title: Agent's Take: What a Baker Mayfield two-year contract extension could look like for Buccaneers quarterback
summary: Tampa Bay reportedly offered Baker Mayfield a two-year extension worth over $100 million, but contract length and guarantee structure stalled negotiations before training camp
full_text:
Baker Mayfield pulled the plug on contract negotiations with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers when a new deal wasn't done by his self-imposed deadline of the start of training camp, which was July 28. Shortly thereafter, information about the contract discussions started to surface.
ESPN's Jeremy Fowler reported at the end of July that the Buccaneers had offered Mayfield a two-year contract extension worth slightly more than $100 million while the quarterback was adamant about a longer commitment. There were structural issues with the offer as the guarantees were considered insufficient.
Mayfield preference for a longer deal was a reasonable demand. It is consistent with the market place. Matthew Stafford , who is 38, is the only quarterback to have ever signed a deal averaging at least $50 million per year with fewer than four new years. The one-year extension Stafford received from the Los Angeles Rams in May is at $55 million per year.
ESPN NFL insider Adam Schefter cited length of contract as a major sticking point for Mayfield during an Aug. 19 appearance on "The Pat McAfee Show." He also said the Buccaneers' offer would have put Mayfield among the NFL's five highest-paid quarterbacks.
Four other quarterbacks besides Stafford have contracts averaging $55 million per year ( Josh Allen , Joe Burrow , Trevor Lawrence and Jordan Love ). Patrick Mahomes and Dak Prescott are the only members of the $60 million-per-year club.
NFL Network insider Mike Garafolo revealed on Aug. 20 to "The Rich Eisen Show" that Mayfield was open to a two-year extension. His camp reportedly countered the Buccaneers with their own two-year proposal before talks broke down.
Mayfield is in the final year of a three-year, $100 million contract, averaging $33,333,333 per year worth up to $115 million with incentives, he signed in March 2024. He is making $40 million in 2026 consisting of a $10 million base salary and a $30 million 10th day of the league year roster bonus. Mayfield's 2026 salary cap number is $39.975 million, which includes $1 million of the $5 million of incentives in 2026 being classified as likely to be earned.
Mayfield's 2026 compensation is being erroneously reported as $27 million in some circles because $13 million of the $30 million roster bonus was prorated on the salary cap during an April 2025 contract restructure. The entire $30 million was paid to Mayfield on June 15.
It would be up to Mayfield's camp to initiate new talks to get something done before Tampa Bay's regular-season opener against the Cincinnati Bengals on Sept. 13 because of his self-imposed deadline. There seemed to be less acrimony in Mayfield's negotiations than with defensive tackle Vita Vea , who requested a trade before signing a one-year, $30 million extension last week.
Former Buccaneers head coach Jon Gruden suggested that could be the case during Monday's appearance on Tampa Bay's 95.7 FM WDAE. "I think they're a lot closer than people realize," Gruden said. "But I expect it to get done, indeed."
Fowler's contract numbers seem plausible because they are in line with the average of Mayfield getting franchise tags in both 2027 and 2028. A $55 million-per-year offer would have to be extremely backloaded with modest guarantees given this dynamic.
Under the NFL collective bargaining agreement's formula for non-exclusive franchise tags, the 2027 quarterback number projects to 14.529% of the 2027 salary cap. That's down from this year's 14.573%.
The 2027 quarterback franchise tag should be $47 million with next year's salary cap being set at just under $323.5 million. The 7.4% growth in the salary cap over the current $301.2 million figure would be consistent with the 7.88% increase from 2025.
A second franchise tag in 2028 at a CBA-mandated 20% increase would be $56.4 million for a two-year total of $103.4 million. The two-year average would be $51.7 million with back-to-back franchise tags.
Structurally, any deal acceptable to Mayfield would likely have to be consistent with other high-priced two-year extensions and two-year contracts. There have been a couple of two-year extensions in 2026 at or near the top of a positional market. Washington Commanders offensive tackle Laremy Tunsil became the NFL's first and only $30 million-per-year offensive lineman in March. The Indianapolis Colts made Jonathan Taylor the league's second-highest-paid running back (now third) at $22 million per year in early August.
Taylor is getting 22.73% of his new money this year in his remaining contract year while Tunsil has 21.59%. The 2027 compensation is fully guaranteed at signing for both players. Tunsil also has 31.48% of his 2028 compensation (his second new contract year) guaranteed for injury that becomes fully guaranteed on the 5th day of the 2027 league year. Taylor doesn't have any guaranteed money in 2028.
The most relevant two-year contract belongs to quarterback Daniel Jones . Jones, who was designated as a transition player by the Colts, signed a two-year, $88 million deal, averaging $44 million per year, in March despite tearing his right Achilles in a Week 14 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars last season. Incentives make the deal worth up to $100 million. There are $60 million in guarantees where $49.49 million is fully guaranteed at signing. Jones is making $50 million, which is 56.81% of the total value, in the first year of his deal.
Another relevant two-year contract was signed by wide receiver Mike Evans in 2024. The Buccaneers gave Evans $41 million over the two years with $35 million in guarantees where $29 million was fully guaranteed at signing. The maximum value of the deal was $52 million thanks to incentives and salary escalators. Evans received 56.1% or $23 million of the $41 million in the first year of his deal.
How the Buccaneers treated Tom Brady , Mayfield's predecessor at quarterback, can't be ignored either. The two-year, $50 million contract Brady signed in 2020 was fully guaranteed. This contract and the one-year extension Brady signed in 2021 contained a no-trade clause and a provision preventing a franchise or transition designation after the expiration of the deals.
In order to prevent Mayfield from playing out his contract, the Buccaneers will need to factor these contractual elements into the equation. The Buccaneers probably have to do something along the following lines at minimum.
Guaranteed for skill, injury & salary cap
Guaranteed for skill, injury & salary cap
Guaranteed for injury; $22.5M guaranteed for skill, injury & salary cap; $22.5M guaranteed for skill & salary cap on fifth day of 2027 league year
Voids on 23rd day prior to start of 2029 league year
Voids on 23rd day prior to start of 2029 league year
Mayfield's $30 million roster bonus isn't being included in the guaranteed money metrics. That's because the $30 million was already paid to Mayfield over two months ago.
The incentives from Mayfield's current contract would carry over into 2026 for the new deal. The same thresholds and dollar amounts as with the incentives would be the salary escalator for 2027 and 2028.
Mayfield has $2.5 million tied to how he performs. He can make $500,000 each for ranking in the NFL's top 10 or NFC's top five in the following categories: passer rating (minimum of 224 pass attempts), touchdown passes, passing yards, completion percentage (minimum of 224 pass attempts) and yards per pass (minimum of 224 pass attempts).
The remaining $2.5 million is tied to Tampa Bay's playoff success and Mayfield's regular-season offensive playtime being at least 75%. Mayfield gets $500,000 for winning a wild card playoff game. It's another $750,000 for winning a divisional playoff game. An NFC Championship game win is worth an additional $500,000. Winning the Super Bowl earns an extra $750,000.
Mayfield's existing fake/dummy 2027 and 2028 contract years are obviously turned into real contract years with the extension. The voiding date of the fake/dummy 2029 contract year moves back two…
author: Joel Corry

title: Renner's 2027 NFL Draft big board: Preseason top 100 as Arch Manning headlines a potentially historic class
summary: If your team needs a blue-chip prospect at a premium position, this could be the draft class for you
full_text:
The hype is real. The 2027 draft class should be in contention with recent classes like 2021 and 2011 for one of the best first rounds of all time.
Unlike the 2026 draft, the elite prospects in this class play the high-value positions you want to target in the top 10. There's a very good chance receiver, edge rusher, offensive tackle and quarterback are the only positions taken in the top 10 next April.
The only question that remains is how deep the draft class will be, with NIL money convincing more and more top prospects to return to school.
While there's no shortage of holes to poke in Arch Manning's 2025 tape, he ends up at No. 1 overall for two big reasons:
Depending on how the 2027 quarterback class shakes out, Jeremiah Smith has a real shot to be the first wide receiver drafted No. 1 overall since Keyshawn Johnson in 1996. You don't need a franchise quarterback to have an effective passing game when you're throwing Smith's way.
Leonard Moore was the best corner in college football as a true sophomore last year and arguably as a true freshman as well. The cons list on his scouting report is minuscule. He could take the year off and still go in the top five .
At the most traits-driven position on the football field, Dylan Stewart is in a physical tier with only a handful of contemporaries over the past decade. It's hard not to get shades of early-career Myles Garrett from the way Stewart knifes into backfields at 6-foot-5, 250 pounds. While he's underdeveloped technically, he can win as an athlete alone.
Trevor Goosby would have been my OT1 had he declared last spring, even with only one full season as a starter under his belt. While he's currently dealing with a bone bruise, if he can show any stretch of play like he did toward the end of 2025, he's a safe bet to go in the top 10 .
Colin Simmons is the most feared speed rusher in the nation. That moniker may not do him complete justice, as he shows some power to his game as well. He racked up 59 pressures and 12 sacks last season.
Jordan Seaton is a graceful offensive tackle who can mirror speed rushers with ease. He allowed only seven total pressures on 314 pass-blocking snaps last season. While he's not a people mover in the run game, he's special on the move.
Ashton Hampton is big, fast and nimble. That's a great combination for a cornerback. He can play man, zone and fill as a tackler. There's not much he can't do on tape.
Drew Mestemaker was the most productive quarterback in college football last season, and it wasn't particularly close. He led the FBS in both yards (4,379) and yards per attempt (9.5). It was no fluke, either.
The 6-foot-4 quarterback has a big arm and a fearless play style from the pocket. His ability to consistently attack downfield was incredibly impressive for his first season as a starter in college or high school.
Cam Coleman's production at Auburn doesn't do justice to his talent level. He's a special mover for a 6-foot-3 receiver. While he could stand to get more consistent in his route running, his floor is very much a first-rounder.
Dante Moore was a likely first-rounder last spring before deciding to return to Oregon. He pairs an effortless release with efficient footwork in the pocket to carve up opponents. Improving his work under pressure is what will get him into the No. 1 overall pick conversation.
Charlie Becker wasn't just a feel-good story down the stretch for the Hoosiers; he's an absurdly talented prospect in his own right. His instant acceleration for a 6-foot-4 receiver, along with hands that didn't drop a pass all last season, is the kind of combination that's hard to stop downfield.
Because defensive tackle is such a strength-based position, it's rare to see freshmen and sophomores dominate there in college. That's why it's easy to be high on David Stone given what he put on tape last fall. He can win with quickness, hands or pure strength -- a tremendous trio for a prospect.
A'Mauri Washington is still more of a freak athlete than a polished defensive tackle, but the 330-plus-pounders who move like him tend to figure it out. There's little you can do as an offensive lineman in the run game when Washington gets a good jump off the snap.
Will Echoles may not have the prototypical traits of the two defensive tackles in front of him on this list, but it doesn't matter when you flip on the tape. Echoles just gets into the backfield and makes plays.
Kade Pieper is one of the most athletic offensive linemen I've ever scouted . He'll be a center in the NFL , but even at guard last year for Iowa, he more than held his own. His grip strength combined with his natural athleticism make him an elite blocker on the move.
Greg Johnson is a prototypical guard with the size and strength to play in the NFL tomorrow. With nearly 2,000 career snaps to his name, he eschewed the NFL last spring to return to Minnesota. If the career progression we've already seen in nearly three years as a starter continues, he'll be a first-rounder.
This far out from the draft, I'm not factoring injuries or off-field issues into my board, but it's worth noting that Ahmad Hardy's future is currently up in the air after being shot at a concert in the offseason . He'll miss Missouri's opener, but the Tigers are hopeful he'll return at some point this season. They need him because he's the most difficult back to tackle in the country .
Sammy Brown is about as clean a prospect as you can be after only two years in college. He was a freshman All-American in 2024 and an academic All-American last year. The rising junior ticks every box you could want to see from a physical and leadership perspective at the position.
Jadan Baugh is a size-speed demon for the Gators. You don't want to be the defensive back tasked with bringing him down with a full head of steam. To top it off, he has exceptional ball skills to be featured in the passing game as well.
Justin Scott came on strong for Miami last season and was a big factor in its run to the title game. Eighteen of his 21 pressures last season came in the second half of Miami's season. He's a penetrator who knows how to create disruption.
After transferring from Purdue, Will Heldt ended up as the most productive Clemson defensive lineman last season. He's a large and bendy defensive end who's only scratching the surface of what he could become.
Kelley Jones is the best pure press corner in the draft class. He ends reps before they start at the line of scrimmage. While he doesn't have a well-rounded skill set, that ability will be highly coveted by certain schemes.
Brauntae Johnson isn't near the prospect that Caleb Downs was, but he has much more of a prototypical frame for the NFL. With a long wingspan and easy playmaking ability, he could easily be the next first-round safety .
Kewan Lacy is a bit smaller than Ahmad Hardy or Jadan Baugh, but that doesn't mean he runs any weaker than those two. He basically never came off the field for Ole Miss last season and finished with the most carries among Power 5 running backs.
Jordan Faison was a Notre Dame lacrosse recruit who walked onto the football team as a freshman, and they haven't been able to keep him off the field since. Despite a smaller frame for the position, he's tough as nails with some of the best ability to get open in the class.
Jamari Johnson is much more of a true inline tight end than former teammate Kenyon Sadiq and could ultimately be coveted in a similar range because of that. His smooth route-running ability combined with his long frame will make him a consistent red-zone weapon at the next level.
Nick Marsh is a throwback receiver who no corner wants to contend with after the catch. His play strength is his calling card, with a unique ability to play through contact. Here's hoping his downfield production takes a jump after transferring from Michigan State to Indiana.
Lance Heard is one of the nastiest offensive linemen in the country. He has some run blocks where defenders…

title: Reasons why the Cardinals released Trey Benson
summary: The Arizona Cardinals are going into the 2026 season with arguably the best running back room in the league. The offense will improve this year with several new pieces in place. The Cardinals went into training camp with a packed and talented running back room. RELATED: CARDINALS SIGN BENSON TO ROOKIE CONTRACT Having selected Jeremiyah […]
full_text: The Arizona Cardinals are going into the 2026 season with arguably the best running back room in the league. The offense will improve this year with several new pieces in place. The Cardinals went into training camp with a packed and talented running back room. RELATED: CARDINALS SIGN BENSON TO ROOKIE CONTRACT Having selected Jeremiyah Love with the third overall pick in this year’s NFL draft added to the talent of the group. Cardinals GM Monti Ossenfort had already signed Tyler Allgeier from the Atlanta Falcons during the free agency period. Bam Knight and Corey Kiner were also re-signed from last year’s roster. However, there were two big question marks: Veterans James Conner and Trey Benson. Both were injured and placed on IR last year. What was their status? Training camp was expected to answer those concerns. At the beginning of last year, both were the starting running backs. And now? On Monday, the questions regarding Benson were answered. The Cardinals released him with a waiver/injury designation. He came to Arizona as a third-round draft pick in the 2024 NFL Draft after two seasons at Florida State when he rushed for 990 and 906 yards in his final two seasons. He also scored 23 touchdowns during this time span, so he knew where the end zone was. Teams don’t usually release third-round draft picks after just two seasons. What were the reasons why the coaching staff gave up on him? Lack of trade market Benson had a great opportunity when Conner went down to injury in Week 3 last year. Unfortunately, Benson suffered a significant meniscus injury the following week and was also placed on IR after surgery. But the recovery has lingered into training camp this year. The #Cardinals have waived RB Trey Benson, who was their 3rd-round pick in 2024. pic.twitter.com/TcEJMmj2qk — Ari Meirov (@MySportsUpdate) August 24, 2026 Benson certainly had trade value – if he was healthy. Certainly, the club wasn’t going to keep all eight running backs on the roster, and he was a third-round pick. During training camp, Benson had a flare-up with his left knee that kept him out of practices. He did not play in any preseason games and wasn’t practicing. The team had an option to place him on IR once again, which would have ended his season. This would have allowed Benson to get completely healthy and come back next year. They could also have kept him on the 53-man roster and then, the following day, placed him on IR, which would have allowed the Cardinals to bring him back at some point during this season. By being sidelined, this eliminated any trade interest. Nobody wants a vehicle that has a blown engine. Too many health issues The injury last year wasn’t pretty. It came at a horrible time in Benson’s athletic career. When Conner went down, it was Benson’s chance to become the starting back for an NFL club, and he went down in the very next game. His practice window opened up, but the coaching staff never reinstated him. Yeah his lower body may just be mush at this point pic.twitter.com/1XWrmsYTjS — tjm (@TMundy_15) August 24, 2026 His meniscus injury has caused issues, which have kept Benson out of practices and games. In his rookie year, he had an ankle injury that caused him to miss the final two games. He was placed on IR because of his injury. As a rookie, Benson finished the season with 291 yards and a touchdown on 63 carries and 59 yards on six catches, so he didn’t tear up the league or get named to the NFL All-Rookie Team. In college, he missed the entire 2020 season with a torn ACL. Benson is a talented back – that is a known commodity. However, all of this points to him being injury-prone, and in all likelihood, that would continue. No club wants to pay a guy to sit on IR, especially repeatedly. Other backs shoved Benson out the door Most NFL teams keep either three or four backs. The Cardinals have eight in camp. That means whoever isn’t named Love and Allgeier must have a great camp and preseason to be retained. Conner has been given the first option to stay. Even though the coaching staff is new and hasn’t gotten comfortable with him, they all know his athletic background. He is a bruising back, so his goal-line presence is a huge plus. He is a nine-year veteran who has rushed for over 6,000 yards with 72 touchdowns scored. And other running backs have shown promise. In the three preseason games, Bam Knight had 12 carries for 58 yards (Panthers), led the team in rushing, 3 carries for 15 yards (Raiders), and no stats against Dallas. He also did not have any kickoff returns, which has been one of his duties in the past. Corey Kiner had 10 carries for 29 yards and a touchdown against the Cowboys; he led all rushers against the Raiders with 10 carries for 59 yards and had 14 carries for 57 yards and one TD in the Hall of Fame Game. Even Evan Hull has shown the coaches something and led all rushers with 11 carries for 51 yards against Dallas. Conner has not carried the ball yet in the preseason. Most likely, the coaches do not want him to become re-injured and will wait until the regular-season games begin. That is, if he remains on the roster. One – or two – of these players have played sound, practiced well, and have shown more promise than a guy who is more likely to end up on IR rather than get 1,000-yards in a season. Running back Trey Benson cleared waivers today and he now reverts back to the Arizona Cardinals injured reserve list. pic.twitter.com/UMwfcKUzKL — Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) August 25, 2026 Benson cleared waivers and reverted to the Cardinals. The decision now is to keep him, place Benson on IR and rehab him in the building, or settle with him and outright release him. If that occurs, he will be on his own to get his body right. That decision matters more to him than the diagnosis does. Most likely, he will head to injured reserve or receive an injury/settlement designation.

title: What to know about Falcons – Dolphins in the preseason finale
summary: The final game of the 2026 preseason kicks off tomorrow night, and when it’s over, all that lies ahead is the first season of Falcons football for Kevin Stefanski, Ian Cunningham, and the host of new players they’ve brought in. We’re nearly there, but there’s this one tune-up to clear first. Here’s what you need […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - OCTOBER 26: Zach Sieler #92 and Jordyn Brooks #20 of the Miami Dolphins tackle Bijan Robinson #7 of the Atlanta Falcons during the second quarter in the game at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on October 26, 2025 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images) | Getty Images The final game of the 2026 preseason kicks off tomorrow night, and when it’s over, all that lies ahead is the first season of Falcons football for Kevin Stefanski, Ian Cunningham, and the host of new players they’ve brought in. We’re nearly there, but there’s this one tune-up to clear first. Here’s what you need to know about tomorrow night. Roster battles to monitor QB3 I firmly believe the team is either going to find a way to keep both players or hold on to Strand, who has looked too good for an assured spot on the Falcons practice squad given how quarterback-starved teams across the league are. Maybe that goes out the window if Strand craters this week. RB3 It’s Tyler Goodson’s job. He was the best back on the field in Week 2 of preseason and has considerable special teams value, so this one is wrapped up. WR5/6 Chris Blair and Dylan Drummond were mentioned as two receivers having very good summers by offensive coordinator Tommy Rees, and they both can play special teams and have experience. Vinny Anthony will have one final shot to make his case for a roster spot instead of a practice squad slot, but we’re not yet sure whether the Falcons will keep five or six receivers to begin with. C2 Maybe James Brockermeyer gets sniped off the practice squad because he was well-regarded coming out of college, but he hasn’t been impressive enough this summer for that to seem incredibly likely. Corey Levin has played guard and center and knows Bill Callahan, so as I keep repeating, the job seems to be his. ILB2 I think it’s Kendal Daniels. Christian Harris only made it into the game very late, working behind JD Bertrand, and may not even be a lock for this roster. Daniels, meanwhile, has been wearing the green dot and looking impressive in preseason action and practices, and figures to be lined up next to Divine Deablo in Week 1. CB2/3 Avieon Terrell is back practicing, but he probably has too much ground to make up ahead of Week 1. With Billy Bowman Jr. still out, Mike Hughes is your starter opposite A.J. Terrell and Darnay Holmes should start in the nickel at the beginning of the season. I expect Avieon Terrell to be a starter by the end of the year, though. What’s new with the Dolphins? Almost everything, and almost everything points toward them being one of the very worst teams in the NFL. They have a new general manager in Jon-Eric Sullivan and head coach in Jeff Hafley, with both men hopping over from Green Bay. They traded away franchise cornerstone Jaylen Waddle to the Broncos and Minkah Fitzpatrick to the Jets, replaced Tua Tagovailoa with Malik Willis, and pulled the Falcons 2021 memorial free agency period out of their hat, signing about 15 guys to one-year deals with none of them exceeding $1.5 million. With a deep draft class, they snagged tackle Kadyn Proctor out of Alabama and cornerback Chris Johnson out of San Diego State in the first round and grabbed linebackers Jacob Rodriguez and Kyle Louis (two Falcoholic draft favorites) and highly-regarded receivers Caleb Douglas and Chris Bell. The foundation for the next quality Dolphins team is partially poured, but right now I would not put more than a few folding chairs on it, much less a house. Miami has a long road back to relevance, one that will start with picks like Proctor, Johnson, Bell, and Rodriguez hitting. What to know about Friday We’ll get a brief look at the starters, including Tua Tagovailoa (who is QB1 for now and still, I think, likely for Week 1) and then the backup brigade in their final opportunity to compete for roles and roster spots. We’ll likely see Cooper Rush for about a quarter and Jack Strand for the rest of the game, if you’re closely monitoring the QB3 battle. After they rocked the Colts reserves a week ago, I’ll be looking to see how the Falcons starters and reserves fare against a Miami team that has a legitimate argument right out of the gate as the league’s team. We’re not going to overcorrect and start panicking if they scuffle a bit, but I would not view it as a tremendous sign if two teams at their most vanilla look fairly even when one of those teams has a roster as decimated as the Dolphins do. Following the game, the Falcons will be making cuts over the next couple of days to get compliant with the Sunday evening deadline for a 53 man roster, and then will populate their practice squad. A lot is going to happen in the next few days, so hopefully you’re locked and loaded in terms of sleep and caffeine. Let us know what you’ll be looking for tomorrow!
author: Dave Choate

title: Falcons training camp 2026: A quick, intense practice on the last day of camp
summary: Today was a short, but intense, practice for the Falcons as they look toward this weekend’s last preseason matchup against the Dolphins. It was Michael Penix Jr.’s third full practice since being medically cleared last week, and he told the media he feels great, and that he’s getting more comfortable and confident each day. But […]
full_text: Jul 29, 2026; Atlanta, Falcons, USA; Atlanta Falcons head coach Kevin Stefanski on the field during the first day of training camp at IBM Performance Field. Mandatory Credit: Dale Zanine-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Today was a short, but intense, practice for the Falcons as they look toward this weekend’s last preseason matchup against the Dolphins. It was Michael Penix Jr.’s third full practice since being medically cleared last week, and he told the media he feels great, and that he’s getting more comfortable and confident each day. But Kevin Stefanski confirmed that Penix will not play in the preseason finale in Miami, and Penix said after practice that his three full practices this week weren’t enough to prepare him for full-speed play (or as close as we get to that in the preseason) this week. Stefanski also said that while this may technically be the last day of training camp, he treats everything up to Week 1 prep as training camp. So hopefully we’ll still get to watch some full practices. I did forget to hit record when both Stefanski and secondary coach Justin Hood were at the podium, but I did get a lot of what they talked about posted in real time. All of my notes from today’s practice are here: Here’s everything you need to know from Wednesday’s practice: Jake Matthews and Jawaan Taylor did not practice on Wednesday, and Stefanski confirmed after practice that it was just a veteran rest day for the two tackles. Da’Shawn Hand was working one-on-one with the athletic performance staff to start practice. Has a huge brace on his knee, but was moving well. The Falcons were running scouted looks against both first-team units, and today was the first time they used specific play cards with the team so everyone can be acclimated to that by the regular season. The first pass I saw Penix throw today was a beauty to Kyle Pitts in the flat. My very favorite play of the day was a little trickeration: Tua was running red zone drills with the 1s, and Bijan was in shotgun. Tua faked the handoff to Bijan, who sold it well even though it was just practice (this was something I noticed on every faked handoff today), and Tua tossed a short lob to Drake London. But wait, there’s more! London pitched it backward to Bijan, who would have likely had a TD in a real-game scenario. Give me this level of fun in-season please. Regardless who was quarterbacking each drill, we saw a decent amount of snaps from the pistol and shotgun and honestly, they didn’t feel terribly predictable. Tomorrow the Falcons will have a walk through, and then they’ll travel to Miami for Friday’s game. Nate Ollie highlights: This was my first time hearing from DL coach Nate Ollie, and I just love his energy. That energy is obvious out on the field, too. He’s super involved with his players and is very vocal about coaching them up. On Za’Darius Smith: “What he’s bringing to the group is infectious. Everybody’s buzzing when he’s around. Even when we were out there at the game (in Indianapolis), he got his iPad. He’s coaching guys up. He’s out there like, man, if you hit this move, you would have got that.” Ollie said that veteran presence is huge for the younger players. On whether or not his unit is where he wants it to be entering Week 1 of the regular season: “There’s always room to improve, we work to improve every single day, but I love the energy these guys are bringing every single day, man. That’s what we’ve gotta have — energy, gotta have juice, especially on the defensive line. Michael Penix Jr. highlights: Penix says he’s feeling good after three days of full practice and he’s excited to be back out there. “I wanted to get back in the rhythm of things. Obviously, whenever you put a d-lineman out there, things start moving a little bit faster. So I’m just getting the speed of the game back down and that aspect.” Penix said it hasn’t been hard to ramp up to full participation in practice. “It’s just more reps,” he said. “It ain’t hard, though, but that’s just what it comes with … it’s exciting for me because now I get more than 8 reps a day.” Penix also said he did take a minor hit when Chris Lindstrom got pushed back into him on Monday. “Obviously, they preach not to let the quarterbacks get hit, but it’s football. You know that those things happen. Accidents happen, but it’s good. I feel good.” On whether or not he feels like he could start Week 1: “Yeah, I feel great. Right now, I’m cleared to do 11 on 11 for practice, but each and every day I’m getting better, getting more confident. I’m not playing this week (against Miami) because obviously I only have three practices under my belt doing the 11 on 11 stuff, but I’ve been feeling really good. Za’Darius Smith highlights: We’d heard through the grapevine that Smith didn’t like talking to the media. We expected a short, gruff presser with minimal answers. It’s a great reminder to not believe everything you hear about others, and don’t assume that if a person behaved a certain way a few years ago, it doesn’t mean they haven’t matured and grown into a person who would react differently today. Za’Darius Smith gave the most open, vulnerable press conference I’ve ever sat through. He retired because he got word that his mother was terminally ill, and he retired because it was the only way to be there for her. Then his grandmother and father also passed away not too long after. His story, and his thoughts on this defense and what it means to him to be an Atlanta Falcon deserve their own post, so I’m going to hold a lot of his quotes and probably will focus on him in Friday’s Opening Drive.
author: Jeanna Kelley

title: Michael Penix Jr. will not play in Falcons’ final preseason game vs. Dolphins
summary: Atlanta Falcons head coach Kevin Stefanski officially announced that former first-round pick Michael Penix Jr. will not be playing in the Falcons’ preseason finale against the Miami Dolphins, according to The Falcoholic’s Jeanna Kelley. Penix was fully cleared last weekend to play in 11-on-11 and team drills, with the hope that he would be able […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GA - AUGUST 14: Atlanta quarterback Michael Penix Jr. (9) warms up prior to the start of the NFL pre-season game between the Denver Broncos and the Atlanta Falcons on August 14th, 2026 at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, GA. (Photo by Rich von Biberstein/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Atlanta Falcons head coach Kevin Stefanski officially announced that former first-round pick Michael Penix Jr. will not be playing in the Falcons’ preseason finale against the Miami Dolphins , according to The Falcoholic’s Jeanna Kelley. Penix was fully cleared last weekend to play in 11-on-11 and team drills, with the hope that he would be able to compete for the starter role in Week 1 alongside fellow quarterback Tua Tagovailoa. With this news, Tagovailoa will likely start on Friday against the Dolphins in Miami. What Does This Mean for Penix? It could mean a couple of things. On the one hand, Penix has not been idle as he recovered; he has been with the team, participating in 7-on-7 periods while continuing to work back from the ACL injury he suffered in mid-November of last year. So, there is the possibility that Stefanski is holding on to his potential franchise quarterback until he is needed in week one against the Pittsburgh Steelers. However, Stefanski has gone on record, stating that he is still not comfortable with Penix potentially taking hits to that knee so soon after being cleared, paving the way for Tagovailoa to start the season under center, despite reports of not doing enough this offseason to lock down the position. Stefanski said Penix just started doing 11s two days ago and he felt like it was too early to put him into a game. #Falcons — Marc Raimondi (@marcraimondi) August 26, 2026 Penix said he does feel comfortable and confident moving around on that repaired knee, and he said he does feel like he could be ready to play Week 1. Stefanski told the media after practice that Tua Tagovailoa will start against his former team this week, Cooper Rush will play next and Jack Strand will close out the game. The Falcons have found themselves in a rough spot at the quarterback position to start the year; it’s no wonder it’s one of the more polarizing stories surrounding the NFL lexicon right now.
author: Saivion Mixson

title: Ravens rookie film review: TE Josh Cuevas flashes versatility
summary: Baltimore’s second preseason game didn’t produce much offense on the scoreboard, but it gave us a better look at several young players who had smaller roles during the opener. Against Minnesota, Josh Cuevas showed why his athleticism and versatility make him an intriguing developmental tight end, offensive tackle Diego Pounds continued to strengthen his case […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MN - AUGUST 22: Baltimore Ravens tight end Josh Cuevas (85) warms up before the NFL preseason game between the Baltimore Ravens and the Minnesota Vikings on August 22nd, 2026, at U.S. Bank in Minneapolis, MN. (Photo by Bailey Hillesheim/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Baltimore’s second preseason game didn’t produce much offense on the scoreboard, but it gave us a better look at several young players who had smaller roles during the opener. Against Minnesota, Josh Cuevas showed why his athleticism and versatility make him an intriguing developmental tight end, offensive tackle Diego Pounds continued to strengthen his case for a roster spot with an impressive performance in the run game, and seventh-round guard Evan Beernsten finally received his first extended opportunity of the preseason. TE Josh Cuevas (Round 5, No. 173 overall) 36 snaps | 21 receiving | 13 run blocking | 2 pass blocking Cuevas’ 36 snaps against Minnesota gave Baltimore an opportunity to use him in several different roles. That allowed the fifth-round pick to show the athleticism and versatility that made him an intriguing addition to the tight end room. The most noticeable part of his performance was what he offered as a receiver. Cuevas flashed his straight-line speed on an underneath drag route, turning a short completion into a 23-yard gain once he got into space. That ability to create yards after the catch is an important part of his evaluation. Baltimore can manufacture opportunities for him underneath and allow his athleticism to take over once the ball is in his hands. Cuevas also showed good awareness against zone coverage, understanding when to settle into open space rather than continuing to run himself into coverage. He also showed the ability to elevate and attack the football vertically, while making a difficult contested catch in traffic. Josh Cuevas lead the Ravens receivers with 46 yards on 3 catches Did a nice job finding soft spots in zone, flashed athletically climbing the ladder for a ball and moving in space. Also noticed his effort as a blocker. pic.twitter.com/V0pZgJS3AB — Yuri (@Yuri_Ravens) August 26, 2026 His effort as a blocker was another encouraging part of the performance. Cuevas isn’t going to consistently overwhelm defenders with raw power, but the willingness is there. He competed through contact and continued working to stay attached to defenders. That matters for a player whose athleticism naturally makes him more appealing as a receiving tight end. The more functional he becomes as a blocker, the less predictable Baltimore becomes when he is on the field. Postgame takeaway: Cuevas’ Week 2 performance provided a good look at his receiving profile. He found openings against zone coverage, picked up yards after the catch, and competed at the catch point. The effort he showed as a blocker was equally important. Cuevas doesn’t need to become a dominant in-line blocker, but becoming reliable enough in that area would give Baltimore considerably more freedom in how it deploys him. OT Diego Pounds (undrafted free agent) 20 snaps | 10 pass blocking | 0 pressures allowed | 92.9 PFF run-blocking grade | 95.7 zone-blocking grade Pounds’ pass protection stood out during Baltimore’s preseason opener, but against Minnesota, it was his work in the run game that became the most impressive part of his performance. Pounds looked particularly natural working within Baltimore’s zone concepts. He showed the ability to run the train tracks, stay square while moving laterally and reach his landmarks without sacrificing control. His movement skills allowed him to get into position before contact, and once engaged, he showed enough power to displace defenders and create movement out of his gap. Diego pounds performed well for a second week in a row He allowed no pressure on 10 pass blocking snaps Last week his pass blocking stood out, but to me this week his run blocking was seriously good. Looks like such a natural athlete in space and being able to work… pic.twitter.com/zOvwAMleHr — Yuri (@Yuri_Ravens) August 26, 2026 The effort after initial contact continued to stand out as well. On one rep, Pounds stayed attached to his defender and drove him roughly 15 yards downfield. Plays like that don’t necessarily tell us much about his technical development, but they do show the temperament Baltimore wants from its offensive linemen. Pounds consistently looks to finish rather than simply completing his assignment and moving on. The grading reflected how effective he was. Pounds received a 92.9 PFF run-blocking grade, including a 95.7 grade on zone runs. More importantly, the film supported why those numbers were so high. His movement skills and comfort blocking in space make him a natural fit for what Baltimore is asking its offensive line to do. Postgame takeaway: Pounds continues to strengthen his case for a spot on Baltimore’s 53-man roster. Allowing zero pressures was another positive step in pass protection, but his comfort operating in space in the run game was the story of Week 2. Given the Ravens’ lack of established offensive tackle depth, Pounds is putting together the type of preseason that could make him difficult to leave off the roster. G Evan Beernsten (Round 7, No. 253 overall) 8 snaps | 77.6 offensive grade, third-highest on team After not getting much of an opportunity during the preseason opener, Baltimore finally gave Beernsten his first real look against Minnesota. Eight snaps obviously isn’t enough to make any definitive conclusions, but there were still a few traits that immediately translated from his college tape. The first was his hand quickness. Beernsten fired his hands immediately after the snap and consistently looked to initiate contact rather than waiting for defenders to attack him. His punch timing was solid, and he showed an understanding of how to establish his hands early in the rep. That initial contact is important for Beernsten because he isn’t going to win consistently through overwhelming length or raw physical tools. His game has to be built around technique, timing and positioning. Rookie Guard Evan Beernsten finally got his feet wet vs the Vikings Impressed by his hand usage, one thing I noted on his report was his quick and active hands. Did a nice job timing his punches. Only 8 snaps so not much to go off of, hope he gets more burn this week pic.twitter.com/1eDwcVieQQ — Yuri (@Yuri_Ravens) August 26, 2026 We saw some of that against Minnesota. Beernsten was quick out of his stance, established contact early and generally looked comfortable during his limited workload. He ultimately finished with Baltimore’s third-highest offensive PFF grade, an encouraging result considering these were his first meaningful preseason snaps. The difficult part of his evaluation is opportunity. Baltimore has already given several other young offensive linemen significantly larger workloads this preseason, leaving Beernsten with very little time to separate himself before roster decisions are made. Eight snaps can give the coaching staff something to build on, but it isn’t enough on its own to dramatically change the roster picture. Postgame takeaway: Beernsten made the most of a very limited opportunity. His quick hands, punch timing and urgency off the snap were all encouraging, and finishing with Baltimore’s third-highest offensive PFF grade gave him a positive starting point. His biggest problem isn’t necessarily his performance—it’s the lack of remaining opportunities. Unless Beernsten produces an exceptional final preseason game, his path to the 53-man roster remains difficult. At this point, he may be playing more to establish himself as a developmental player Baltimore wants to keep around than to outright win a roster spot. Final Thoughts Baltimore’s offense didn’t generate many points against Minnesota, but Week 2 still provided useful information about several rookies fighting to…

summary: The Baltimore Ravens’ final 2026 preseason game against the Washington Commanders is set to kick off at 6 p.m. ET on Friday. 53-man roster cuts will take place just two days later, making the contest a key battleground for several backend roster spots, not to mention the starting center competition. So, today, Baltimore Beatdown wants […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MD - AUGUST 15: Cole Payton #10 of the Philadelphia Eagles carries the ball against Adisa Isaac #50 of the Baltimore Ravens during the second half of the preseason game at M&T Bank Stadium on August 15, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens’ final 2026 preseason game against the Washington Commanders is set to kick off at 6 p.m. ET on Friday. 53-man roster cuts will take place just two days later, making the contest a key battleground for several backend roster spots, not to mention the starting center competition. So, today, Baltimore Beatdown wants to know: which Raven has the most on the line heading into Friday night’s matchup against the Commanders? Nikhil’s take: There are a few options that come to mind here. 2025 fifth-round pick Carson Vinson is being pushed by undrafted rookie Diego Pounds for the swing tackle job. Fourth-year running back Rasheen Ali has to prove he is worth of a roster spot. And the math in the defensive line room indicates that at least a few players are competing for a job. But third-year outside linebacker Adisa Isaac, a former third-round pick who has barely played in the last two years due to injury, may already be on the outside looking in. He was sidelined for a stretch this offseason and has rarely flashed in training camp, especially compared to Ethan Burke. The undrafted rookie out of Texas has received positive reviews from coaches, consistently makes plays in practice, and had a mini-breakout in the Ravens’ win over the Vikings on Saturday. A new coaching regime may not be as attached to a Day 2 pick from two years ago, so Isaac may still need to solidify his spot on Friday night. Now, it’s your turn! title: Ravens news: OC Declan Doyle will call plays from coaches’ booth
summary: Welcome back to Loose Feathers, a regular round-up of the latest news and analysis about the Baltimore Ravens. In today’s edition, we cover a key decision from offensive coordinator Declan Doyle, the end of the Pro Bowl game, and a way-too-early 2027 mock draft pick. Let’s dive in! Declan Doyle will call Ravens’ offensive plays […]
full_text: Baltimore Ravens offensive coordinator Declan Doyle during a news conference on Wednesday, Feb. 18, 2026, in Owings Mills, Maryland. (Brian Krista/Baltimore Sun/Tribune News Service via Getty Images) Welcome back to Loose Feathers, a regular round-up of the latest news and analysis about the Baltimore Ravens. In today’s edition, we cover a key decision from offensive coordinator Declan Doyle, the end of the Pro Bowl game, and a way-too-early 2027 mock draft pick. Let’s dive in! Declan Doyle will call Ravens’ offensive plays from coaching booth Ravens offensive coordinator Declan Doyle’s biggest preseason decision is his starting center. He has yet to pick between his options, but he was more decisive about another key choice: his game day play-callingn operation. Doyle felt good about how he called plays from the coaches’ booth in the first preseason game and initially planned to go down to the field for the second game in Minnesota. But, recognizing that he only had two more dress rehearsals for the regular season, Doyle went with his gut and settled on the booth for the season. Declan Doyle August 25 press conference I am going to go up in the booth. So, I had the Philly experience up there; it felt like it was really clean and it went really well. What I was kind of looking for was the communication between myself and the coaching staff, the communication with the quarterback, especially…I have a direct line to [Lamar Jackson] and then also, I really have a lot of faith in [quarterbacks coach Israel Woolfork] down on the field. What I found was it was really pretty simple to be able to communicate to him, to the quarterback, what the quarterback was feeling back to me. I thought our staff did a great job down on the field. … …So, I am going to go back up there in game three, and we will roll from there. But it is something that I talked to other coaches around the league about, other play callers. I talked to [Buffalo Bills head coach] Joe Brady specifically, I talked to some other guys, and the advice that they gave basically was, ‘Go where you feel comfortable being able to communicate to the staff [and] being able to solve problems in a clean and efficient manner.’ The Pro Bowl (game) is dead. NFL Will No Longer Hold Pro Bowl – Sam Robinson (Pro Football Rumors) On life support earlier this decade, the Pro Bowl changed to a flag-football game with accompanying skills challenges. After tepid interest, the NFL is doing away with the event altogether. The league will not hold a Pro Bowl moving forward, The Athletic’s Jonathan Jones reports . Players will still receive acknowledgements as Pro Bowlers, though Jones indicates alternates for the game — a pervasive league honors component that has increasingly minimized the achievement — will no longer be recognized. That will provide some clarity, as recent years — due in large part to player enthusiasm for the event dwindling — have brought a wave of questionable Pro Bowl accolades. Way-too-early Ravens mock draft pick 2027 NFL mock draft: Reid’s preseason first-round predictions – Jordan Reid (ESPN) 30. Baltimore Ravens Ahmad Moten Sr., DT, Miami Back-to-back Miami defensive linemen! Moten is one of my favorite players in this draft and would fit in seamlessly in new Ravens coach Jesse Minter’s defense. Moten is already first-round-worthy as an interior pass rusher, as his first-step quickness and penetration abilities are top-notch. He’ll have to take a major step as a run defender to cement a place in Round 1, as he sometimes gets dislodged from his gaps. But with Calais Campbell turning 40 next week and Nnamdi Madubuike’s long-term status up in the air, Moten would be a good fit.
author: Nikhil Mehta

title: Ex-Michigan LB Michael Barrett joins Ravens, reunites with Jesse Minter
summary: The Baltimore Ravens signed linebacker Michael Barrett on Wednesday, reuniting him with Jesse Minter, his defensive coordinator for two years at Michigan. The Ravens badly needed linebacker depth with Jamon Johnson, Carl Jones Jr., and Reid Williford all dealing with injuries. Jones and Williford have been absent for more than a week, while Johnson left […]
full_text: UNIVERSITY PARK, PA - NOVEMBER 11: Michigan linebacker Michael Barrett (23) celebrates after a stop during the Michigan Wolverines versus Penn State Nittany Lions game on November 11, 2023 at Beaver Stadium in University Park, PA. (Photo by Randy Litzinger/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens signed linebacker Michael Barrett on Wednesday, reuniting him with Jesse Minter, his defensive coordinator for two years at Michigan. The Ravens badly needed linebacker depth with Jamon Johnson, Carl Jones Jr., and Reid Williford all dealing with injuries. Jones and Williford have been absent for more than a week, while Johnson left Saturday’s preseason win over the Vikings. That forced second-year UDFA Jay Higgins and undrafted rookie Dominic DeLuca to play nearly the entire game. Barrett, who has a baseline familiarity with Minter’s scheme after running it at Michigan, should be able to step in and take preseason snaps on Friday against the Commanders. Barrett, 26, was the Wolverines’ starting linebacker during both of Minter’s seasons in Ann Arbor. His 137 tackles trailed only Junior Colson – who Minter later coached with the Chargers – during that time and he added in a mix of splash plays: 8.5 tackles for loss, 6.5 sacks, two interceptions, three passes defended, three forced fumbles, and two recoveries. Barrett’s contributions to Michigan’s championship-winning defense in helped get him drafted in the seventh round of the 2024 draft by the Panthers. Carolina traded him to the Seahawks for veteran cornerback Mike Jackson, only for Seattle to waived him during final roster cuts, re-sign him to the practice squad, and release him shortly after Week 1. Barrett spent time on the Browns’ and Packers’ practice squads in 2025 and signed with the Raiders for the 2025 offseason. After being waived, he moved to the UFL, first joining the Birmingham Stallions but ultimately appearing in seven games for the St. Louis Battlehawks during the 2026 season. To make room on the roster, the Ravens placed center Danny Pinter on injured reserve following his season-ending knee injury suffered during joint practices in Minnesota. Later in the day, Willford, an undrafted rookie, was waived with an injury designation, leaving one spot open on Baltimore’s roster.
author: Nikhil Mehta

title: Ravens wideouts battle physical Commanders secondary at joint practice
summary: At the beginning of the Ravens’ joint practice with the Commanders, it seemed like Baltimore’s offense would be in for a long afternoon. The Commanders’ cornerbacks consistently stymied the Ravens’ wideouts in 1-on-1 reps from the five-yard line with rookies Ja’Kobi Lane and Elijah Sarratt both failing to score a touchdown. Lane in particular struggled […]
full_text: OWINGS MILLS, MD - AUGUST 26: Ja'kobi Lane #6 of the Baltimore Ravens makes a catch during the Washington Commanders and Baltimore Ravens joint practice at Under Armour Performance Center Baltimore Ravens on August 26, 2026 in Owings Mills, Maryland. (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images At the beginning of the Ravens’ joint practice with the Commanders, it seemed like Baltimore’s offense would be in for a long afternoon. The Commanders’ cornerbacks consistently stymied the Ravens’ wideouts in 1-on-1 reps from the five-yard line with rookies Ja’Kobi Lane and Elijah Sarratt both failing to score a touchdown. Lane in particular struggled with physical press coverage at the line of scrimmage and lacked precise footwork in his release. Rashod Bateman was the only member of his unit to score multiple touchdowns in the period – he found the end zone three times via clean route-running wins. Next came 7-on-7 work from the 10-yard line. Lamar Jackson overshot an open Justice Hill on a wheel route on the first play, but he completed his remaining five passes with touchdowns to: Tight end Mark Andrews, who caught the ball short of the goal line on the next play but adjusted for a score on a similar concept a few plays later. Bateman, who ran an easy 7-yard in route and walked in untouched. Lane, who extended out for a catch in a tight window. Tight end Josh Cuevas, who adjusted to a ball throw slightly behind him and made a sliding catch. In 11-on-11 work, Ravens offense struggled to find the end zone during both red zone periods. In the first, the run game was solid; Derrick Henry had plenty of open holes and the Commanders defense wanted nothing to do with him. Jackson took multiple passes into the flat but did find Justice Hill across the middle for a touchdown. In the second period, the offensive line allowed pressure on three straight plays, with Jackson spinning into a scramble on one and finding a checkdown the other two times. On his last play of the afternoon, the two-time MVP threw an uncharacteristically bad interception, lofting up an easy ball for Commanders cornerback Mike Sainristil. Jackson was trying to put it behind the defense for LaJohntay Wester, but he may have been a little trigger-happy. He had more time to make a better throw – or decision, as Bateman was open on the right side of the field. Between the red zone sessions was full-field 11-on-11 work. Bateman, who was serving as Baltimore’s de facto WR1 with Zay Flowers sidelined, heated back up in this period, finding soft spots in zone coverage and racking up yards after the catch on a few screens. Devontez Walker had the longest play of the day, catching a 20-yard crosser, turning the corner, and outrunning the Washington secondary for a 60-yard touchdown. After practice, head coach Jesse Minter confirmed that the absence of Flowers and several other players, including second-round outside linebacker Zion Young and second-year cornerback Bilhal Kone, was due to minor, short-term injuries. The Ravens will kick off their final preseason game against the Commanders at M&T Bank Stadium in Baltimore on Friday night at 6 p.m. ET. The contest will be crucial in deciding the starting center competition between Jovaughn Gwyn and Ethan Pocic as well as the final spots on the 53-man roster, which will be set at 6 p.m. ET on Sunday.

title: Ravens Reacts Survey: which undrafted rookie will make the 53-man roster?
summary: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Ravens fans and fans across the country. The Baltimore Ravens are known for finding diamonds in the rough when signing undrafted rookies. In 21 of the last 22 years, a UDFA has made […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - AUGUST 22: Ethan Burke #45 of the Baltimore Ravens looks on before the preseason game against the Minnesota Vikings at U.S. Bank Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Ravens fans and fans across the country. The Baltimore Ravens are known for finding diamonds in the rough when signing undrafted rookies. In 21 of the last 22 years, a UDFA has made the 53-man roster, including three in 2025: Keyon Martin, Reuben Lowery, and Jay Higgins. (Lowery retired this offseason, but Martin and Higgins are poised to keep their spots for a second year.) Heading into training camp, it was unclear if the Ravens would have room on their roster for an undrafted rookie. But several have played their way into consideration for a 53-man roster spot, though Baltimore Beatdown’s staff is largely agreed on their favorite: Zach’s take: The Ravens’ best undrafted rookie signing has to be Ethan Burke up to this point. It was hard to picture any UDFA making the roster during the summer because of stacked this roster was and the large draft class. But the former Maryland lacrosse commit has generated a lot more buzz than Adisa Isaac and Kaimon Rucker so far through two weeks. He consistently made plays in training camp and broke out in Saturday’s preseason win in Minnesota with two tackles, two pressures, a sack, a tackle for loss, a pass breakup and a forced fumble on just 34 snaps. It’ll be hard to keep him off the roster as the fifth edge if the Ravens roster that many, which is to be expected. Dustin’s take: I have to go with outside linebacker Ethan Burke as the Ravens’ best undrafted rookie signing this year. Burke has a real shot the make the team as the fifth outside linebacker following a strong preseason, particularly his recent game against the Vikings. The former Texas Longhorn has shown real pop as a pass rusher on the edge through two preseason games. Burke’s main competition as the fifth outside linebacker is former third-round pick Adisa Isaac. Isaac is entering his third season and has struggled to stay on the field to this point in his career. While Isaac is still a promising prospect, Burke has given Baltimore more reason to go with him when comparing how the two players have performed this preseason. summary: Buffalo Bills tight end Dalton Kincaid is no stranger to injury woes. Having dealt with various levels of knee pain in the aftermath of a torn PCL during the 2024 NFL season, it sometimes feels as though Kincaid is always injured. Now, there’s more recent news that Kincaid may have been dealing with a new […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - AUGUST 22: Dalton Kincaid #86 of the Buffalo Bills looks on prior to a preseason game against the Cleveland Browns at Huntington Bank Field on August 22, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images Buffalo Bills tight end Dalton Kincaid is no stranger to injury woes. Having dealt with various levels of knee pain in the aftermath of a torn PCL during the 2024 NFL season, it sometimes feels as though Kincaid is always injured. Now, there’s more recent news that Kincaid may have been dealing with a new injury. Before you rush to the comments section, by all accounts and especially per Kyle Trimble (@BangedUpBills) who noted that it appears Kincaid hasn’t been limited by the observed injury . However, Trimble noted back on July 30 that Kincaid may have suffered a right ring or pinky finger injury based on the tape mechanism he sported at the start of training camp. Fast-forward to this week, and Dan Fetes confirms that Kincaid had indeed broken his right pinky finger at some point in camp. That brought about a bit of an uncomfortable pause in the room before discussing that even with the splint on, Kincaid’s training camp this summer has been so good the injury’s gone largely unnoticed. On a similar theme, Kincaid hasn’t worn a knee brace in camp, and he’s been a big part of the offense’s plans in the early going. Despite Kincaid having picked up a new injury (and one that could have happened in many different ways), it appears to be nothing to worry about at this point in time. Need reassurance? Just check out any highlight video of Kincaid’s summer work. Will this positively translate to major steps forward in the regular season? Time, as only it can do, will tell. A fully healthy Kincaid is certain to be a problem for NFL defenses, and many people have observed a potentially new/different level being unlocked by Kincaid this offseason. Below, you can check out all the commentary from “Buffalo Plus LIVE” on Kincaid’s latest injury and his game overall, conveniently time-stamped for you at the moment of the relevant conversation. @danfetes confirmed on his @BuffaloPlus podcast last night that Dalton Kincaid had broken his R pinky. Noticed this back on 7/30 which means it could have happened the 1st day of TC. title: Buffalo Bills fans approve of team signing DT Greg Gaines
summary: If you suspected I forgot about sharing results from Buffalo Rumblings’ latest Reacts poll, fear not. The results weren’t ready before I skipped town to hit the beach for a few days. Now back and surrounded by far less sand, seagulls, and jellyfish, I’m here to share the info you’ve all been anxiously expecting. You […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - AUGUST 22: Running back Raheim Sanders #35 of the Cleveland Browns is tackled by Greg Gaines #97 of the Buffalo Bills during the second quarter of the preseason game at Huntington Bank Field on August 22, 2026, in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Jason Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images If you suspected I forgot about sharing results from Buffalo Rumblings’ latest Reacts poll, fear not. The results weren’t ready before I skipped town to hit the beach for a few days. Now back and surrounded by far less sand, seagulls, and jellyfish, I’m here to share the info you’ve all been anxiously expecting. You may recall that last week we decided to gauge fan opinions on the Buffalo Bills’ signing of defensive lineman Greg Gaines . Or, if you’ve been out to sea too long, you may be wondering: “Who’s Greg Gaines”? A defensive tackle by position and a classic nose tackle by trade, Gaines comes to One Bills Drive to help fill an important role. Buffalo was in dire need of reinforcements after the news that defensive tackle Phidarian Mathis is set to miss the team’s first three games while suspended thanks to violating the NFL’s banned substances protocol. Despite the presence of Tommy Akingbesote as roster depth at the position and prior to adding Gaines, Mathis was widely viewed as the team’s only viable one-tech defensive tackle. We know now that Akingbesote wouldn’t get a bigger opportunity with Buffalo thanks to his release as a corresponding move to adding Gaines. So is Gaines just a fringe contributor, someone who may only see a few snaps a game? Gaines himself said that he passed up opportunities elsewhere, seeing real opportunity as a good fit for the scheme new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard intends to run. No, Gaines is unlikely to start over either Ed Oliver or Deone Walker in a perfect world. However, rarely is anything perfect. That means Gaines could find himself playing significant snaps at some point during the 2026 season either due to scheme or roster needs. For now, let’s see how you all voted regarding the Bills’ decision to sign Gaines. In looking at the total numbers, 75% of voters approve of the signing. Broken down further, 21% of voters gave Buffalo’s addition of Greg Gaines an “A” grade. For those of you savvy in math and the idea of approval, you now know that means 54% of voters gave Gaines’ signing a “B” grade. That’s the largest percentage of votes, and reflects a segment of the fan base that’s reasonably optimistic this move was made to improve the roster. Perhaps surprisingly, tied with the percentage of “A” voters are those who gave the signing a “C” grade (21% of voters). You might term this the “wait and see” group, which is understandable on many levels. Depending on what you thought of Akingbesote and any shot he may have had, his dismissal could play into the 4% of voters who gave the addition of Gaines a “D” (1%) or “F” (3%) grade. Maybe those fans are bummed that president of football operations/general manager Brandon Beane didn’t get something done with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers to trade for defensive tackle Vita Vea. It’s also possible that people are betting on Gaines playing little role for the Bills this season, thus viewing Gaines as anything other than a needle mover for the defense. title: We’ll have to monitor if Texans will be without right tackle vs. Bills Week 1
summary: Earlier this week during a joint practice with the Panthers, Texans newly signed right tackle Braden Smith was carted off the field, and now we have more details on his injury. According to ESPN’s Adam Schefter, the veteran with 110 games of NFL experience suffered a foot injury and isn’t expected to be out long-term: […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - JUNE 10: Braden Smith #71 of the Houston Texans arrives for the Houston Texans mandatory minicamp at Houston Methodist Training Center on June 10, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Jack Gorman/Getty Images) | Getty Images Earlier this week during a joint practice with the Panthers, Texans newly signed right tackle Braden Smith was carted off the field, and now we have more details on his injury. According to ESPN’s Adam Schefter, the veteran with 110 games of NFL experience suffered a foot injury and isn’t expected to be out long-term: Texans RT Braden Smith, who was carted off from practice this week, suffered an injury to his plantar fascia. He could miss “a few weeks”, per a source, but it is not considered a long-term injury. pic.twitter.com/3gswSucqnp — Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) August 27, 2026 This is a major win for the Texans, a club that over the past two seasons has been very aggressive in an attempt to rebuild its offensive line. Smith was a second-round pick of the Colts in 2018 out of Auburn and quickly acclimated to the professional game in Indianapolis. While he’s missed time with injury in all eight of his NFL seasons to date, he’s always played in double-digit contests each year. He signed a two-year, $20 million contract in Houston this past offseason and turned 30 in March. A gritty, ultra-physical blocker, Smith has allowed allowed more than 30 pressures in the regular season once, and that came in 2019. The timeline of “a few weeks” for his foot injury makes him potentially available for the Bills and Texans contest Week 1. The game will be 18 days after Smith suffered this injury. If Smith cannot go, expect either 33 year old Trent Brown or third-year pro Blake Fisher, the latter of whom has mostly been a liability in pass protection in his first two seasons across 855 total snaps, to replace Smith at right tackle. The week of Bills-Texans — after Labor Day — we’ll have to closely monitor whether or not the veteran will be ready to get back on the field ahead of the regular-season opener.

title: Buffalo Bills 2026 scouting report: safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson
summary: The Buffalo Bills are no strangers to quality safety play. For the better part of the last decade-plus, Micah Hyde and Jordan Poyer held down the last level of the defense, and each player made an All-Pro team at least once in their time with the club. Now, both Poyer and Hyde are no longer […]
full_text: ROCHESTER, NEW YORK - JULY 29: C.J. Gardner-Johnson #22 of the Buffalo Bills signs autographs for fans at St. John Fisher University during training camp on July 29, 2026 in Rochester, New York. (Photo by Joe Hrycych/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills are no strangers to quality safety play. For the better part of the last decade-plus, Micah Hyde and Jordan Poyer held down the last level of the defense, and each player made an All-Pro team at least once in their time with the club. Now, both Poyer and Hyde are no longer with the club. Hyde is officially retired, and Poyer remains unsigned after a productive 2025 season with Buffalo. He has said publicly that he would like to retire as a member of the Bills, and he also knew coming into last season that his playing days were numbered. It doesn’t seem likely that Poyer will play again. With both of Buffalo’s top safeties for most of the ‘20s at the end of their careers, it’s time for a new crop of players to take the mantle and continue the run of strong play Bills’ fans expect from the positional grouping. In today’s installment of our “91 players in 91 days” series, we discuss a veteran signed to help a new defense take hold this season. _____________________________________________________________________________ Name: C.J. Gardner-Johnson Number: 22 Position: S Height/Weight: 5’11” 208 lbs. Age: 28 (29 on 12/20/2026) Experience/Draft: Selected by the New Orleans Saints in the fourth round (No. 105 overall) of the 2019 NFL Draft College: Florida Acquired: Signed with Buffalo on 3/13/2026 Financial situation (per Spotrac): Gardner-Johnson signed a one-year deal worth $3.5 million this offseason; of that total, $3.015 million is guaranteed. The latter number will be the dead cap charge Buffalo carries if Gardner-Johnson is released. His cap hit for the season is $2.4 million if he makes the 53-man roster. 2025 Recap: Gardner-Johnson was traded to the Houston Texans from the Philadelphia Eagles in March, and while he dealt with a leg injury in training camp that caused him to miss time, he opened as one of Houston’s two starting safeties. He started the Texans’ first three games, all losses, totaling 15 tackles. After that game, Gardner-Johnson was released. Reports vary about why he was released—the Texans said it stemmed from his inability to adapt to DeMeco Ryans’ defensive scheme and his pointing fingers at teammates for coverage mistakes rather than accepting blame himself. Gardner-Johnson denied those allegations. He signed with the Baltimore Ravens practice squad on October 7, but was released a week later without having made an appearance for the team. Gardner-Johnson then signed with the Chicago Bears on October 29; he replaced slot corner Kyler Gordon, and he played very well with the Bears overall. In ten games, he totaled 51 tackles, three sacks, five tackles for loss, two interceptions, four pass breakups, one forced fumble, and five QB hits. In Chicago’s final regular season game, he suffered a concussion, which caused him to miss the Bears’ victory in the Wild Card Round over the Green Bay Packers. He returned to action the following week, totaling four tackles in Chicago’s 20-17 overtime loss to the Los Angeles Rams in the Divisional Round. Positional outlook: Gardner-Johnson is one of six players listed at safety on the current roster. Cole Bishop, Damar Hamlin, Geno Stone, Jalen Kilgore, and Wande Owens are the others. Sam Franklin is listed at defensive back, but he is a safety when he’s not doing his main work on special teams. Jordan Hancock is also listed at defensive back, and he is a safety/slot corner hybrid. 2026 Offseason: Gardner-Johnson was carted off the field with a calf strain on August 1, and while initial fears that he suffered an Achilles tear were proven false, the injury has held him back a bit. Two days after he returned from that calf injury, he suffered another leg injury. Head coach Joe Brady did not provide a timeline for the injury, but he didn’t seem concerned that it would lead to a long-term issue. 2026 Season outlook: If Gardner-Johnson is healthy, he has the ability to serve multiple roles in new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard’s defense. He is perfectly capable of playing the deep-third of the field, but he can also match man-to-man with both tight ends and wide receivers, and he can also sneak in an blitz hot off the corner to cause chaos in the backfield. Overall, Gardner-Johnson is a complete football player who has an edge that, frankly, the Bills might have been lacking over the last few years. There’s no question that he’ll start alongside Cole Bishop as long as they both are healthy. The problem is that, at present, neither of them is healthy. Minor preseason dings don’t worry me, but the opportunity to play in a new scheme before the real games start is something I hope that most, if not all, of Buffalo’s defensive starters can take advantage of at some point in these next few weeks. Gardner-Johnson’s injury history is extensive, containing foot, knee, calf, and pectoral injuries that have caused him to miss time. He also suffered a lacerated kidney during a November 2022 contest. He’s played just one full slate of games in his career, and that was his rookie season in 2019. If he’s healthy, he has the potential to be a great add for the Bills this season. However, staying healthy has proven to be a challenge for him throughout his career.

title: Buffalo Bills should look to sign this former Chargers offensive lineman
summary: If the Bills want to upgrade the guard and, especially, tackle depth on their roster, I have just the blocker for them. Jamaree Salyer, formerly of Chargers and most recently of the Dolphins. Right now, the presumed swing tackle on the Bills roster is third-year pro Tylan Grable, who only has 146 regular-season snaps on […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA - JANUARY 11: Jamaree Salyer #68 of the Los Angeles Chargers during an AFC Wildcard game between the New England Patriots and the Los Angeles Chargers on January 11, 2025, at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Fred Kfoury III/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images If the Bills want to upgrade the guard and, especially, tackle depth on their roster, I have just the blocker for them. Jamaree Salyer, formerly of Chargers and most recently of the Dolphins. Right now, the presumed swing tackle on the Bills roster is third-year pro Tylan Grable, who only has 146 regular-season snaps on his professional resume to date, and the overwhelming majority of those reps have come in Week 18 the past two seasons. He dealt with an injury in camp that forced him to miss the preseason opener, and while he did get back onto the field a week ago in Cleveland, Grable hardly looked up to the task of successfully blocking Browns outside rushers in the preseason. Swing tackles across the league aren’t starters for a reason, yet the Bills can’t feel incredibly confident in Grable’s ability if he’d be needed to play this season. There’s plenty of uncertainty with the former sixth-round pick at this stage of his development. Like Grable, Salyer was a sixth-round pick, and a few days into free agency this past March, he signed a one-year deal in Miami but was placed on injured reserve with a knee injury on August 16. The Dolphins are releasing G/T Jamaree Salyer with an injury settlement, per source. The team previously placed him on season-ending IR (knee). Salyer, who started 40 games for the Chargers, plans to be healthy and sign with a team in-season. — Jeremy Fowler (@JFowlerESPN) August 25, 2026 Counting the playoffs, Salyer has 67 games of NFL experience under his belt. He’s a uniquely built blocker listed at 6’4” and 325 pounds — although he was 6’3” at the 2022 NFL Combine — therefore his frame is more of a prototypical guard than tackle. I vividly remember scouting Salyer ahead of the 2022 NFL Draft, he was a collegiate tackle who everyone — including myself — believed was best-suited at guard at the next level. However, the Chargers essentially had no choice but to place Salyer at left tackle early in his rookie season after Rashawn Slater was lost for the season in Week 3. And Salyer thrived in his debut NFL campaign at left tackle protecting the blindside of Justin Herbert from Week 4 onward, including Los Angeles’ wild-card game against the Jaguars. Altogether, Salyer logged 1,029 snaps that rookie season and was a pleasant surprise, particularly in pass protection. While the only game in which he did not allow a pressure was his first, in Week 4, Salyer surrendered more than five pressures in just one contest. In 2023, Salyer played the entire season in Los Angeles at right guard, which totaled 1,144 snaps but lost his starting status ahead of the 2024 campaign but got on the field at left tackle, right tackle, and right guard. A season ago, Salyer saw 509 snaps of game action for the Chargers at those three positions and allowed a career-low 22 pressures. Lastly, there’s familiarity with Salyer from a few current Bills players. He blocked alongside Sedrick Van Pran-Granger and paved lanes for James Cook at Georgia. We aren’t sure how healthy Salyer is now or when his knee will be back to 100%. But if the Bills are searching for more stable depth at tackle and guard ahead of the beginning of the regular season, Salyer should strongly considered.
