Nestled within that bigger narrative were multiple individual ones, including that […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - JANUARY 11: New England Patriots defensive tackle Leonard Taylor III (93) runs during an NFL wild card playoff game against the Los Angeles Chargers at Gillette Stadium on January 11, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Rags-to-riches stories are commonplace in the NFL, and the New England Patriots wrote their own in 2025. Coming off consecutive 4-13 campaigns, they manufactured a lightning-fast turnaround under first-year head coach Mike Vrabel, and ended up advancing all the way to the Super Bowl. Nestled within that bigger narrative were multiple individual ones, including that of defensive tackle Leonard Taylor. He went from the depths of one of the worst teams in football to the biggest stage in the NFL last year, and is now trying to add more chapters to his story. Hard facts Name: Leonard Taylor III Position: Defensive tackle/Interior defensive line Jersey number: 93 Opening day age: 24 (5/29/2002) Measurements : 6’3 1/2”, 305 lbs, 9” hand size, 33 7/8” arm length, 80 5/8” wingspan, 5.12s 40-yard dash, 7.68s 3-cone drill, 4.71s short shuttle, 30” vertical jump, 9’1” broad jump, 7.60 Relative Athletic Score Experience NFL: New York Jets (2024-25), New England Patriots (2025-) | College: Miami (2021-23) A standout defensive lineman at Miami Palmetto in Pinecrest, FL, Taylor was ranked a five-star college recruit and his offers looked accordingly. His first scholarship opportunity came courtesy of the University of Miami back when he was still a high school sophomore, and he later saw other high-profile schools such as Alabama, Ohio State and Tennessee all enter the mix. Miami remained in the race throughout, however, and was able to secure him coming out. In three seasons with the Hurricanes, Taylor saw action in 31 games with 19 starts. A one-time honorable All-ACC selection, he registered six sacks as well as 61 tackles and an interception during his college career. While he could have stayed put for another season, he decided to skip his senior campaign to enter the NFL Draft — a decision that did not result in him getting selected: he failed to hear his name called, and he instead had to enter rookie free agency. Taylor subsequently signed with the Jets, with whom he spent the first one and a half seasons of his career. He later joined the Patriots midway through the 2025 season, bringing his career total to a combined 23 regular season and playoff games. He has 36 tackles and 1.5 sacks on his résumé. Scouting report Strengths: Taylor is a well-put-together interior lineman whose long limbs and adequate height allow him to be used in a multi-purpose fashion. He combines his frame with some good moving skills, both laterally and when working up the field. His quickness can catch offensive linemen off guard and allows him to exploit gaps before they can close, while he also has the motor to simply will himself to positive results. He plays with some powerful hands, both in terms of applying an initial punch and bringing down ball carriers. He also has shown some real strides as a tackler since his college days. Weaknesses: Taylor never lived up to his five-star status coming out of high school, in part due to some shortcomings that still exist to this day. Among them is his lack of agility and lower-body flexibility. He also continues to struggle with keeping his pad level low, and can too easily find himself out-leveraged and moved off the point of attack; that has been a particular problem in the run game, where his consistency and ability to control gaps has been lacking. His rush plan also could use some fine-tuning given that his hands tend to be all over the place especially after first contact. 2025 review Stats (Jets) : 2 games (0 starts) | 47 defensive snaps (12.3%), 13 special teams snaps (7.5%) | 3 tackles, 0 missed tackles, 1 TFL | 0 penalties Stats (Patriots): 7 games (0 starts) | 122 defensive snaps (13.3%), 17 special teams snaps (4.3%) | 9 tackles, 1 missed tackle (10.0%) | 7 QB pressures (1 hit, 6 hurries) | 1 field goal block | 0 penalties Season recap: Spending his entire rookie campaign on the Jets’ active roster even as an undrafted free agent, Taylor’s career got off to a promising start. However, he was unable to build any momentum from that point on, at least in New York. Working under a new coaching staff, he appeared in just two games over the first six weeks of the season. His eventual release in mid-October was therefore not much of a surprise. Neither was Taylor finding a new home fairly quickly after clearing waivers: just two days after getting cut by what was then an 0-6 Jets team, he was signed to the Patriots’ practice squad. Taylor spent the remainder of the 2026 there, but along the way saw some serious playing time. He was elevated to the game day roster on three occasions during the regular season — the maximum allowed under NFL rules — and four times in the playoffs, appearing in a combined seven contests for his new club and playing 122 defensive snaps. Of those 122 snaps, 70 came in the playoffs as a de facto injury replacement for rookie Joshua Farmer. While still only New England’s No. 5 interior lineman in playing time share in the tournament, the Patriots trusting him in the sport’s ultimate perform-or-else setting speaks for itself. Taylor himself was able to show why the team kept calling his number, registering three quarterback pressures in the playoffs and making one of the its biggest plays. GOT A HAND ON IT 🙅‍♂️ 📺 CBS pic.twitter.com/qQXfoCAsVu — New England Patriots (@Patriots) January 25, 2026 Taylor getting a hand on Broncos kicker Wil Lutz’s potential game-tying 45-yard field goal in the late fourth quarter of the AFC Championship Game forced the ball off its intended course and past the uprights. This allowed the Patriots to retain a narrow 10-7 lead they would hold on to all the way to the final whistle. As a consequence, Taylor helped his new team punch its ticket to the Super Bowl just three months after being let go by arguably the worst one in the league at that point. That fact alone made his second year in the league a success, and one of the best plot lines of New England’s 2025 season. 2026 preview Position: 3-/4-/5-technique defensive tackle | Ability: Depth player/Role player | Contract: Signed through 2026 (2027 RFA) What will be his role? Taylor spent his first training camp in New England working as a second-string interior lineman primarily focused on rushing the passer. He found some success in that area against his teammates, during joint practices, and in preseason. Based on his usage over the summer, he projects as a pass-first rotational backup at the defensive tackle position. What is his growth potential? Taylor has some athletic skill and an NFL-caliber frame, but — just like in college — has failed to put it all together and become a consistent contributor. Chances are he never will be, at least from an all-around three-down perspective, but he can still build a career off of providing value as a package and depth player. Does he have positional versatility? Like other 300-plus-pound defensive tackles, Taylor offers limited versatility. He can play multiple techniques up front, but is best suited to take the field on late downs and in obvious passing situations. He also showcased his special teams abilities last season and should be able to regularly line up alongside the field goal and extra point blocking teams. What is his salary cap situation? Taylor was one of several practice squad players to sign a one-year futures contract with the Patriots after the Super Bowl. The deal consists entirely of a $1.075 million base salary that is non-guaranteed and simultaneously functions as his cap number. How safe is his roster spot? Despite spending significant time with the second-string defense in training camp, Taylor finds himself on the roster bubble. His pass-first skillset offers an…

title: Joining Patriots all about familiarity, value for newly-signed Greg Van Roten
summary: The New England Patriots’ interior offensive line depth suffered a blow during the preseason opener against the Indianapolis Colts, prompting the club to look for alternatives. They signed three players in total, with one of them standing out among them: Greg Van Roten, a veteran of 12 NFL seasons and a player who very well […]
full_text: Foxborough, MA - August 25: New England Patriots guard Greg Van Roten speaks to reporters after practice at Gillette Stadium on August 25, 2026. (Photo by Danielle Parhizkaran/The Boston Globe via Getty Images) | Boston Globe via Getty Images The New England Patriots’ interior offensive line depth suffered a blow during the preseason opener against the Indianapolis Colts, prompting the club to look for alternatives. They signed three players in total, with one of them standing out among them: Greg Van Roten, a veteran of 12 NFL seasons and a player who very well could find himself on the 53-man roster come the regular season. For the Patriots, signing Van Roten made plenty of sense. Not only does he bring immense experience to a backup group lacking just that following the Ben Brown and Andrew Rupcich injuries, he also has familiarity with offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels after the two overlapped in Las Vegas in 2023. “There is a lot of carry-over,” Van Roten told reporters following the Patriots’ final practice of training camp on Tuesday. “Really just a matter of forgetting some of the things that aren’t the same, and trying to re-learn some of the things because I was with Josh in 2023. So, it’s been a few years. But the system is similar. It’s just everyone has little kind of idiosyncrasies and nuances to how they want things done.” The familiarity between Van Roten and the Patriots does not end with McDaniels and his system. The 36-year-old, who is now the oldest player on the team’s roster, also has started alongside two of his new teammates before: Alijah Vera-Tucker and Morgan Moses, New England’s left guard and right tackle, respectively, were part of the New York Jets’ starting O-line alongside Van Roten in 2021. For Van Roten, who is mostly a right guard but also has the versatility to play on the left side or line up at center, this preexisting connection helps with the transition. “It’s huge just because you don’t have to make up so much time,” he explained. “We’ve had plenty of games together and years together, so we have experience. We have our ways of communicating and just knowing — I know how Morgan’s going to set, I know how Alijah’s going to set, because we’ve had countless practices and games together.” Van Roten signed with the Patriots earlier this month, but it was not the first time the two sides had already touched base. He was in Foxborough for a free agency visit two weeks before officially putting pen to paper. That visit gave him a first glimpse of the Patriots’ new facilities and allowed him to reconnect with some of the people he knows within the organization — a taste of what was to come. “I have a lot of familiarity with players and coaches in the building, so it was a cool experience just kind of catching up with some people I haven’t seen in a long time,” he said. “And then being up here, I played a ton of games actually in New England over my career. I think it might be the one team I played the most. I have family that lives up this way in New England. It’s not home for me, but it’s not far off.” Knowledge of New England as a team and a region is one thing, but the business side of the NFL also dictated where Van Roten ended up. And the Patriots made sure it was with them: they signed him to a one-year, $3 million contract well above the veteran’s minimum one could have projected for a player unsigned since March. In Van Roten’s eyes, this speaks for itself. “You want to go where you’re valued, and the Patriots valued me more than other teams,” he said. “It’s a great organization. It speaks for itself. I’ve had a rough couple of years with different teams, so I’m excited to be somewhere with the tradition that they have here.”
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: 6 winners and losers from Patriots’ Kayshon Boutte-Jaylen Reed trade
summary: Considering the last few months of speculation, the New England Patriots trading Kayshon Boutte did not come as too big a surprise. Neither was them sending the fourth-year wide receiver to a Houston Texans team that had just lost fellow wide receiver Jayden Higgins to a torn ACL. What might have come as a bit […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - SEPTEMBER 28: Drake Maye #10 of the New England Patriots celebrates with teammates Kayshon Boutte #9 of the New England Patriots and Mack Hollins #13 of the New England Patriots after scoring a touchdown against the Carolina Panthers during the second quarter in the game at Gillette Stadium on September 28, 2025 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Jordan Bank/Getty Images) | Getty Images Considering the last few months of speculation, the New England Patriots trading Kayshon Boutte did not come as too big a surprise. Neither was them sending the fourth-year wide receiver to a Houston Texans team that had just lost fellow wide receiver Jayden Higgins to a torn ACL. What might have come as a bit of a surprise, and the general consensus around the move reflects this, was the return: second-year safety Jaylen Reed and a seventh-round draft choice in 2028. We have already looked at what the move means for the Patriots from a big-picture perspective and their wide receiver group in particular . Now, let’s focus on who on the team is better or worse off because of it. Winners WR Kyle Williams: Williams served as the Patriots’ backup X-receiver behind Boutte last season, and did show some promise in his limited opportunities as an injury replacement. However, with both Boutte, A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs all on the roster as perimeter targets this summer, he was relegated mostly to second-string duty. The team is still high on him, and Monday’s trade further strengthens his position on the team — something the first post-Boutte practice on Tuesday already reflected. WR Mack Hollins: When it comes to actually replacing Boutte’s contributions as the No. 4 wide receiver on the team, Mack Hollins might be the frontrunner. The veteran has not been a particular standout in training camp, but his abilities as a big-bodied red area target and a blocker in the run game will allow him to see regular action. He is not the same player type, but is an established commodity in the New England offense who, similar but not quite like Boutte, has good chemistry with Drake Maye. WR Efton Chism III: Before the Boutte trade to the Texans was finalized, the Patriots had seven roster-worthy wide receivers on their roster. The seventh among those, and therefore the one on the fringes of the 53-man team, was Chism. While a solid player whose versatility can be an asset, he could have ended up losing his roster spots to needs elsewhere. However, it now seems like a fairly safe bet that he will make it onto the team. Zak Kuhr: Talking to reporters since the trade was made official, Patriots assistant coaches expressed their excitement about getting Reed aboard and working with it. They also highlighted his physical play style and versatile skillset — two assets that will likely also appeal to the team’s defensive coordinator. Kuhr likes to call an aggressive game and move his players all over the formation to create favorable matchups. Reed should be a perfect fit to the unit in that regard. Losers QB Drake Maye: Boutte was never a bona fide No. 1 wide receiver, but he and Drake Maye developed a nice chemistry going back to the latter’s rookie season in 2024. Maye trusted Boutte on deep shots down the field, and the former sixth-round draft pick delivered some spectacular plays in their two seasons working together (and this year’s training camp as well). The receiver group around New England’s franchise quarterback is still very deep, but the Maye-Boutte connection was still a fun one to watch. (Speaking of fun, how about a fun fact? The first and last touchdown pass from Maye to Boutte both came against his new team, the Texans, and both versus All-Pro cornerback Derek Stingley Jr.) The depth safeties: Even before training camp started, the hierarchy at the safety position was set. There were starters Craig Woodson and Kevin Byard, and everybody else. That second group competed for what was unlikely to be more than two spots on the team, but that outlook has now changed. With Reed effectively a roster lock alongside Woodson and Byard, the other depth safeties — in particular Dell Pettus, John Saunders Jr. and Mike Brown — have now been put in a difficult spot.
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: What the Patriots saw in trade acquisition Jaylen Reed
summary: As the New England Patriots went through their draft preparation ahead of the 2025 NFL Draft, Penn State safety Jaylen Reed came across their radar. The safety ended up coming off the board 187th overall in the sixth round to the Houston Texans. But the Patriots continued to monitor him. “We followed his career last […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - JANUARY 18: Jaylen Reed #23 of the Houston Texans lines up during an NFC Divisional Playoff game against the New England Patriots at Gillette Stadium on January 18, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images As the New England Patriots went through their draft preparation ahead of the 2025 NFL Draft, Penn State safety Jaylen Reed came across their radar. The safety ended up coming off the board 187th overall in the sixth round to the Houston Texans. But the Patriots continued to monitor him. “We followed his career last year with Houston,” executive vice president of player personal Eliot Wolf said Tuesday. “When we determined that he might be available, he was someone that we wanted to acquire.” The Patriots did just that on Monday, trading wide receiver Kayshon Boutte to the Texans for Reed and a 2028 seventh-round draft pick. Reed now joins a safety room that includes Kevin Byard, Craig Woodson, Dell Pettus and John Saunders Jr. with just two weeks remaining before the season opener. His immediate role, however, remains to be determined as he works to learn New England’s defense. “That will kind of be up to him at this point, coming in, learning the system,” Wolf said. “He’s supposed to be really smart, so we’ll see if our reports on that are true. But talking to him this morning, he’s really eager and excited to be here.” During his rookie season with the Texans, Reed appeared in just seven regular-season games, drawing one start. He did, however, start each of Houston’s two playoff games — including a Divisional Round loss to the Patriots — something that stood out to Wolf. “Thought it was pretty remarkable that, as a rookie who hadn’t played much during the regular season, they trusted him enough to play the majority of the playoff games,” Wolf said. As for what kind of player New England is adding, safeties coach Scott Booker recalled watching Reed ahead of last year’s draft. “Good player, physical player,” Booker said. “A guy that was definitely on our draft board. Obviously, we didn’t go that route. But definitely a guy that I talked to in the pre-draft situation. Like his personality and happy he’s part of us.” Despite playing just 173 defensive snaps last season, Reed showed the ability to play the deep portion of the field, while his physicality can make him an asset closer to the line of scrimmage. That versatility could prove valuable for a Patriots defense that has spent the offseason searching for the right fit alongside Byard and Woodson as a big nickel in three-safety packages — something that has become more common across the league as offenses play in heavier personnel. New England has cycled through several options on the backend, but have not appeared to find the right fit. Booker and defensive coordinator Zak Kuhr were not ready to put any expectations on Reed’s fit in the defense, but his skill set provides an intriguing option in that role. “Since we just got him, I’m not going to make any predictions of where he’s going to play and all that type of stuff,” Booker said. “We’re going to try to get him up to date on all our terminology and all of our calls as soon as possible and see where he fits in.” Reed also saw extensive time on special teams for the Texans last season, playing 113 snaps across multiple units in the kicking game. With the Patriots losing three of their top five special teams players in terms of snaps from last season, Reed should be provided with an opportunity to assume a core role. Upon his arrival at the facility Tuesday, Reed already pledged to Wolf that he would be more violent on special teams — which was music to special teams coordinator Jeremy Springer’s ears. “A safety that’s violent, plays fast — every time you see one of those they can play in a lot of different spots,” Springer said. “So I’m excited for that.”
author: Brian Hines

title: Saints rookie report: Preseason Week 3
summary: WR Jordyn Tyson  DNP: Still injured DT Christen Miller Miller returned to practice from his injury that he suffered against the Rams, which means he should be able to play in the Saints’ last preseason game. So far, Miller has arguably been the best rookie so far, and that’s even when he didn’t play in […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - AUGUST 22: Bryce Lance #18 of the New Orleans Saints during warm up before a preseason game between the New Orleans Saints and the Los Angeles Rams at SoFi Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Harry How/Getty Images) | Getty Images WR Jordyn Tyson DNP: Still injured DT Christen Miller Miller returned to practice from his injury that he suffered against the Rams, which means he should be able to play in the Saints’ last preseason game. So far, Miller has arguably been the best rookie so far, and that’s even when he didn’t play in week 2 and missed a good amount of game 1. In the little time he has played, Miller looked like one of the best run defenders on the roster and really fit in Brandon Staley’s scheme. For the young DT, he will not have to wait long to become a starter. It’s clear how important he is to the defense, even if it’s just preseason. TE Oscar Delp TE Oscar Delp has had a slow start to his preseason and is now dealing with an injury. Not the best combination for a rookie, and even if the hamstring issue is minor, Delp is likely going to miss game 3. OG Jeremiah Wright Week 2 was a big test for rookie offensive lineman, and although the entire offensive line struggled (including Wright at times), he did decent. Not ready to start, but showed enough to feel good about his future. Game three should be more of the same. Wright is likely going to start at RG, and again, it is going to be an opportunity for him to perform. If he continues to improve as he has, it could be the first time we see a starting-level performance out of him. WRs Bryce Lance and Barion Brown More standouts for the Saints roster, Bryce Lance and Barion Brown have been some of the most exciting players for New Orleans. Brown was sat for Week 2, which is a sign the Saints view him as a high-level starter going into the season, but Lance did play. After being injured in Week 1, Lance had a big challenge ahead of him against the Rams, and he did do well. It wasn’t a big performance for him, only catching two passes, but those catches were good. Game 3 is going to be fun to see both these players, but if the starters don’t play, Brown will likely be sat again. DBs Lorenzo Styles Jr. and TJ Hall Jr. It was not a good week for the Saints’ pass defense, and every player struggled, but Styles and Hall were able to get a pass deflection each. Still, clearly, these two players will likely be special teams players right away.

summary: Tampa Bay Buccaneers The Buccaneers had a pretty low-scoring game this week against the Kansas City Chiefs, but they were able to get the win in the end. One of the shining parts of this roster so far in preseason has been QB Jalon Daniels. He did really well in Week 1 and led the […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CA - AUGUST 22: Matthew Stafford #9 of the Los Angeles Rams meets with head coach Kellen Moore of the New Orleans Saints following an NFL preseason game between the New Orleans Saints and the Los Angeles Rams on August 22, 2026, at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Greg Fiore/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Tampa Bay Buccaneers The Buccaneers had a pretty low-scoring game this week against the Kansas City Chiefs, but they were able to get the win in the end. One of the shining parts of this roster so far in preseason has been QB Jalon Daniels. He did really well in Week 1 and led the team to this win in Week 2. Also, first-round pick Rueben Bain Jr. had a good game and completely dominated the opposing RT on one play. In addition, since last week’s state of the NFC South, DT Vita Vea was signed to a contract extension, although only for 1 year. The DT should be staying in Tampa Bay, but if the year goes wrong, that could change. Carolina Panthers Unlike last week, when the Panthers lost by two scores to the Buffalo Bills, Carolina got the win this time. Battling with the Jacksonville Jaguars, Carolina’s QBs, consisting of Kenny Pickett, Bryce Young, and Kyle Trask, had a pretty good day. Pickett was the main QB for the game, finishing with 137 yards and 1 touchdown. Next game, the Panthers will be playing the Houston Texans in their fourth and final preseason matchup. The starters did play a bit in their third preseason game, but maybe they will play more in the final game. Atlanta Falcons Out of all the NFC South teams this week, the Falcons had the most success. They beat the Indianapolis Colts by 28 points, and QB Jack Strand looked really good. The rookie, who is a UDFA, has been an impressive part of Atlanta’s preseason and may legitimately be a dark horse QB moving forward. Michael Penix is beginning to ramp up back to being able to play, and Tua Tagovailoa is ready to play again, so the final preseason game should feature these two battling against each other. New Orleans Saints And now we have the Saints. Instead of getting a win, the Saints were shut out 34-0 by the Rams. It was one of those performances that are hard to forget, even if you try. Of course, it’s just preseason, but it was ugly. It was even worse because of the injuries and the fact that little information was gained in position battles. QB Zach Wilson and Spencer Rattler both struggled and will not have a major game in front of them in Week 3. The backup job is wide open, to the point that if both of these two have bad performances again, the Saints could be making another addition to the QB room. Kellen Moore and the staff have already not wasted time bringing in new players and reinforcements, but maybe the work needs to continue.

title: Our defense vs. their offense: Dallas Cowboys
summary: Less than one week after an awful 34-0 loss to the Los Angeles Rams, the New Orleans Saints will now shift their focus to the team’s final preseason game against the Dallas Cowboys. On the flip side, Dallas is coming off of a 34-13 victory over the Arizona Cardinals. Let’s take a look at the […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CA - AUGUST 22: Brennan Presley #81 of the Los Angeles Rams runs up the middle during an NFL preseason game between the New Orleans Saints and the Los Angeles Rams on August 22, 2026, at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Greg Fiore/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Less than one week after an awful 34-0 loss to the Los Angeles Rams, the New Orleans Saints will now shift their focus to the team’s final preseason game against the Dallas Cowboys. On the flip side, Dallas is coming off of a 34-13 victory over the Arizona Cardinals. Let’s take a look at the Saints’ defensive matchup for this upcoming game. Through two preseason games, the Dallas offense has lived up to expectations even without many starters playing up to this point. Former Tennessee quarterback Joe Milton III has performed masterfully as he competes for the QB2 spot behind Dak Prescott. He has managed to lead the Cowboys to the fifth-highest scoring offense at 25.5 points per game. Dallas also ranks tenth in passing yards per game at 219.5 and first in the league with 156 yards per game on the ground. Meanwhile, the New Orleans defense has struggled to keep opponents out of scoring position, allowing 29 points a contest, a mark that ranks 31st in the league. Both of the teams that the Saints have faced previously this preseason, the Jacksonville Jaguars and Los Angeles Rams, are ranked within the top 12 in the NFL for scoring. Dallas is projected to have one of the better offenses in the league for the 2026 season. With Prescott at the helm and a number of weapons at his disposal such as CeeDee Lamb, George Pickens, Javonte Williams, Jake Ferguson, etc., the Cowboys are likely to put up a lot of points this year. After getting emabarassed by the Rams last Saturday, it will be interesting to see how the defense responds. This will be one of the final opportunities that those vying for roster spots will have to impress the coaching staffs and prove they deserve to be on the final 53-man depth chart.

title: Saints vs. Cowboys: Quarterback Matchup
summary: The New Orleans Saints take the field on Friday for the final dress rehearsal of the preseason in a matchup against the Dallas Cowboys. This matchup should not turn into the Royal Rumble that took place last week during the joint practice session between the two teams. The Saints are coming into the game following […]
full_text: OXNARD, CALIFORNIA - AUGUST 18: Tyler Shough #6 of the New Orleans Saints runs during joint practice against the Dallas Cowboys at River Ridge Playing Fields on August 18, 2026 in Oxnard, California. (Photo by Ric Tapia/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New Orleans Saints take the field on Friday for the final dress rehearsal of the preseason in a matchup against the Dallas Cowboys. This matchup should not turn into the Royal Rumble that took place last week during the joint practice session between the two teams. The Saints are coming into the game following one of their worst performances of the preseason. The Saints gave Zach Wilson the opportunity to start last week vs. the Rams, and his play was not that inspiring. Rattler finished the game, although his wasn’t much better. Kellen Moore said that Tyler Shough and most of the starters will sit out of this game, which is wise given the growing number of injuries, as it’s best to have them ready for Week 1 vs. Detroit. Wilson and Rattler are both competing for the No. 2 spot, and so far, neither one of them has really taken the job. Wilson had his moments against the Jaguars, but the regression that took place against the Rams has to be noticed. Rattler hasn’t been terrible, but he also has not been good. Rattler finished the game against the Rams 14-of-23 for 141 yards with an interception that was returned 100 yards. So, his interception was returned for nearly the same amount of yardage that he threw for. Wilson finished the day with six completions on 12 attempts for 55 yards and an interception as well. The confidence in the backups is not high right now, but this week will be an opportunity for them to show that last week was a fluke and not the norm. As for the Cowboys, they are locked into a backup quarterback battle as well. However, there seems to be more confidence in their backup situation, as Joe Milton and Sam Howell are apparently “neck and neck” in that race, according to head coach Brian Schottenheimer on Monday. Schottenheimer said that over the past two games, Milton has played beautifully and Howell has made some really good plays as well. The two quarterbacks have alternated the starting role over the past two weeks, so it will be interesting to see who gets the nod against the Saints if Prescott is held out. In his start last week against the Cardinals, Milton finished 9-of-13 passing for 179 yards and two touchdowns while adding another touchdown on the ground. Not to mention, he had zero turnovers. Howell, on the other hand, finished that game 7-of-10 for 65 yards with one interception. In the game vs. Seattle, Milton finished 12-of-15 for 107 yards and one touchdown. Howell finished 8-of-12 for 94 yards and one touchdown. Both finished with nearly identical passer ratings in that game, with Milton at 118.6 and Howell at 118.1. The Cowboys are undefeated so far in the preseason, and their quarterback play is a big reason why. Can the Saints get what would be their first and only win of the preseason in the finale on Friday and put a blemish on the Cowboys’ preseason record? In order to accomplish that, the quarterback play for the Saints needs to step up and remain consistent throughout the entire game. It should be a fun game in Dallas.

title: NY Giants assistant GM Brandon Brown: ‘Meritocracy’ has raised the floor
summary: Meritocracy. From Dictionary.com, here is what it means. New York Giants assistant GM Brandon Brown said this week that one of the most important things head coach John Harbaugh has brought to the Giants is the idea of meritocracy — players earning what they get based on what they do now, rather than what they […]
full_text: Brandon Brown | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Meritocracy. From Dictionary.com, here is what it means. An elite group of people whose progress is based on ability and talent rather than on class, privilege, or wealth. A system in which such persons are rewarded and advanced. New York Giants assistant GM Brandon Brown said this week that one of the most important things head coach John Harbaugh has brought to the Giants is the idea of meritocracy — players earning what they get based on what they do now, rather than what they have or have not accomplished in the past. “Harbs has preached meritocracy, right?,” Brown said. “So, what has got you here is not necessarily going to keep you here, and you’ve got to have daily deposits.” The idea of meritocracy is something every coach talks about. The dirty little secret, or perhaps not so secret, of the NFL is that meritocracy on an NFL roster is rarely real. Players with big paychecks usually play even if there is a better player on the roster at their position. Their paycheck, after all, has to be justified. First- or second-round draft picks get far more opportunities than undrafted free agents, even if teams tell you — as they always do — that how a player got to a team doesn’t matter. It does. Almost always. Teams will often go to great lengths to prove they weren’t wrong to use premium draft capital on a player. The fact that Harbaugh’s Giants are running a true meritocracy is impressive. And should help to make the on-field product better. Brown said that what Harbaugh has done is “raise the floor” of expectations from players. “It’s just being objective. It’s not having any governor on guys. It’s earning it,” Brown said. “And as you guys have seen through the practice rotations in terms of at certain positions, which guys are getting more reps, which guys are getting less reps, maybe that flips on a certain day. It’s all a part of the meritocracy of earning it.” There is no better example on the roster of a player benefiting from this meritocracy than Deonte Banks. Yes, Banks is a former first-round pick. After two miserable seasons, though, it looked like Banks was a failed cornerback who would hang around the NFL because of his big-play ability as a kickoff returner. Harbaugh, though, had an “I want to see these guys for myself” approach with failed high picks like Banks, Evan Neal, Jalin Hyatt, and the now-traded Josh Ezeudu. From early in the spring, Banks has been impressive. Many of the things that seemed to be missing the past two seasons — like being sound in technique and assignments, and being aggressive in run support and willing to tackle — have been evident. The thought all along has been that Banks and veteran Greg Newsome were competing for the CB2 job across from Paulson Adebo. Now, judging by the reps being doled out in practices, Banks and Newsome could push Adebo and his team-high $24.199 million cap hit to the bench. That would be a development that seemed impossible in the spring. “I think he [Banks] just has belief in himself right now,” defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson said this week. “He has a good group of DB coaches in that room that believe in him. The players believe in him, and he’s playing with confidence. He’s out there, he’s making the plays he’s supposed to make. He’s detailed on his assignments, being where he’s supposed to be, and that’s giving him an opportunity to make plays. “As long as he keeps doing that, he’ll continue to get better.” There are other examples across the roster: The idea that Chauncey Golston, who floundered without a real role a year ago, seems to have emerged as a starting base defensive end. He has made plays all summer, and that is being recognized. The competition that has developed between practice squad player Bryan Hudson and veteran offensive lineman Lucas Patrick for the job backing up John Michael Schmitz at center. The competition for both roster spots and playing time at wide receiver. Odell Beckham might make the roster, but it will be because he has earned it. Not because of his name. Former undrafted free agent Dalen Cambre could make it, too. Trading guard Daniel Faalele, a player who started for Harbaugh for two seasons with the Baltimore Ravens, showed Harbaugh would not be emotionally attached to a player when there were others available who could do that job. The Giants appear likely to go with undrafted long-snapper Ben Mann and undrafted placekicker Dominic Zvada. Because both have earned the opportunity. Brown said the idea of meritocracy extends across the organization. “Harbs makes you earn it,” Brown said. “When you go into a team meeting room, first thing you see is a big sign on the back wall that says, ‘Earn the Right.’ It’s right in front of the room, and it just doesn’t extend to players. It’s to staff, and it’s understanding a good idea can come from anywhere, and the way that Harbs seeks and solicits opinions keeps you on your A-game. “Every day you want to make a deposit. Every day you want to have an idea or thought or something to contribute to making a good decision. Again, he’s hard on the coaches in terms of teaching and getting the technique right, and also on the personnel department along with (Senior Vice President and General Manager) Joe (Schoen) in terms of, hey, we have all of our contingency plans ready to go, and we understand what the marketplace looks like, and if it’s something that comes about that we’re not a part of, we’ve done our due diligence, but we’re never going to sit on our hands.”
author: Ed Valentine

title: Will Giants’ starters play vs. Jets? We don’t know, but they should
summary: New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh told Boomer and Gio on WFAN that he was “waffling” about whether or not to play quarterback Jaxson Dart on Friday night in the preseason finale against the New York Jets. On Wednesday afternoon, Harbaugh told media that he would “just leave it up in the air right […]
full_text: Jaxson Dart | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh told Boomer and Gio on WFAN that he was “waffling” about whether or not to play quarterback Jaxson Dart on Friday night in the preseason finale against the New York Jets. On Wednesday afternoon, Harbaugh told media that he would “just leave it up in the air right now.” “We’ll see where we’re at,” Harbaugh said. “There would be things to be gained for those guys to play defensively as well, from a communication standpoint. But there’s risk. It’s just a balancing act of what we gain the most from with the least amount of risk. That’s what we’ve got to figure out.” One of the winningest NFL head coaches of all time, Harbaugh doesn’t need Big Blue View’s help making decisions. I am going to offer it, anyway. Play the starters, John. At least on offense. They don’t need to play into the third quarter, like many front-line players used to do in Week 3 when NFL teams played four preseason games. A quarter or a couple of series worth of work, though, should be beneficial. Jaxson Dart is a second-year quarterback leading a team learning a new offense that is asking him to do things he did not do in college or as an NFL rookie. Practice is nice. Game reps are better. If Dart and other front-line Giants who played in the Week 1 game against the Minnesota Vikings don’t play Friday night, they will go from Aug. 15 to Sept. 13 — the date of the season opener vs. the Dallas Cowboys — without game action. Harbaugh, of course, understands the value of game reps. He knows going so long without game action is not ideal, especially for an offense like the Giants that is not already established. I asked him early in the week if that played a role in how he would approach getting players ready for the season-opener. “Most definitely. Most definitely. You have to factor that in and consider that,” Harbaugh said. “Playing together in a game, communicating together in a game, those things are valuable things that it’s better to have some experience with before you get into the game that counts, so to speak. “So, yeah, that’s part of it.” Harbaugh was asked again on Wednesday about players going that long without competition, with the exception of the single joint practice against the Miami Dolphins. “Well, that’s a big factor. I think that’s exactly right. I mean, that is the factor,” Harbaugh said. “That’s the thing that – I don’t know if concern is the right word because a lot of teams do it, but you haven’t played in a game, now we’re going to go play in a game under the lights, high stakes, it’s going to be loud. All those things are going to factor in, and they haven’t been out there in that setting for a while. And the setting they were in isn’t anything like the one they’re going to be in either. So, that, to me, is your point. It’s exactly right. That is the factor.” Harbaugh worked the Giants hard — by modern NFL standards — during the Giants’ time in West Virginia and for the first week or so after returning to New Jersey. He had said he was happy that the team was “calloused” and ready for NFL competition after that work. Practices this week were all unpadded and were shorter than the 2½-hour workouts that were common earlier in the summer. There is more of a regular-season tempo to the work the Giants are doing now. The danger, of course, is that the Giants will lose the edge they have developed by the time the opener against Dallas rolls around. The injury risk is also real, and why teams often opt not to play their best players in the final preseason game. Even if that impacts how well prepared they may be for the beginning of the season. “You get some injuries, and you just try to make the argument that you go to the season with your best players healthy, that’s the most important thing,” Harbaugh said. “It’s a 17-game season, it’s a long season. Yes, you may not be as sharp as you’re going to be a couple games in, but it’s a long season. And the other team is in the same boat you’re in … People work back towards trying to avoid the injuries.” Harbaugh said the other debate is over the value of a brief stint for players rather than extended work. “That’s the other side of the argument now,” Harbaugh said. “How much are you going to play them? In the old days, they would be out there for three quarters in the third preseason game. “How much is six plays, 10 plays, how much is that really worth? That’s part of the whole balancing act.” The view here is that any game snaps for this still-developing Giants’ offense are good, valuable snaps. Provided, of course, nobody gets hurt.

summary: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know the day before the Giants play their last preseason game against the New York Jets. Albert Breer Empties His Giants Notebook From Training Camp | SI.com Jaxson’s Dart’s benefitting from an experienced, battle-hardened staff with Matt Nagy as coordinator, and Greg […]
full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know the day before the Giants play their last preseason game against the New York Jets. Albert Breer Empties His Giants Notebook From Training Camp | SI.com Jaxson’s Dart’s benefitting from an experienced, battle-hardened staff with Matt Nagy as coordinator, and Greg Roman, Brian Callahan, Willie Taggart and Tim Kelly as top lieutenants. One big difference for Dart: He’s going from one-word calls to longer, more-traditional West Coast verbiage, which has been both a challenge and, as he sees it, a benefit as he settles in for his second year. As Dart puts it, he needs to know the jobs of all 11 guys anyway, so having to run through everyone’s responsibility should give him more command of the offense. And yes, he’s aware that he needs to hit the deck quicker than he did a year ago, and he’s worked through tape with the coaches to better understand when he needs to prioritize living to see another down. As for Nagy, what’s really interesting to me is this is the first time he’ll get to focus on just being a play-caller—all of his previous experience calling an offense came as a head coach. John Harbaugh on the growth of Abdul Carter John Harbaugh gives Abdul Carter a resounding A+ for his performance on and off the field: pic.twitter.com/UzCGOf9Mgw — WFAN Sports Radio (@WFAN660) August 26, 2026 10 NFL players on roster bubbles going into the 2026 season | PFF RB Tyrone Tracy Jr., New York Giants. Tracy has operated as New York’s backup running back over the past two seasons, posting at least 740 rushing yards in every campaign with a cumulative 74.0 PFF rushing grade. However, he’s endured a shaky preseason, producing a 40.0 overall PFF grade thanks to allowing a sack (and big hit) on Jaxson Dart as well as fumbling in Week 2. Before the second preseason contest, the Giants signed Najee Harris as depth behind Cam Skattebo, complicating Tracy’s role in the team’s backfield. While Tracy could still make the roster if John Harbaugh elects to retain four running backs, his spot seems tenuous, especially with Devin Singletary (75.0 PFF receiving grade) also shining in August. Tyrone Tracy not dwelling on mistakes with changing Giants reality looming | New York Post Tyrone Tracy Jr. believes he can be a two-strike hitter. Guilty of committing one high-profile mistake in each of the first two Giants preseason games — a missed pass block that left Jaxson Dart vulnerable to a big hit and concussion check against the Vikings, plus an untouched red zone fumble against the Dolphins — Tracy is itching for his next opportunity rather than sulking about how quickly his two-year NFL résumé has been tarnished. NFL offensive rookies: Best and worst case for 17 players in 2026 | NFL.com WR Malachi Fields. Best-case scenario: Fields earns a starting job over Darius Slayton. The Notre Dame product uses his size (6-foot-4, 222 pounds) and strength to become a solid possession target capable of winning one-on-one battles in the red zone. Worst-case scenario: Despite a solid camp, Fields gets caught up in the glut of receivers behind Malik Nabers and fails to establish himself as a reliable, productive option during the season. Projected stats: 46 catches for 503 yards, 4 TDs. National media continues to be impressed by Arvell Reese View this post on Instagram CBS Sports NFL roster rankings 2026: Sorting the league’s bottom half from 32-17 | CBSSports.com 23. New York Giants. The bad: Defensive interior — With Dexter Lawrence II gone, Shelby Harris, DJ Reader and Darius Alexander are set to start on the interior. Remember, this Giants team allowed a league-high 5.3 yards per carry last season. The massive Reader was the most double-teamed player in the NFL last year, according to Next Gen Stats. He’s 32-years-old now, and didn’t record a sack in 2025. The Giants have been managing his workload, as they are with the 35-year-old Harris. Alexander, on the other hand, is the young buck at 25 years old, but has been far from a standout in the two preseason games. So, will this run defense be improved in 2026? The question: Quarterback — Jaxson Dart is a fun quarterback, but can he be a good quarterback? He became just the third rookie to ever throw 10 touchdowns while rushing for eight more scores, but he is also about to start paying rent to the blue medical tent. Apart from needing to play smart, Dart’s completion percentage also ranked outside the top 20 at 63.7%, and J.J. McCarthy and Spencer Rattler threw for more yards per game than Dart did. He’ll need to be better as a passer, but he is certainly capable. What Giants, Jets really think about living and playing in New Jersey | ESPN.com Perhaps the biggest surprise came when Giants rookie cornerback Colton Hood went to pump gas. New Jersey is the only remaining state where it is illegal to pump your own gas. That’s generally an eye-opener for those who have never been to the Garden State. “I was surprised. The dude came out and I don’t think he spoke English. He was just talking to me and I honestly couldn’t understand what he was saying. I’m just like, ‘Bro, I can pump my own gas. OK, bro!’ He was like, ‘No.’ I told him I can do it. I got it myself. title: Dennard Wilson: Consistency, confidence are key for Deonte Banks
summary: The biggest question regarding the New York Giants heading into 2026 has been whether their defense can rise above its dismal performances in 2024 and 2025. It was a bit of a surprise when the Giants hired former Tennessee Titans defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson when names like Jim Leonard or Wink Martindale were being bandied […]
full_text: Deonte Banks is one of the Giants in a competition for playing time. | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The biggest question regarding the New York Giants heading into 2026 has been whether their defense can rise above its dismal performances in 2024 and 2025. It was a bit of a surprise when the Giants hired former Tennessee Titans defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson when names like Jim Leonard or Wink Martindale were being bandied about. However, Wilson is both familiar with the “Ravens” style of defense and has a history of producing excellent secondaries. One of the prime concerns regarding the Giants’ roster was their defensive secondary. In particular, those on the outside were concerned about the cornerback position opposite Paulson Adebo . It was widely expected that Greg Newsome II would be the starting corner opposite Adebo, with rookie Colton Hood rotating in and eventually supplanting him. Instead, the Giants have rotated their starting corners with Adebo, Newsome, Deonte Banks , and Hood all getting reps with the starters. “Right now, I see a bunch of young men trying to get better,” Wilson said. “Every day they’re going out there and they’re competing against our offense. You’ve seen them in the games that we had in the preseason and in the preseason practice. They’re coming out there and trying to detail their work. Right now, everybody’s fighting to play, and I like where they’re all at.” One of the biggest surprises of camp has been that not only has Tae Banks gotten starting reps, he’s done well enough to be a consistent starter and bump Adebo down to more of a second team role. Banks was widely dismissed as a draft bust coming into the off-season, but has played with a level of confidence and physicality that we haven’t consistently seen since his rookie season. “I think he just has belief in himself right now,” Wilson said. “He [Banks] has a good group of DB coaches in that room that believe in him. The players believe in him, and he’s playing with confidence. He’s out there, he’s making the plays he’s supposed to make. He’s detailed on his assignments, being where he’s supposed to be, and that’s giving him an opportunity to make plays. As long as he keeps doing that, he’ll continue to get better.” “I think it’s a combination of everything,” Wilson continued, when asked what’s changed for Banks. “Just like anybody in life, if you believe in somebody and you have a group of people believing in a player, or if you have your own kids and you believe in your kids, they come out more inspired. It’s a little bit of that, and he’s taking the personal pride to play better, to be better on the field, to be more consistent. It’s a little bit of both, but I give the kudos to the young man. He’s really doing a great job of just trying to be the best version of himself.” Banks’ athletic ability has never been in question, and he has consistently produced tight coverage when allowed to play to his strengths. If the coaches now have him playing with the confidence and physicality to be the best version of himself, that could be a very good player. In addition to ‘confidence’, the other watchwords in Wilson’s remarks were ‘consistency’, ‘versatility’, and ‘accountability’. In fact, ‘accountability’ was the first word Wilson used to describe new MIKE linebacker Tremaine Edmunds . “He holds everybody accountable,” Wilson said. He’s vocal on the field. He brings a toughness, and he also brings a calmness to the defense. He’s a very intelligent player. He can make all the adjustments, and then when he lines up and plays, he runs and hits. Everything that he does in a pass game is good for us. He takes over the middle of the field because of height and size and instincts. We’re glad we have him, and we love that he’s here.” The combination of Edmunds and Arvell Reese could be a very interesting linebacker duo for the Giants. Likewise, Wilson also complemented the rise of versatile defensive lineman Chauncey Golston , who is pushing for a starting job in front of those linebackers. “For us, we look at our defense as positionless,” Wilson said. “The more you can do, the more opportunities you get to play. And Chauncey’s a very consistent player. He plays with great technique and detail, and you see it every day. Chauncey’s just like some of the other guys; we can move him around and put him in different spots.” Wilson taking the time to mention Edmunds’ ability in coverage and Golston’s versatility along the defensive front gives us a glimpse into Wilson’s defensive philosophy. He’s already mentioned being positionless, which implies that the defense will use versatile players to change looks on the fly. Not only does that create opportunities to scheme pressure, it allows the defense to dictate to the offense. Likewise, in mentioning Edmunds’ ability in coverage, it tells us a couple things about where the Giants are expecting to be attacked. There has been a recent trend for offenses to use play-action passes to attack the intermediate and middle areas of the field. That’s a departure from earlier eras of offensive football in which play-action fakes were used to set up deep passes. That’s one of the reasons why big safety hybrids, like Seattle’s Nick Emmanwori, have become such valuable assets. Wilson suggests that the presence of Edmunds and rookie WILL Arvell Reese can have a similar impact for the Giants. That also suggests that the structure of the Giants’ coverage shells will be designed to take away deep shots, leading to offenses trying to find explosives in the middle of the field, rather than against the secondary. “Some of the play-action passes, it’s hard for quarterbacks to throw it over top of them, especially when their eyes are right,” Wilson said, talking about Reese and Edmunds. “When they get their depth, they’re long. They’re big guys. So, it just clogs their windows. Both of them are very athletic in their zone drops. They do a great job of matching and taking windows away, and then ultimately, they have the athleticism to break on the ball. They have a unique trait or unique skillset, and it’s good for the New York Giants.”

title: NY Giants tales from the timeline: A dominant performance in Week 2
summary: The New York Giants have one preseason game left before the 53-man cutdown. Many players on the back end of the roster received ample playing time in the Giants’ 26-3 victory over the Miami Dolphins. Josh Ezeudu played 47 snaps for the Giants in Miami and was then traded to the Kansas City Chiefs for […]
full_text: The New York Giants have one preseason game left before the 53-man cutdown. Many players on the back end of the roster received ample playing time in the Giants’ 26-3 victory over the Miami Dolphins. Josh Ezeudu played 47 snaps for the Giants in Miami and was then traded to the Kansas City Chiefs for a 2028 seventh-round pick. Some possible starters received snaps, but most of the first-team rested. Nevertheless, we saw a Jameis Winston rushing touchdown, 81 J.C. Davis snaps, and a suffocating defense versus a Malik Willis-less — already bad — Dolphins’ offense. Here are some tales from the timeline after preseason Week 2. Defensive football! Arvell Reese played 10 snaps and continued to show his physical nature. He fit the WS B-Gap to blow the FB up at the LOS. The RB bounced and was tackled for a loss. pic.twitter.com/wwro9UhY5Y — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) August 23, 2026 Arvell Reese played 10 snaps for the Giants and showed his physicality against the Dolphins’ 21 personnel package; Reese took on the fullback at the line of scrimmage and created no rushing room in the B-Gap. Reese’s fit in the 4-hole to the weak side forced Jaylen Wright (5) into the arms of three Giants’ defenders. The upgrade at linebacker for the Giants will secure the continuity of the defense, which should inspire discipline and confidence. Tyler Nubin breaks on a seam ball from the deep half. He almost comes away with the interception. pic.twitter.com/mPLp5KJAVY — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) August 22, 2026 Tyler Nubin (27) breaks on a football just outside his opposite hash. New York ran Cover-2 third-and-10, and Nubin initially opened to his deep half responsibility, but quickly turned to almost intercept the seam pass. Tyler Nubin tied the Minnesota Golden Gophers’ interception record with 13 and has yet to secure a regular-season interception through two seasons. I love how Dru Phillips responded to the slot-fade he surrendered. Phillips with back-to-back impact plays to shut down the Dolphins offense. Phillips' physical nature is one thing that can't be denied. pic.twitter.com/cgUPWZmk9E — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) August 22, 2026 I like Dru. He was a good value for the #Giants . He'll have a role and be an asset in it. His presence will improve the overall run defense vs. 11 P. He's good around the LOS. It's not that he can't cover. He just has to win these 50/50s. He's there often, just not finishing. https://t.co/lYB9TvgdAH — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) August 23, 2026 Dennard Wilson is going to be FUN! 3rd & 11, and the #Giants loop McFadden (41) into the C w/ Dru (22) hitting the D (lol). The 4i takes the OT, leaving MIA vulnerable. Dru is best attacking, earns a FF. A good coach maximizes his players' traits. Dennard Wilson gets this. pic.twitter.com/WcDCJbXW6W — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) August 23, 2026 Dru Phillips (22) has always been effective around the line of scrimmage. He’s had 63 STOPs over his two-year career. He surrendered a 30-yard catch earlier in the drive above, but he bounced back by showcasing his strength. He does, though, need to get better in coverage to earn a larger snap share in Wilson’s scheme. Exceptional play by Greg Newsome II to keep his arm free and contain on the outside against this boundary jet-sweep. pic.twitter.com/yzmPTL8DV1 — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) August 23, 2026 Greg Newsome II (20) saw snaps for the Giants after missing preseason Week 1. He earned a PBU on the first drive and then had this excellent execution of contain defense on this boundary jet-sweep. Newsome II is in contention to start for the Giants agianst Dallas in Week 1. The rookie defensive lineman pushed the center back and remained disciplined; he kept the blocker at a distance with his extension, and he got his eyes on his target. Good patience and good finish. title: Giants sign TE Josiah Deguara and WR Kobe Prentice
summary: The New York Giants signed a pair of players to fill out their offense on Wednesday. The team announced Wednesday afternoon that they’ve signed tight end Josiah Deguara and wide receiver Kobe Prentice. Prentice, 22, was originally signed as an undrafted free agent out of Baylor by the Carolina Panthers after the 2026 NFL draft. […]
full_text: Tight end Josaih Deguara runs with the ball for the San Francisco 49ers. | Getty Images The New York Giants signed a pair of players to fill out their offense on Wednesday. The team announced Wednesday afternoon that they’ve signed tight end Josiah Deguara and wide receiver Kobe Prentice . Prentice, 22, was originally signed as an undrafted free agent out of Baylor by the Carolina Panthers after the 2026 NFL draft. He spent the first three years of his collegiate career playing for the Alabama Crimson Tide before transferring to Baylor for his final season in 2025. Prentice is an undersized but athletic receiver who will likely fill in for Calvin Austin III, who suffered a torn ACL in Tuesday’s practice. Standing just 5-foot-9, 184 pounds, Prentice is a bit bigger than Austin, though he isn’t quite as athletic as Austin. That said, Prentice has good speed (4.39-second 40-yard dash), explosiveness (36-inch vertical), and acceptable quickness (7.16 second 3-cone drill). Deguara, meanwhile, is an experienced tight end with “move” versatility . The 29-year-old was drafted by the Green Bay Packers out of Cincinnati in the third round of the 2020 NFL draft. Though Deguara’s rookie season was ended early by a torn ACL, he spent the next four years (2020-2023) with the Packers. He then played for the Jacksonville Jaguars (2024) and Arizona Cardinals (2025). He was signed by the San Francisco 49ers to a one-year deal in 2026, but was released on Aug. 24th. Deguara has played in 77 games with 12 starts, averaging 8.9 yards per catch and scoring 3 touchdowns. Prentice and Deguara likely take the roster spots opened by the trade of Joshua Ezeudu to the Kansas City Chiefs and the injury to Austin.

title: Scouting Jets edge defender Nate Lynn
summary: The Jets recently signed edge defender Nate Lynn, who has already made an impact in preseason. Today, we break Lynn down in detail. The 24-year old Lynn is listed at 6’3” and 256 pounds and was undrafted out of William & Mary in 2024. He is yet to make his NFL debut despite some solid […]
full_text: Aug 21, 2026; Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, USA; New York Jets defensive end Nate Lynn (92) sacks Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback Drew Allar (16) during the fourth quarter at Acrisure Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Charles LeClaire-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Jets recently signed edge defender Nate Lynn, who has already made an impact in preseason. Today, we break Lynn down in detail. The 24-year old Lynn is listed at 6’3” and 256 pounds and was undrafted out of William & Mary in 2024. He is yet to make his NFL debut despite some solid preseason performances following a decorated college career at the FCS level. Background Lynn was a zero-star recruit in high school despite always having been big for his size and adjusting well to playing against older competition. At the end of his high school career, he got offers from three schools and opted to attend William & Mary where he started off as a rotational lineman and registered 14 tackles with 1.5 tackles for loss in 12 games as a freshman. His second season was disrupted by the pandemic, as the Tribe only played three games in a truncated schedule. He had seven tackles with one for a loss and broke up a pass. 2021 was a breakout campaign for Lynn, who was named as a first team FCS all-American after racking up 52 tackles, 12 sacks and six forced fumbles in 10 games. In 2022, Lynn was productive again with 61 tackles, eight sacks and four forced fumbles. This time, he was a third team all-American. He finished up a career where he set several school records by recording 58 tackles and eight sacks in 2023, earning second team all-American honors. He was also a first team all-CAA selection in 2021, 2022 and 2023. Having not been invited to the combine, Lynn went undrafted, but the Detroit Lions picked him up as an undrafted free agent and he had a solid training camp. As preseason began, Lynn made an impact in his first game as he had a sack and initially was also credited with a strip sack, although the replay booth reversed this to an incomplete pass. Unfortunately, though, he suffered a season ending injury and had to spend the entire season on injured reserve. In his second season, Lynn was again productive in preseason with 11 tackles and a sack in four games, albeit mostly against backups. However, he was released in final cuts and not retained. The Titans added him to their practice squad after the bye week but never elevated him and, despite signing him to a futures deal after the season, they cut ties with him in April. The Jets signed Lynn just over a week ago, but he already made a big impact in his first appearance with them in preseason. Let’s move onto some more in-depth analysis of what Lynn brings to the table, based on in-depth research and film study. Measurables/Athleticism As noted, Lynn was big for his age as a youngster, but he was initially an interior defender at the collegiate level, a role he was undersized for. He has good size for an edge role at the NFL level, although he lacks ideal length. At his pro day, Lynn’s workout numbers were slightly below average for his size across the board. He ran a 4.85 in the 40-yard dash and posted 20 bench press reps along with underwhelming explosiveness and agility numbers. Usage As noted, Lynn started off on the interior, playing primarily as a defensive tackle or 3-4 defensive end during his first two seasons. He still lined up inside over the next three years, although his primary role was on the edge and by the end of his career he was playing almost exclusively outside. Motor Lynn brings aggressiveness and effort in the trenches and has proven capable of handling a starter’s workload by playing almost 700 snaps in 2022, including over 70 in two games. Here is an example of his hustle and effort in pursuit: Pass rush Lynn had a terrific pressure rate in college, along with a knack for finishing plays. Impressively, he’s also achieved the same kind of pressure rate in preseason action with four sacks in six games. He showcases good burst off the edge and displays an ability to dip and bend. However, he can also bring power as a bull rusher or on speed to power moves. Run defense Lynn has good strength to enable himself to hold his ground and set the edge in the running game. However, he can be controlled at the point of attack at times. His performance grades on analysis sites such as Pro Football Focus were excellent in college and, while they haven’t been as consistent in preseason action, he has been in on several run stops near the line. He has the ability to shoot gaps and beat blocks with his quickness but it will be important for him to show he can hold his ground on the edge and penetrate upfield when engaged with a tight end on stretch plays. Technique Lynn has a good first step but the key to his success is that he has good technique, based around patient and disciplined hand usage. He pulled off an impressive spin move on one of his two sacks in his first Jets game, but this wasn’t the first time he has done that at the NFL level. It’s a move he has also pulled off at times in college. Special teams In college, Lynn’s only role on special teams was rushing kicks and punts and he failed to generate any production within that role, while also being called for one penalty. At the pro level, he’s also blocked on the kickoff return units and covered kicks. He already shown a good knack for the latter as he’s been credited with a tackle three times in just eight plays. He showcased excellent physicality on this play from last week’s game. Tackling Lynn has an impressive knack for forcing fumbles as he had 10 in his career, including six in one season. He hasn’t managed to do this in any of his preseason appearances so far, although he did have one strip sack overturned by the replay booth. Missed tackles were a bit of a concern, as he had 25 in his last two college seasons combined. However, his missed tackle rate was much lower in his second season and he’s only missed one in preseason action. Coverage Dropping into coverage wasn’t something that Lynn was asked to do in college, although he did bat down a few passes at the line and was credited with a pass break-up. In the Jets game last week, Lynn dropped with a receiver on this incompletion and was right with his man even though this would perhaps be categorized as a drop. Instincts/Intelligence Lynn notes the importance of making pre-snap reads in terms of recognizing formations and also noted that in his pre-game preparation, he would study the usual drop depth of opposing quarterbacks so he knew what depth to aim for when rushing. He showcased his ability to make instant reads and react well on this short pass. However, he also jumped offside four times in his final college season. Lynn was praised for his good academics while in high school. Attitude/Demeanor From being a zero-star high school recruit, to the death of one of his former coaches and mentors, and then suffering a serious injury in the middle of a breakout debut preseason game, Lynn has had to deal with plenty of adversity to make it this far. He obviously has good toughness, determination and character, and was a team captain in his final season at William & Mary. On-field discipline wasn’t a concern early in his career, as Lynn had just one defensive penalty in his first three seasons. However, as his playing time increased, he had 12 in his final two years. Three of his penalties in his final season were personal fouls: Roughing the passer, unnecessary roughness and unsportsmanlike conduct. Injuries Lynn is now healthy having suffered a torn ligament in his shoulder two years ago that landed him on season-ending injured reserve. During that time, he still attended meetings and leaned on the veterans on the Lions’ defensive line to learn how better to look after his body. title: How will Frank Reich impact Garrett Wilson’s usage as Jets offensive coordinator?
summary: Zack Rosenblatt of The Athletic penned a glowing profile on first year Jets offensive coordinator Frank Reich. I would imagine quite a few first year coaches are having similar profiles written about them as training camp comes to a close. This is a period of great optimism in the NFL. Indeed, much of the article […]
full_text: New York Jets wide receiver Garrett Wilson (5) catches a pass during a preseason opening game between the New York Jets and Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Friday, Aug. 14, 2026, at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, NJ. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Zack Rosenblatt of The Athletic penned a glowing profile on first year Jets offensive coordinator Frank Reich. I would imagine quite a few first year coaches are having similar profiles written about them as training camp comes to a close. This is a period of great optimism in the NFL. Indeed, much of the article is generic praise for Reich. A few things stated by Jets wide receiver Garrett Wilson did stand out to me, though. Modern offenses, he says, have become overcomplicated, bright-eyed masterminds trying to show everyone how smart they are. Wilson thinks they sometimes fail to see what’s right in front of them. “With receivers like Terrell Owens, his coaches knew they had a special talent,” Wilson says. “We’re not going to overcomplicate it. It’s man coverage, let’s throw a fade to Terrell Owens. The last 10 years you’ve seen that fall off and it’s all about everyone’s plays.” To Wilson, early days with New York Jets offensive coordinator Frank Reich have felt like a blast from that past. Reich is coaching the kind of football Wilson always dreamed of playing. He felt it from their first conversation, when Reich had clearly already studied him, understood which routes and plays best suited his skill set, and shared his plan to deploy the star receiver. It’s awfully early to say that Reich is going to get more from Wilson than other coaches. I don’t consider Mike LaFleur, Nathaniel Hackett, or Todd Downing to be particularly brilliant offensive minds, and Wilson still produced 1,000 yard seasons playing for them. The Jets haven’t shown much so far in preseason. Their starters have only played two series on offense. I have started to detect one subtle trend in the play calling, though. Wilson has been on the field for five passing plays on third down. On four of these plays, the Jets have come out in a 3×1 formation with three eligible receivers on one side and a single receiver on the other. On each of these plays, Garrett Wilson has been the single isolated receiver on his side. Isolating Wilson gives him more room to operate. He’s more likely to get a one on one and less likely to get caught up in traffic, which allows him to feast on his route running. On early downs with the first team offense, the team has varied its formations. We haven’t seen much of Wilson isolated. They have saved it for the critical third down plays, the ones that decide whether a drive continues or ends. Of course this is a minuscule sample size. It is possible the Jets do things differently in the regular season. But there is plenty of logic in making this a third down staple. It puts the best receiver on the team in position to make plays on the most important downs.
