title: Eagles Training Camp Practice Notes: Some hints for the final preseason game?
summary: Wednesday marked the seventeenth and final Philadelphia Eagles training camp practice ahead of the 2026 NFL season. Here’s what I observed down at the Jefferson Health Training Complex! EAGLES PRACTICE NOTES UP NEXT: Here’s the upcoming schedule (all times listed Eastern):
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - JULY 30: Makai Lemon #9 of the Philadelphia Eagles looks on during training camp at Jefferson Health Training Complex on July 30, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images Wednesday marked the seventeenth and final Philadelphia Eagles training camp practice ahead of the 2026 NFL season. Here’s what I observed down at the Jefferson Health Training Complex! EAGLES PRACTICE NOTES The final practice of camp was a lighter one. No pads. EAGLES INJURY REPORT: DID NOT PARTICIPATE TE Eli Stowers (hamstring) OT Markel Bell (thumb/leg) TE Grant Calcaterra (back) CB Jakorian Bennett (knee) S Cole Wisniewski (concussion) LIMITED PARTICIPATION: CB Jonathan Jones (shoulder) Jones was upgraded to limited after missing a big portion of training camp. REMOVED FROM THE INJURY REPORT: OG Landon Dickerson (not injury related/rest) returned to practice after missing Tuesday night. Dickerson did look to be lumbering off the field after a rep in team drills while Drew Kendall came in for the next play. I don’t think Dickerson got newly injured as much as he’s just physically diminished to some extent. No one can question his toughness but I’m not feeling amazing about his chances of bouncing back to his Pro Bowl form. CB Mac McWilliams (shoulder) was upgraded from limited to full go. OT Lane Johnson, DT Jordan Davis, and TE E.J. Jenkins appeared to get banged up on Tuesday night but they were not listed on Wednesday’s injury report. Good to see. IN-PRACTICE INJURY (?) OG Willie Lampkin returned to practice on Tuesday after missing Monday with a stinger. Doesn’t seem like he’s 100%. Willie Lampkin just came off the field visibly frustrated and had a quick conversation with a trainer. He’s staying out here, but he’s stretching out his neck. He just came back from a stinger. #Eagles — EJ Smith (@EJSmith94) August 26, 2026 JALEN HURTS UPDATE: 7-on-7 red zone: A Hurts pass to DeVonta Smith on a curl route was broken up by Riq Woolen. Hurts sailed a pass to Dallas Goedert up the seam high and out of the back of the end zone. Hurts hit DeVonta over the middle for a touchdown. Hurts looked to Darius Cooper as a late read and threw high of him with Woolen smothering the receiver anyway to prevent any kind of jump ball opportunity. 11-on-11: Hurts had a couple good short completions to DeVonta and Hollywood Brown. He threw a pass towards the end zone into traffic that got knocked down by Quinyon Mitchell (Jihaad Campbell may have also tipped it first). Hurts overthrew DeVonta in the end zone. The passing offense as a whole looked out of sync at times. Hurts threw a pass to a crossing Johnny Mundt where the timing wasn’t there. BACKUP QUARTERBACK COMPETITION UPDATE: Tanner McKee has been doing a good deal of dink and dunk this summer and Wednesday was no different. There were a lot of short completions before he capped off a drive with a touchdown throw to Tank Bigsby, who got open as McKee rolled to the right. Seemed like McKee should’ve found him streaking open sooner but the result was ultimately good. McKee was slightly off target on some throws to Brandon Hayes ( who was released on Thursday morning ) before finishing camp with a touchdown pass to Erik Ezukanma to beat Shaun Wade in coverage. Andy Dalton had the most flashy completion of the day when he hit a crossing Stone Smartt in stride to beat really tight coverage from Michael Carter II. Dalton did throw a touchdown to Quez Watkins but it looked like Ty Robinson was in position to sack the quarterback from the interior. If practice is any indication, the Eagles are going to try to manufacture Lemon touches in this offense. They have yet to prove fruitful. But I expect the effort to get him involved early and often will be there. There was a rep on Wednesday where the Eagles only had 1o players on the field for offense. Lemon didn’t realize he was supposed to be out there and had to be called over by his teammates. The Eagles did some pre-practice and post-practice walkthrough periods that looked like the team preparing for Friday night’s game. Lemon took part in those, so, it’s looking like he might play (at least for a little bit) against the Cincinnati Bengals. McKee was also first up at quarterback in those periods with Dalton following him. Star of the summer Jalyx Hunt easily beat a Johnny Mundt block to be in position for a TFL on Saquon Barkley. Cam Latu had a really bad drop. Darius Cooper failed to make a grab on a Dalton ball that was thrown a bit high of him. It seemed like Andre’ Sam may have gotten a hand in there to break up the pass and tip it into the air for a Michael Carter II interception. Elijah Moore failed to make a contested grab while being covered by Ambry Thomas. Dameon Pierce has had some nice runs and a good catch since returning to practice. He’s missed too much time to make the roster but it could be good to keep him around on the practice squad. Shaun Wade got beat multiple times and also got called for defensive holding in the end zone. It’s been a very quiet offseason for the Eagles’ final pick in the 2026 NFL Draft, Keyshawn James-Newby. He’s missed a lot of time due to injury. But KJN flashed on Wednesday by being in position for a strip-sack on Dalton after beating Myles Hinton around the edge. Hinton’s stock is way down. Has not had a good summer. The Eagles ran a special teams scenario where Jake Elliott was lined up for a 60-yard kick and the field goal block unit was prepared for a return, with Will Shipley lined up deep in case of a miss that fell short. The ball was snapped but Elliott did not attempt a kick, with Braden Mann instead standing up from his holding position and chucking the ball downfield to Shipley. Kinda weird. Mann’s got a good arm, by the way. Training camp is over! Thanks for following along with our daily coverage here at BGN. If you’re new, we hope you stick around! If you’re not new, thanks for your continued support! Sorry for the delay in getting these notes published. I had to run around and get some things done prior to attending PHLY’s The Ospreys award show last night, where it was announced I’ll be joining their game day coverage programming this season! Excited to be doing Eagles pregame/postgame shows as part of their team. UP NEXT: Here’s the upcoming schedule (all times listed Eastern): Thursday, August 27 — Walkthrough closed to media access Friday, August 28 — Eagles vs. Bengals (8:00 PM start) Saturday, August 29 — Rest day Sunday, August 30 — 53-man roster cuts deadline at 6:00 PM

title: Vic Fangio’s perspective on why Jalen Hurts keeps throwing interceptions in training camp
summary: The Eagles had their final practice of training camp on Wednesday, and defensive coordinator Vu Fangio spoke to reporters before heading over to the field. He talked about battles for the final roster spots and why he enjoyed joint practices last week so much. Fangio also was asked about Jalen Hurts throwing so many interceptions […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - JULY 30: Philadelphia Eagles defensive coordinator Vic Fangio is shown during the Philadelphia Eagles training camp on July 30th, 2026 at Jefferson Health Training Complex in Philadelphia, PA. (Photo by Terence Lewis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Eagles had their final practice of training camp on Wednesday, and defensive coordinator Vu Fangio spoke to reporters before heading over to the field. He talked about battles for the final roster spots and why he enjoyed joint practices last week so much. Fangio also was asked about Jalen Hurts throwing so many interceptions this camp, and he explained that it was a good thing for the defense, but also isn’t something he’s worried about from the QB. “[Jalen Hurts is] learning a new offense. He’s trying things, seeing what’s available and what isn’t available. I don’t think that’s going to carry over [to the regular season].“ Here’s what else the DC had to say: On final roster decisions When asked if his mind is made up with the roster spots, he noted that players can still sway decisions on Friday night, but ultimately, it’ll be up to Howie Roseman and Nick Sirianni. The DC later noted that two guys who could benefit from the final preseason game are S Maximus Pulley and DB Kapena Gushiken. “Special teams does play a factor. The last few spots are always a story in and of itself. It might be a guy that’s not ready to play, and you might not think he’s ready to play the entire year, but you want him. Sometimes that happens. Sometimes it’s a guy that you think can help us in a pinch if we need it. As I said, special teams is a big thing. Just numbers, too. There’s minimal numbers you need at every position. You need five or six defensive linemen to make the roster. You need eight to nine outside backers and inside backers to make the roster minimum. The numbers is part of it also.” Fangio also admitted that the competition at safety between Marcus Epps and Michael Carter is still close. He noted that Carter is doing a good job, but it’s all still new to him and he needs more exposure and reps. Still, the DC does think Carter can eventually do the job. He also liked the depth Andre Sam provides at safety. “[Andre Sam] knows our defense from the safety position. He’s reliable in that regard. He’s trustworthy, and I think he’s a guy that will have a spot somewhere along the line, but we like him.“ He talked about being happy with the CB depth, saying he was comfortable with Quinyon Mitchell and Tariq Woolen, and he hopes to get Jonathan Jones back from injury soon. The DC said Mac McWilliams has made strides but is dealing with an injury of his own, and noted Kelee Ringo was also making strides. And then, they still have to fill the sixth CB spot. On Riq Woolen’s training camp “Overall, good. He’s had his moments where he can get a little sloppy. We need to eliminate those and hopefully once the regular season starts, that will happen. We like him. I like him a lot. I like the player. I like the person. I like being around him and I like coaching him.” Fangio later spoke about how Woolen has done well with adapting to the Eagles’ style of zone defense, and he’s continuing to get better at it. On DT Ty Robinson “Everybody’s a little different, but you see it every year — some guys, they’re struggling, struggling, struggling. Something happens that they’re able to turn the corner a little bit. It just so happened that it was [Ty Robinson] in the first preseason game, and he carried it over to last week. Hopefully, this will continue. Now, he’s got to be able to do it against the frontline players too.” Fangio later admitted that Robinson has likely solidified a spot among the defensive tackle rotation this season. On the Eagles-Patriots joint practices “I thought those two practices against the Patriots were our two most beneficial and valuable practices the entire year, entire camp. Just like I said before, it’s a different style offense, so that was great in and of itself. They have a good group of receivers that was good to go against. Way different offensive scheme than ours, great to go against. Those were two really, really good practices. We had, I think like 80 some plays the first day, 50 [or] 60 maybe the second day with a red zone focus. Fantastic practices.” On Jalyx Hunt Fangio was asked about Hunt and whether he’s exceeded expectations when they drafted him, and the DC said that his production is what they expected and hoped for, and now those expectations are even greater. “Am I surprised? Is this unexpected? That’s who [Jalyn Hunt] is.”

title: Eagles News: Za’Darius Smith reveals why he left Philadelphia last year
summary: Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … Za’Darius Smith retired last season to be with his mother before she died – PFTZa’Darius Smith’s retirement took the Eagles by surprise last season and the veteran outside linebacker explained the decision in his first press conference since coming out of retirement to join the […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MO - SEPTEMBER 14: Philadelphia Eagles defensive end Za'Darius Smith (52) before an NFL game between the Philadelphia Eagles and Kansas City Chiefs on September 14, 2025 at GEHA Field at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, MO. (Photo by Scott Winters/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … Za’Darius Smith retired last season to be with his mother before she died – PFT Za’Darius Smith’s retirement took the Eagles by surprise last season and the veteran outside linebacker explained the decision in his first press conference since coming out of retirement to join the Falcons. Smith said on Tuesday that family matters led to the decision to step away from the game because it was the only way he could be with his mother during a difficult time. “I wasn’t supposed to retire ,” Smith said. “I wasn’t going to tell the story, but I’m going to tell it. I got a phone call from my mom’s doctor telling me that she don’t have much longer to be on this Earth. I let the team know. Obviously they wasn’t trying to let me leave, but that was the only thing I had left — to retire. So I retired.” Eagles-Patriots Film Review: Ty Robinson showing signs of life! – BGN Robinson certainly showed signs of life against the Patriots. He finished with four tackles, two sacks, three tackles for loss, and three quarterback hits. Not bad! More importantly for me, though, was that the style of performance looked familiar. This was the version of Robinson we saw in college, which I will get into later. Before getting into Robinson’s performance, let’s start with Kelee Ringo. I was critical of Ringo after the opening preseason game because he remains one of the most frustrating players on the roster. The physical talent is obvious, but he has struggled to translate those traits into consistent play within this particular scheme. This was a better performance. Ringo makes an excellent play on the ball on the Patriots’ opening series, staying connected to the receiver and using his length and athleticism to contest the catch. If anything, I think he will be disappointed that he doesn’t pick this off because he has great hands. I am still not convinced everything will come together for Ringo in Fangio’s defense. Technical and processing issues keep popping up, and the fit has never looked completely natural to me. However, there is a capable NFL cornerback in there if he can become more consistent. The talent is too evident to dismiss. Which makes him even more frustrating… Eagles positional group review: Better or worse since the start of training camp? – PhillyVoice Jalen Hurts aside, the plan at QB2 is weird and confusing. Andy Dalton is not a QB2 anymore, and for some strange reason he has gotten significantly more reps with the second-team offense than Tanner McKee has this offseason. Clearly, the team thinks less of McKee than the fans and media do. If I had to guess, the Eagles’ QB2 this season will be McKee, and Dalton won’t be on the roster, whether he’s traded or outright cut. But who knows? Until that actually happens, Dalton is the QB2. Verdict: Worse 👎 (mainly because of the strange QB2 situation). Short Term vs Long Term – Iggles Blitz Eli Stowers is off to a slow start. That has some people questioning why Howie chose him, knowing this team had Super Bowl potential. Was adding a project a smart move? That is debatable. But Howie did this with his eyes wide open. He valued Stowers potential enough to make the move. Howie thinks Stowers can be an impact player that is a major factor for the Eagles in the future. We don’t know how much Stowers will be able to do this year. The problem with Stowers isn’t a lack of talent. He’s struggling because he is thinking too much. I’ve used this example before. Think about driving. You hop in a car and take off without doing much thinking. A 16-year old who is new has to think about every step. They lack experience. The veteran driver does things without even realizing what they are doing. It is more instinctive than thinking. Stowers is like the young driver. Things aren’t natural for him right now. He’s not able to take advantage of his natural ability. I think Stowers will overcome this. He’s stayed late to work on the JUGs machine. His effort on STs is good. His effort as a blocker has improved. Stowers is doing what he can to play better. The more reps he gets, the more natural he’ll play. He needs time, reps, and coaching. NFC East Preview: Is This the Cowboys’ Year? – The Ringer I think that the defense will carry this team to a bunch of wins early on, and the hope has to be that the offense can eventually find its footing and catch up. In some ways, this offseason has worked out great for Hurts’s standing among Eagles fans. They’ve rallied behind him after the Brown drama and will point out to any unsuspecting hater that Hurts balled out in both of his Super Bowl appearances and that the team has won 76 percent of the games he’s started over the past four seasons. He’s their guy, and they very badly want this new experiment to work. The biggest factor that will determine whether the Eagles are just a good team or a legit Super Bowl contender is the offensive line. There’s a scenario in which this group bounces back after a down season.[1] There’s also a scenario in which this group struggles in a new scheme without Stoutland pulling the strings and the 2026 Eagles end up looking a lot like the 2025 Eagles. Bottom line: The defense offers a high floor, and the offense will determine the Eagles’ ceiling. I still see enough talent here for another division crown. Projected record: 11-6. Eagles practice observations: Trending up and down at the completion of camp; cornerback greatness – Inquirer Trending down. Hollywood Brown. He’s probably on the 53-man roster, and may end up getting more playing time if Lemon needs developing. But Brown hasn’t popped like the speedster was expected to. He may need some time to adjust to a new scheme. Andy Dalton. The veteran quarterback didn’t ask to be traded here. That doesn’t excuse his spotty play in an offense he had experience with. But it’s hard to see why the Eagles felt it necessary to push McKee and cut into his repetitions in a new scheme. Maybe Dalton can turn it on at the end to win the job. Landon Dickerson. No one can deny the left guard’s toughness and what he’s already accomplished. He still has gas in the tank. But of the five starting O-linemen, he may not be an ideal fit in the new wide-zone blocking scheme. As for whether he can make it through the season, that is to be determined. An example of Dickerson’s sluggishness in the new scheme came on Wednesday when he was late to the second level and Campbell plugged Barkley. Jalen Hurts: ‘I’m in a good spot’ in new offense with season nearing – NBCSP Jalen Hurts has had to shoulder a lot this summer as the Eagles make a massive offensive shift to run a new scheme under new OC Sean Mannion. As training camp ended on Wednesday, where is Hurts’ command of this offense? “I feel like I’m in a good spot,” Hurts said after Day 17 of camp. “Feel like I’m in a good spot. It think it’s about really looking at the experiences. The experiences don’t mean anything until you reflect on them and grow from them and you start to apply them. So we’re very widespread in what we’re doing right now and I think that’s good. And so when we can hone it down and kind of see who we are, establish exactly what the identity is for us, it’ll come together. So still very early.” 2026 NFL season: Ranking all 32 teams’ watchability, excitement – ESPN 15) Philadelphia Eagles. When have the Nick Sirianni-led Eagles not been dramatic? When they’re good, running back Saquon Barkley has score-from-anywhere potential. Quarterback Jalen Hurts has a beautiful deep ball along the sideline, and receiver DeVonta Smith is a more-than-capable beneficiary of A.J. Brown’s departure.…

summary: Philadelphia Eagles owner Jeffrey Lurie (official title: “Chairman and CEO”) is being inducted into the Eagles Hall of Fame this season, according to a team announcement. Lurie will be formally honored at halftime of the Eagles’ Week 7 home game against the Dallas Cowboys on Monday Night Football. His statement: “Being selected to the Eagles […]
full_text: Feb 9, 2025; New Orleans, LA, USA; Philadelphia Eagles owner Jeffrey Lurie hoists the Vince Lombardi Trophy after defeating the Kansas City Chiefs in Super Bowl LIX at Ceasars Superdome. Mandatory Credit: Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn Images | USA TODAY Sports via Reuters Con Philadelphia Eagles owner Jeffrey Lurie (official title: “Chairman and CEO”) is being inducted into the Eagles Hall of Fame this season, according to a team announcement. Lurie will be formally honored at halftime of the Eagles’ Week 7 home game against the Dallas Cowboys on Monday Night Football. His statement: “Being selected to the Eagles Hall of Fame is one of the greatest honors of my life. It is truly rewarding to know that I will now join a distinguished group of legends who have all made significant contributions to this organization. From the very moment I became owner, I have been deeply committed to delivering a champion – both on and off the field – that our fans and city can be proud of. This franchise has given so much to me and my family over the past 32 years, and for that, I will be forever grateful. I would like to thank the selection committee for their support and am humbled that they felt I was deserving of this recognition.” There are a lot of bad owners in sports. Lurie is clearly not one of them. And the Eagles have two Super Bowl victories to evidence as much. While many owners will merely talk about their commitment to winning, Lurie has put his money where his mouth is … literally. The Eagles have been one the NFL’s top spending team during his time in Philly. In addition to seeing strong on-field results, the Eagles are very active in the community (see: the Eagles Autism Foundation, among many other initiatives). Lurie’s leadership is a huge reason why many Eagles fans can say they’re proud of their favorite football team and the success they’ve sustained for an extended period of time. It does seem kind of funny to be inducting yourself* into the team’s Hall of Fame that you own, but, hey, nobody can dispute that he deserves to be there. Lurie is one of the greatest figures in Eagles franchise history. Next stop: Canton, Ohio? *Note: Worth noting: There's a selection committee that determines who should be in the franchise's HOF. This wasn't Jeffrey naming himself into the HOF, specifically. (Although he is the owner, I doubt they would object.) Regardless, it's a worthy honor. Lurie changed the franchise… https://t.co/BG0acwe7BP — Zach Berman (@ZBerm) August 26, 2026

title: Why Jalen Milroe’s development isn’t over, but it’s becoming a concern
summary: A few days ago, I wrote about my expectations for Jalen Milroe entering the preseason. At the time, I thought the most realistic goal for the Seahawks’ second-year quarterback was fairly simple: close the gap on Drew Lock and make the competition for the QB2 job a legitimate one. So far, that hasn’t happened. The […]
full_text: A few days ago, I wrote about my expectations for Jalen Milroe entering the preseason. At the time, I thought the most realistic goal for the Seahawks’ second-year quarterback was fairly simple: close the gap on Drew Lock and make the competition for the QB2 job a legitimate one. So far, that hasn’t happened. The reports coming out of training camp were encouraging in one regard. The Seahawks believe in Milroe and remain invested in his development. At the same time, head coach Mike Macdonald and Brian Fleury has made it clear that Milroe needs to show more as a quarterback if he wants to earn opportunities in more situations. Through two preseason games, that hasn’t really changed. Against the Dallas Cowboys, Seattle’s offense struggled, but Lock still looked more comfortable than Milroe. Against the Tennessee Titans, the gap was significantly larger. Milroe had a terrible game, finishing with two interceptions and another sack on fourth down. Outside of a few runs, he produced very little offensively. That doesn’t mean the Seahawks should give up on the project. Two preseason games are not enough to make that kind of decision, especially with a quarterback as young as Milroe. Everyone knew when Seattle drafted him that he would need time to refine his game. A bad preseason doesn’t suddenly change that. But there is a difference between understanding that a young quarterback needs development and seeing whether that development is actually happening. And so far, even compared with more conservative expectations for where Milroe should be at this point, he appears to be behind. The biggest issue isn’t necessarily his arm. It’s his willingness to use it. Seattle has actually put Milroe in some of the situations that I thought would make the most sense for him. Rollouts, play-action concepts and plays that reduce the number of reads he has to make while keeping his ability to run as part of the equation. But Milroe hasn’t consistently pulled the trigger. Whether it’s a lack of confidence or simply an attempt to play as conservatively as possible and avoid turnovers, the result is the same. He’s passing up opportunities to make plays, both as a passer and as a runner. That was particularly evident against the Titans. On the first interception, Milroe takes too long to deliver the ball, allowing the linebacker to read his eyes and get into the passing lane. That’s the kind of mistake that can happen with a young quarterback, but it’s also exactly the type of processing issue he needs to improve. Jalen Milroes escapa da pressão, mas demora para passar a bola e claramente, sem sinergia com o WR manda o passe atrás e gera uma interceptação para acabar com o jogo. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-08-27T01:30:15.426Z On the second interception, Milroe escapes the initial pressure (which came from Beau Stephens), keeps moving and once again finds some space to make a play. However, he hesitates for too long before delivering the ball. There is clearly no chemistry between him and wide receiver Emmanuel Henderson, and the pass ends up behind the receiver, who falls and allows the defender to make the interception that effectively ends the game. On 4th down sack- No one is open;- Holding on Nick VannettBut… – THROW IT MAN! — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-08-27T01:23:51.033Z The fourth-down sack was arguably even more frustrating. Milroe escapes the pocket trying to get away from the pressure, but instead of creating more space, he moves toward the linebacker who is sitting in a spy position. That makes the sack increasingly imminent. And once that happens, Milroe has to understand that holding onto the ball at all costs isn’t the right answer. Throw it. Maybe the defensive back intercepts it and takes it the other way. Maybe Nick Vannett, who appeared to be held on the play, makes a contested catch and converts the fourth down. There are plenty of possible outcomes, including a turnover. The one thing that’s certain is that getting sacked on fourth down ends the possession. That’s part of the development Milroe needs. He doesn’t have to play recklessly, but he also can’t be so afraid of making a mistake that he stops giving himself opportunities to make plays. That’s particularly concerning because running the football has been his best contribution so far, and he rushed just once in the Titans game. If the passing window isn’t there, Milroe has the athletic ability to turn a broken play into positive yardage. But there have been too many moments when he hesitates to make that decision as well. The Seahawks can put him in favorable situations. They can simplify his reads. They can use his legs as a designed part of the offense. Eventually, though, Milroe has to pull the trigger. That’s why I still expect Seattle to give him significant playing time against the Kansas City Chiefs. Based on how the Seahawks approached the previous preseason finale against the Green Bay Packers, the plan seemed to be giving Milroe as many reps as possible and allowing him to work through these situations. After what happened against the Titans, however, it will be interesting to see whether Seattle sticks with that plan. None of this means Milroe’s career is over. Quarterbacks sometimes take much longer than expected to figure things out. Malik Willis, for example, had a career defined more by lows than highs early on, moving from the Titans and eventually around the league before getting an opportunity to show more with the Packers. That eventually helped him earn a significant contract with the Dolphins last year. Geno Smith is an even better reminder of how unpredictable quarterback development can be. After years of struggles and opportunities that didn’t work out, he eventually put together a solid season and changed the trajectory of his career. Sam Darnold followed a similar path. He entered the NFL as the No. 3 overall pick after a strong run at USC and was widely considered a legitimate franchise quarterback prospect. Things didn’t work out with the Jets, and his career went through Carolina and San Francisco before he eventually found stability with the Vikings and later the Seahawks. Milroe doesn’t have anything close to Darnold’s draft pedigree or the same level of hype coming out of college. But that’s not really the point. The point is that quarterbacks can develop late. Milroe’s second season is not going to determine whether he can become an NFL starter. There are too many variables between now and then, and the Seahawks aren’t going to make a final judgment based on a couple of preseason games. But the clock does start moving. Drew Lock’s contract is set to expire after this season, while Sam Darnold enters the final year of his deal in 2027. The Seahawks will eventually have to decide whether to extend Darnold, bring in another quarterback or address the position through the draft. Milroe will be part of that equation. And that’s why this preseason matters, even if it isn’t definitive. The goal was never for Milroe to become a finished quarterback in August. The goal was to see progress. The goal was to see him close the gap on Lock, become more comfortable operating the offense and show the Seahawks that the enormous physical talent they invested in can eventually translate into quarterback play. So far, he hasn’t done enough of that. There is still plenty of time to change the narrative. But Milroe needs to start showing the Seahawks why they should keep believing in the project.

title: 3 things we learned (and 1 big question) about Brian Fleury’s Seahawks offense
summary: Once Klint Kubiak took over as head coach of the Las Vegas Raiders this offseason, one of the biggest questions on the minds of Seattle Seahawks fans was how much change we’d see offensively with Brian Fleury taking over as coordinator. On the latest episode of the Sea Hawkers Podcast, Derek Coleman, a.k.a. “Coach DC”, […]
full_text: RENTON, WASHINGTON - JULY 25: Offensive Coordinator Brian Fleury of the Seattle Seahawks looks on during practice at Virginia Mason Athletic Center on July 25, 2026 in Renton, Washington. (Photo by Jack Compton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Once Klint Kubiak took over as head coach of the Las Vegas Raiders this offseason , one of the biggest questions on the minds of Seattle Seahawks fans was how much change we’d see offensively with Brian Fleury taking over as coordinator. On the latest episode of the Sea Hawkers Podcast , Derek Coleman, a.k.a. “ Coach DC ”, sat down to examine two preseason games and what early tape shows about Fleury’s offense versus the Super Bowl winning version Kubiak installed last year. For the full, detailed conversation tune into the video embedded below. Here are the biggest takeaways. 1. The Ace formation is back After Kubiak left, Coach DC wondered whether Seattle would keep it. The early film says yes. Kubiak’s 12-personnel “Ace” formation includes two tight ends and two receivers aligned in a balanced, mirrored 2-by-2 set. Same spacing and width to both sides. It was a highly effective formation from which to run play action. Fleury has already shown the formation, including multiple times in this past game against Tennessee. Continuity here matters and “Ace” remains a versatile, high-success package that fits this tight end room and stresses defenses the same way it did a year ago (at 12:02 in the video below) . 2. More running-back motion and shotgun option concepts One of the first things Coach DC noticed with Fleury’s offense was increased running-back motion just before the snap, a look more common in San Francisco. The back often motions toward the two-receiver side, forcing second-level defenders to widen and helps to open up throwing lanes underneath. Combined with it is a heavier diet of shotgun run concepts and option-style reads than last year’s under-center-heavy attack. The quarterbacks appear to be reading the edge or second-level defender. While Sam Darnold has the athleticism to keep it occasionally, as he showed in the Super Bowl, don’t expect high-volume quarterback runs. However, used sparingly, these wrinkles can help create some easy yards (4:06 below) . 3. The Seahawks offense looks like a Shanahan-Kubiak hybrid, not a reset Formations and run concepts overlap more than they diverge. During the show, Coach DC described a Venn diagram with a large shared middle. Play-action boot to the field after run action to the boundary is still there. Protection answers so far do not look locked into the rigid Shanahan style that got exploited in a Super Bowl loss to the Chiefs. It appears that retaining John Benton could be a key here, evolving around the same core principles while adding motion and shotgun options (10:46) . The thing remains unclear: How the ball gets distributed Expect a spotlight early on in the season as to how much Seattle’s tight ends are featured. Coach DC says AJ Barner could be a 70- to 75-catch player, with 6-10 touchdowns, as a featured pass catcher — approaching Trey McBride’s level of productivity. But Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Rashid Shaheed, Cooper Kupp, Tory Horton, a commitment to the run game, and an emerging Elijah Arroyo will all need touches, too. Considering the Shanahan tree likes to get the running back room involved more in the pass game as well, it’s more likely that Barner doesn’t get that high level of volume. Arroyo’s development as a blocker will also determine how often both tight ends stay on the field together. So the question remains: how many of those targets will exist over 17 games? Coach DC covers many other questions in the episode including losing Jake Bobo and Robbie Ouzts as chess pieces (21:42) , Jalen Milroe’s decision-making during his second preseason stint (7:48) , and additional details surrounding Fleury’s offensive formations (34:54) . Early tape suggests Fleury is keeping what worked and adding a few new tools. Check out the full discussion below.

title: Why Mason Richman is an overlooked Seahawks injury
summary: The Seattle Seahawks have taken some significant hits over the past week. Jake Bobo, a fan favorite who had carved out a meaningful role in Seattle’s receiver rotation, was placed on injured reserve with a torn ACL. Bud Clark, one of the team’s most intriguing defensive prospects, also landed on IR. Then there was Mason […]
full_text: SAN JOSE, CALIFORNIA - FEBRUARY 06: Mason Richman #78 of the Seattle Seahawks during a practice ahead of Super Bowl LX at San Jose State University on February 06, 2026 in San Jose, California. (Photo by Eakin Howard/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Seattle Seahawks have taken some significant hits over the past week. Jake Bobo, a fan favorite who had carved out a meaningful role in Seattle’s receiver rotation, was placed on injured reserve with a torn ACL . Bud Clark, one of the team’s most intriguing defensive prospects, also landed on IR . Then there was Mason Richman. Of the three, Richman is probably the loss that has received the least attention. That’s understandable. Richman was a seventh-round pick in 2025 and was never expected to walk into Seattle as a starter. But his development was becoming increasingly interesting, and his versatility was giving the Seahawks something that is difficult to replace. Mason Richman was quietly becoming valuable Richman played tackle at Iowa, but Seattle has been able to move him around the offensive line, giving him experience at tackle, guard and center, including work at center last season. That versatility was a major reason he remained on the roster. And there were clear signs of progress this preseason. Richman had been receiving positive feedback throughout camp, and his first two preseason games showed a player who was noticeably more advanced than he had been a year ago. The performances weren’t perfect, but the improvement was considerable, particularly in terms of his strength and technique. His development was also showing up in the run game. On power concepts, Richman was frequently used as a puller, where he was asked to execute important blocks at the second level. Those plays don’t necessarily mean a backup offensive lineman is about to become a starter. They do show, though, that the coaching staff was increasingly comfortable trusting him with meaningful assignments. That matters when you’re talking about offensive line depth. A player who can play multiple positions doesn’t have to start to provide real value. He gives the coaching staff flexibility when injuries happen and allows the team to carry fewer specialists on the active roster. Richman was becoming that type of player. Now he’s gone. The two trade candidates The Seahawks don’t have many offensive linemen who could realistically attract trade interest, but two names stand out: Olu Oluwatimi and Christian Haynes. Olu is the more obvious candidate. He has starting experience at center, which immediately gives him value to teams looking for help at the position. He’s also nearing the end of his contract, potentially making him an attractive short-term option for another team. And that’s important because you don’t trade a player just because you’re willing to move him. Another team has to see something in him. Olu has that selling point: he has started games at center in the NFL. That makes him a legitimate trade candidate. It also makes Seattle much less likely to want to move him. Haynes has a different argument. He hasn’t lived up to the expectations that came with being a third-round pick during his first seasons in Seattle. However, there have been signs of improvement this preseason. That could make him an intriguing reclamation project for another team. Haynes still has the physical tools and draft pedigree that could convince a different coaching staff that there is more to unlock. A different scheme or developmental environment could potentially put him in a better position to succeed. That makes both players realistic names to at least consider in trade discussions. But Richman’s injury makes moving either one much harder. Why Richman changes the equation Start with Olu. If Seattle trades him, the center depth becomes extremely thin. After Jalen Sundell, the obvious remaining option is Federico Maranges. And what we’ve seen from Maranges this preseason hasn’t exactly provided much confidence that he is ready to step into a larger role. Richman potentially offered another option because he had already been getting work at center. Now that option is gone. Beau Stephens and Bryce Cabeldue don’t appear to provide an immediate solution either. Stephens is still a rookie, while Cabeldue has fallen considerably down the depth chart. More importantly, neither has been getting the kind of center work that would give Seattle confidence in using them as emergency options there. That makes an Olu trade extremely difficult to justify. The situation with Haynes is slightly different. Trading him would leave Seattle with Stephens and Cabeldue as the primary guard depth behind the starters. That’s not necessarily impossible, but it’s a much bigger gamble than it would have been with Richman available. The Seahawks could have felt better about moving Haynes if another player on the depth chart had been developing at center or showing enough positional versatility to cover multiple spots. Richman was the player closest to providing that insurance. His injury removes that possibility. Final Thoughts Mason Richman wasn’t a starter. He wasn’t a high draft pick. But he was becoming a valuable piece of Seattle’s offensive line depth precisely because he could do things that the players around him couldn’t. He could play tackle, guard and center. He was improving. And the Seahawks were beginning to trust him with important assignments in the run game. That versatility gave Seattle options. Now it doesn’t. Oluwatimi may have enough value to attract a trade offer because of his starting experience at center. Haynes may attract interest from a team that believes it can unlock more from a former third-round pick. But the Seahawks have to consider what happens after the trade. Move Olu, and the center depth becomes Federico Maranges. Move Haynes, and the guard depth becomes Stephens and Cabeldue. Neither scenario looks particularly comfortable. That’s why Richman’s injury may matter more than the player’s role on the depth chart would suggest. The Seahawks didn’t lose a starter. They lost flexibility — and in a roster where trade options are already limited, that could prove to be the bigger loss.

title: NFL, NFLPA announce new 1-game suspension rule for repeat on-field offenders
summary: With every new season comes a new focus around the officiating of games, from revised rules around lowering the crown of the helmet to pass interference calls. Ahead of the 2026 season, the NFL and NFLPA have agreed to five new points of emphasis around the health and safety of the game, as well as […]
full_text: SEATTLE - SEPTEMBER 23: A penalty flag lies on the field during the Seattle Seahawks game against the Cincinnati Bengals at Qwest Field on September 23, 2007 in Seattle, Washington. The Seahawks won 24-21. (Photo by Otto Greule Jr/Getty Images) | Getty Images With every new season comes a new focus around the officiating of games, from revised rules around lowering the crown of the helmet to pass interference calls. Ahead of the 2026 season, the NFL and NFLPA have agreed to five new points of emphasis around the health and safety of the game, as well as clearly defined penalties around any offenses. The points of emphasis as announced by the league and its players association on Wednesday are: -Hip Drop Tackle -Horse Collar Tackle -Launching -Hit on a Defenseless Player -Blindside Block The hip drop tackle, in particular, has been a major topic in recent years as it has continued to lead to serious injury. Last season, Commanders linebacker Frankie Luvu received a ( later rescinded ) one-game suspension for repeated hip-drop infractions, the last of which was one on the Seahawks’ Jaxon Smith-Njigba. According to Wednesday’s announcement, players who commit three offenses in any of the five points of emphasis will receive a one-game suspension. Players who commit only one violation will receive half of their fine back at the end of the season. Another big note is that violations will carry over season-to-season. All players, however, will begin the 2026 season with no previous violations.

title: What incoming Seahawks owner Vinod Khosla said in his first press conference
summary: The Seattle Seahawks are just about at the finish line as far as transitioning franchise ownership from the Allen family to the Khosla family. In a special league meeting in Atlanta on Wednesday, NFL owners unanimously approved the Khoslas as the next owners of the reigning Super Bowl champion. While the $9.612 billion sale is […]
full_text: Toronto , Canada - 18 June 2024; Vinod Khosla, Founder, Khosla Ventures, backstage of Centre Stage during day one of Collision 2024 at the Enercare Centre in Toronto, Canada. (Photo By Vaughn Ridley/Sportsfile for Collision via Getty Images) | Sportsfile via Getty Images The Seattle Seahawks are just about at the finish line as far as transitioning franchise ownership from the Allen family to the Khosla family. In a special league meeting in Atlanta on Wednesday, NFL owners unanimously approved the Khoslas as the next owners of the reigning Super Bowl champion . While the $9.612 billion sale is not expected to close until early September, a press conference was still held to introduce the would-be new owners, which includes Sun Microsystems co-founder and venture capitalist Vinod Khosla, his wife and would-be controlling owner, Neeru, and their son, Neal. Their daughter, Nina, was also part of the event. Here’s what was said in the first presser! We’ll presumably get a press conference again when the sale is closed and they’re inside the VMAC building. Vinod Khosla’s opening statement “It’s a great honor to be here. I do want to start by thanking Jody Allen and the Allen Trust for trusting us with this franchise. Roger has been incredibly helpful, and the NFL staff has been incredibly helpful in getting here. As Roger said, it’s pretty simple when the team is functioning as well as it is today. How often do you get to buy a franchise that just won the Super Bowl? So, we are incredibly lucky and humbled by this gift, I would say, from the Allen Trust. “Having been to Lumen Field and watching the 12s everywhere, I do want to thank them for their passion and fervor, and the community in Seattle is incredibly valuable, so we hope to engage a lot more with the community also. “The task ahead is actually pretty simple: keep the winning streak alive, get another Super Bowl. That’s simple. In general, our approach is generally going to be long-term focused, that’s our inclination always. So, keep winning, take a long-term approach, and learn a lot. We don’t know enough, and the other owners have been incredibly welcoming and willing to teach us, so we’ll learn a lot. We’ll learn from management and see what they are recommending. So we’ll just be in learning mode for quite some time.” The Khosla family’s ties to the San Francisco 49ers, football fandom Vinod Khosla : “Well, we are huge fans of football and these opportunities, especially Super Bowl winning teams, seldom come along. So, we were very excited to have the opportunity and I’ve been tied to the Seattle tech community for a long time and so it was pretty easy to make the jump.” Neeru Khosla : “To add to that, if I might add to that, see that guy on my left? Not this one, [our son Neal Khosla]. He’s been a big fan of sports and in particular football. So he’s wanted forever to get involved in in actually strategizing and kind of doing something about that. So he’s the one who actually really pushed us into doing this. He’s worked really hard. So I’m very proud of him.” Vinod Khosla : “We’ve been very passionate about football for a long time. I would say we’ve been going to home games at the 49ers since [he was] five. Maybe half of all home games since he was five. And so football is definitely a passion. “I also happened to come to this country in ‘76 when the Steelers were winning the Super Bowl. So actually I was originally and still am a big Steelers fan also. Little known fact, but I still watch all the Steelers games, too.” Vinod Khosla’s message to Seahawks fans “I just want to say a big thank you for being such a passionate fanbase. It’s actually pretty incredible, it’s the best fanbase in the country of any NFL team. The 12s are such an iconic brand, it’s hard to not be honored and humbled by inheriting that and being part of that fanbase.” Vinod Khosla on the future of Lumen Field “Well, first, Lumen Field is iconic and very much a part of the Seahawks brand. “So, that’s all I will say for now. Obviously we are not owners yet and we need to learn a lot more but we will work with management and with others, and the community in Seattle to hopefully preserve this iconic brand.” Watch the full video below! Video And yes, by the way, he is active on social media. Super excited to join 12’s everywhere and the Seattle community and winning another Super Bowl!!! https://t.co/ZXs8g1wavP — Vinod Khosla (@vkhosla) August 26, 2026

title: Kenneth Walker III dealing with swollen ankle, won’t play Friday against Seahawks

Kansas City Chiefs head coach Andy Reid announced Walker III is dealing with […]
full_text: Former Seattle Seahawks running back and 2025 Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker III opted for the big money from the Kansas City Chiefs this offseason , but any thought of him facing off against his old team this week appears to be shelved. Kansas City Chiefs head coach Andy Reid announced Walker III is dealing with a swollen ankle and will not play in the team’s preseason finale at home against Seattle on August 28. Andy Reid said Patrick Mahomes, Josh Simmons, Jack Cochrane, Ashton Gillotte, Jimmy Holiday, Chris Oladukon & CJ Hanson will not play Friday against the Seahawks. Garrett Nussmeier will start. Reid said Kenneth Walker III has a swollen ankle. — Nate Taylor (@ByNateTaylor) August 26, 2026 Although Walker III has been a non-participant in the Chiefs last two practices, Reid added the swelling was merely due to his cleat and he is not expected to be sidelined long-term. Star quarterback Patrick Mahomes and 2025 first-round pick Josh Simmons are among other starters being held out, so it’s not likely that Walker would have played anyway, although Reid has not completely ruled out some starters like Xavier Worthy and Rashee Rice getting game time. “I’m going to evaluate it in the next couple of days,” Reid said (via Arrowhead Pride ). “They’ve worked their tails off this week and have taken a lot of reps, so that’s been good for them. full_text: SAN FRANCISCO, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 28: Vinod Khosla, Founder of Khosla Ventures, speaks onstage during TechCrunch Disrupt 2024 Day 1 at Moscone Center on October 28, 2024 in San Francisco, California. (Photo by Kimberly White/Getty Images for TechCrunch) | Getty Images for TechCrunch The Seattle Seahawks are one step closer to having new ownership. Over a month after an agreement was reached with the Khosla family to purchase the Super Bowl champions for a league record $9.612 billion, franchise owners voted to approve the sale. A three-quarters majority (or 24 out of 32 possible votes) was needed for ratification and they received a unanimous vote. The Khoslas have been unanimously approved as the new owners of the Seattle Seahawks https://t.co/YQ89ZSJGYV — Jonathan Jones (@jjones9) August 26, 2026 While Sun Microsystems co-founder Vinod Khosla is the face of the ownership group, his wife Neeru would serve as the controlling owner. In a matter of days, the Seahawks’ 30-year span of ownership of Paul Allen and later the Paul G. Allen trust (led by Paul’s sister Jody) will come to an end. If not for Paul, Seattle would probably not have an NFL team right now, much less a two-time Super Bowl champion. It was Paul’s directive to sell his assets and donate the proceedings to philanthropic causes, so the sale was bound to happen. In the eight years since Paul’s passing, Jody has navigated through some (comparatively speaking) rougher seasons without playoff wins to end the era of Allen ownership on the highest of high notes. More is expected to be revealed soon, and Field Gulls will have updates either within this article or a new one.

full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - FEBRUARY 11: Fred Warner #54 of the San Francisco 49ers celebrates a defensive stop with Dre Greenlaw #57 during the first half against the Kansas City Chiefs during Super Bowl LVIII at Allegiant Stadium on February 11, 2024 in Las Vegas, Nevada. We’re two years removed from a 2023 season that was one of the most aesthetically pleasing years of any team in the NFL. Everything came easy offensively. Kyle Shanahan is hoping that’s Brock Purdy’s life in 2026. It’ll be the best supporting cast for Purdy since ‘23. He has a legitimate WR1. And unlike in years past, Purdy has a pair of wide receivers who thrive in contested situations. The depth in the backfield should make Christian McCaffrey better. Kaelon Black and Jordan James should be sneaky good contributors, and not just in 2026. If the 49ers can find a left guard who can hold his own, the offense has a chance to be special. ESPN’s Benjamin Solak compiled a watchability list , ranking every team based on quality offenses, star players, competitive games, and explosive plays. Surprisingly, the 49ers checked in low on the list. They were 20th, one spot below the Colts and one spot in front of the Panthers: The 49ers under coach Kyle Shanahan — so long as the offense is decently healthy — have always been pleasantly view-worthy. Even a quarterback injury can’t slow Shanahan down — those early-season Mac Jones games in 2025 were hilariously fun. Even as running back Christian McCaffrey , now 30, diminishes in athleticism and tight end George Kittle returns from a right Achilles tear , I’ll believe in a bad 49ers offense only when I see it, and not a moment before. San Francisco played in only six one-score games last season — fewer than any other team — thanks in large part to a porous defense that was among the bottom 10 in most metrics. Fortunately for the Niners, bad defense and good offense can make for surprisingly watchable games. Take their Week 16 primetime game against the Colts in December. It was the only watchable Philip Rivers game after he came out of retirement to be Indianapolis’ quarterback at 44 years old … and it was because the 49ers’ defense was shaky enough to make it so. The 49ers should be healthier on both sides of the ball this season, so they might just be a boring version of pleasantly good. But 25% of their games are against NFC West rivals, the Rams and Seahawks, and those contests always deliver. If August has taught us anything, it’s that the 49ers will not be boring. The defense will be somewhat of a wildcard. The front four will be the deepest it’s been in some time. Osa Odighizuwa is still a move that is flying under the radar — Solak didn’t even mention him. Role players like Sam Okuayinonu and Keion White won’t need to be overextended. Having your two best players, Nick Bosa and Fred Warner, takes pressure off the other nine players on the field.

title: Brock Purdy labeled as ‘supporting cast dependent’ in latest QB tier rankings
summary: When it comes to quarterback rankings, San Francisco 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy hasn’t always gotten the respect he deserves. Entering the fifth year of his NFL career, Purdy remains a fringe top-10 quarterback who has continued to elevate his game with his athleticism and propensity for extending plays. He remains a high-quality anticipator, his efficiency […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - AUGUST 20: Brock Purdy #13 of the San Francisco 49ers warms up before the preseason game against the Los Angeles Chargers at SoFi Stadium on August 20, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Luke Hales/Getty Images) | Getty Images When it comes to quarterback rankings, San Francisco 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy hasn’t always gotten the respect he deserves. Entering the fifth year of his NFL career, Purdy remains a fringe top-10 quarterback who has continued to elevate his game with his athleticism and propensity for extending plays. He remains a high-quality anticipator, his efficiency metrics in Kyle Shanahan’s system continue to stand out, and his sack avoidance has become even better. Now, there are obviously still some flaws in his game, namely his propensity for turnover-worthy plays (41 turnovers in 49 career games), but Purdy has shown he can elevate the 49ers offense, even when the supporting cast isn’t as strong (see: 2025 season). Still, in controversial NFL analyst Steven Ruiz’s rankings , Purdy was labeled as a “supporting-cast dependent” quarterback in a tier that includes eight other quarterbacks. Ruiz had three quarterbacks in his “elite” tier: Patrick Mahomes, Josh Allen, and Lamar Jackson. Another five made his “franchise carriers” tier: Matthew Stafford, Joe Burrow, Drake Maye, Dak Prescott, and Justin Herbert. The following tier, “on the doorstep”, consisted of four more quarterbacks: Caleb Williams, Trevor Lawrence, C.J. Stroud, and Jordan Love. Purdy fell into the tier after that, which also included Sam Darnold, Jared Goff, Kyler Murray, Jayden Daniels, Jalen Hurts, Baker Mayfield, Bo Nix, and Daniel Jones. What’s the definition of being in this tier? “This group can produce like top-10 quarterbacks provided the conditions around them are just right,” Ruiz wrote. “Some in this group require pristine pass protection. Others need an innovative play-caller or a stacked receiving corps. But when those needs aren’t met, they play more like bottom-10 quarterbacks. This is the middle class of NFL passers. “The fanbases for these quarterbacks are all thinking the same thing: Why is my guy lumped in with these scrubs?” For Goff, he mentioned the inability to handle pressure. For Murray and Daniels, it’s health-related. Then, there are the three quarterbacks who have made a Super Bowl: Darnold, Hurts, and Purdy. “This tier also includes three quarterbacks who have played in a Super Bowl, and two of them have won it,” Ruiz said. “Sam Darnold is the defending Super Bowl champ, and he’s coming off a clean postseason run, but he also led the NFL in turnovers last season. Jalen Hurts has led mediocre passing games in three consecutive seasons despite a wealth of surrounding talent. And Brock Purdy has battled injuries and inconsistency since breaking out in 2022 with a superstar supporting cast and Kyle Shanahan calling the plays.” Now, detractors of Purdy can point to his injury history. He has dealt with a UCL tear, a shoulder/oblique injury (that didn’t cost him any games), and turf toe throughout his NFL career. But last season was truly the first year where he missed substantial time, as Purdy played in 16 and 15 games in 2023 and 2024, respectively. Purdy’s interception rate is the main detractor in his game, as he had four multi-interception games last season, while throwing one in eight of his 11 games played. But he proved last year that he could produce even without a strong supporting cast. Due to injuries, Purdy was throwing to a receiving core that included Demarcus Robinson and Kendrick Bourne as starters for parts of the year. At the moment, it feels like Purdy is just outside or right near the Top 10 conversation, but he has continued to level up his game while still having some of those head-scratching moments.
author: Rohan Chakravarthi

title: 49ers 53-man rundown: Will there be any bold moves on cutdown day?
summary: The San Francisco 49ers’ final roster cuts will be here in the blink of an eye. Most roster spots are locked up. However, there are still positions that need weeding out for the preseason finale. The Niners will use Thursday night’s game to determine whether any of the players fighting for a roster spot can […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - JULY 27: James Thompson Jr. #75 of the San Francisco 49ers works out during training camp practice at SAP Performance Facility on July 27, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers’ final roster cuts will be here in the blink of an eye. Most roster spots are locked up. However, there are still positions that need weeding out for the preseason finale. The Niners will use Thursday night’s game to determine whether any of the players fighting for a roster spot can contribute to their roster, whether it’s the final 53 or the practice squad. Today, we’ll walk through each position to determine if there will be any bold moves by the 49ers. Quarterback Kurtis Rourke won’t play in the preseason finale. Does that mean Mac Jones sees an extended run? Probably not. The team isn’t going to risk an injury to their backup — Jones could field trade offers during the first half of the season — behind backup offensive linemen. Teams like the Falcons have to be keeping tabs on Jones. The 49ers know that. We asked you whether the 49ers can afford to keep three quarterbacks . My answer is an easy yes. I don’t think that’s a bold prediction. Maybe Mac plays the first quarter, and Adrian Martinez takes over for the final three quarters. That would be unfortunate for the receivers. Verdict: No bold moves, keep three quarterbacks. You can always place Rourke on the short-term Injured Reserve if you need to keep him, but he isn’t going anywhere. Running back The 49ers won’t have to do any roster gymnastics at running back, thanks to Christian McCaffrey and Jordan James returning to practice. Kaelon Black showed plenty of promise in his preseason debut. James and Black should get carries on Thursday. James might get a longer look since he missed so much of August. It’ll be a good opportunity for both players to get enough work in without overdoing it. I’d like to see Black and James work in tandem in the first half, with Sincere McCormick and Khalil Herbert taking over in the second half. Verdict: No surprises when it comes time for cuts. McCaffrey, Black, James, and Kyle Juszczyk. The team can elevate Sincere McCormick from the practice squad on game day if need be, while the Isaac Guerendo experiment either ends or he lands on the Injured Reserve. Wide Receiver No Mike Evans or Jacob Cowing tonight, as both recover from groin injuries. The 49ers social media team had a video of Cowing on Wednesday. He’s making the roster. There’s also no need to play Deebo Samuel, De’Zhaun Stribling — although he could use the reps — and Demarcus Robinson. Those are the five receivers with seats on a plane to Australia. Christian Kirk is an Injured Reserve candidate. Jordan Watkins can return, but he only covered kicks in the second preseason game. Tonight, he’ll have to make the difficult plays on offense and perhaps do a little bit of everything on special teams to stick around. Verdict: I think the mildly bold move is to roll with five receivers. Use your practice squad elevations if you need a special teamer. But realistically, Watkins isn’t going to contribute on offense. If the 49ers are hovering at or below .500 around Thanksgiving, it won’t be because they waived Watkins in August. It’ll allow the team to bulk up in the trenches. Tight End George Kittle returning changes everything. You don’t have to roster a player who is either inexperienced or untrustworthy. Instead of using a platoon rotation between Jake Tonges and Luke Farrell, they stay in their respective roles. It may take a couple of weeks for Kittle to get into football shape, but defenses will be forced to play him 1-on-1, and the run game will benefit from having Kittle in the game, which will do wonders for the offense. Verdict: Only three tight ends. Nothing to see here. Offensive line Dominick Puni re-entered the concussion protocol. Austin Pleasants (knee) and Robert Jones (unspecified) will make the trip to Australia. That was Kyle Shanahan’s way of telling us they’ll make the roster. Brett Toth has had a concussion since the first week of August. What do the 49ers do with that? Vederian Lowe will likely begin the season on the Injured Reserve. Pleasants makes the team as the swing tackle, with Jones, Carver Willis, and Puni as the guards. Willis will play tonight because he needs as much exposure as he can get ahead of Week 1. Reps are gold for Willis. Verdict: The 49ers keeping Enrique Cruz and Connor Colby wouldn’t be surprising due to the uncertainty along the line. But the bold move here would be to part ways with both and upgrade on the waiver wire. Defensive line It seems like after every practice you hear something about James Thompson making a play or impressing in some capacity. At his size, with his quickness, I doubt the Niners risk losing him. My bold prediction for this group is CJ West outplays Alfred Collins this year. West is the ideal run stopper this defense needs. The defensive tackle group has a chance to be as good as it’s been in several years — especially if Gracen Halton performs as he did in the preseason. Sebastian Valdez and Bryson Eason are battling to make the roster tonight. It’s difficult to imagine any of the edge rushers taking a spot, though. Verdict: The number of vested veterans you can do a handshake deal with and release on cutdown day to keep a young player like Eason or Valdez makes sense. The bold move would be to keep both. A lot like the offensive line, the 49ers may find a better option at edge rusher, with Mykel Williams starting on the PUP, after other teams make their cuts. Edge rusher is another spot where the answer may not be on the roster. Linebacker Fred Warner, Dre Greenlaw, and Jaden Dugger are going to start. Dugger quickly leapfrogged Nick Martin, who still looks a little lost, but will make the roster after making a splash play on special teams in the second preseason game. Tatum Bethune and Luke Gifford are your special teamers, and that’s the linebacker room. Verdict: The bold move here would be to part ways with Gifford and roll with one of the young linebackers to complete the youth movement. Unlikely, but it’s an idea. Expect Garret Wallow and Larry Worth III to land on the practice squad, with Wallow getting the call on game days for special teams purposes. Defensive backs Renardo Green’s injury is the only concern for this group. If his hamstring lingers into the regular season, it means Jack Jones will start. Jones starting will be entertaining. One series you’ll love him. The next you’ll be begging for Green. Deommodore Lenoir and Upton Stout are the other starters, with Ephesians Prysock being the final cornerback. There’s no argument for Nate Hobbs, as he hasn’t played. Perhaps he’s an Injured Reserve candidate. Green isn’t the only starter with a hamstring concern. We haven’t seen Malik Mustapha in the preseason. There is no competition anymore at safety because of it. That means the 49ers enter 2026 with Marques Sigle and Ji’Ayir Brown penciled in at safety, with Ashtyn Davis covering kicks. It goes without saying that this unit can stand to upgrade, but where are those coming from? These are positions where you either draft well at or spend big in free agency. Verdict: No surprises in August, but a bold move would be to make a splash ahead of the deadline for a corner or a safety. My read is that the 49ers are banking on their defensive line to do much of the heavy lifting this season.

title: NFL and NFLPA just handed refs a loaded three-strike rule
summary: NFL officiating crews now have even more (subjective) power to determine game outcomes and—to a greater extent—a season. The NFL and NFLPA made a joint statement Wednesday, saying players who commit three of the violations below in a season will be suspended one game: This is not a combination, from what it says. Basically, a […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA - AUGUST 13: A flag is thrown during a preseason game between the New England Patriots and the Indianapolis Colts on August 13, 2026, at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Fred Kfoury III/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images NFL officiating crews now have even more (subjective) power to determine game outcomes and—to a greater extent—a season. The NFL and NFLPA made a joint statement Wednesday , saying players who commit three of the violations below in a season will be suspended one game: Hip Drop Tackle Horse Collar Tackle Launching Hit on a Defenseless Player Blindside Block This is not a combination, from what it says. Basically, a player has to commit three blindside blocks to get the suspension, not two blindside blocks and a launch. That said, this is extremely dangerous and subjective (not to mention unclear) for how these penalties are checked off as strikes. It’s not clear if players need to be flagged for the strike to occur. It’s also not clear if an incorrect call made during a game is an automatic strike or is lifted the week after the game. Hip drop tackles, horse collars, and launching are self-explanatory. Where it gets murky is the hit on a defenseless player and the blindside blocks. The former has numerous plays called incorrectly because of the speed of the game, and no fines are handed out as a result. The latter is a bit more solid, but it still leaves a lot of subjectivity in what is or isn’t a blindside block. The bigger issue is when three egregious calls stack up on one player, and they get suspended. This is more concerning for running quarterbacks who have taken advantage of the rules in the past and can now get a player suspended by baiting them into it. Then there’s timing. Three flags in a season is fine—problem is, what are we classifying as a season? Is it the regular season, with players having a clean slate in the playoffs? What happens if a safety has two hits on a defenseless player in the regular season, then commits it during an AFC/NFC Championship game? Are they suspended for the Super Bowl? What about regulating whether the call was correct on the field? Can we trust the NFL to vet these after the fact given what’s at stake? Here’s another situation to consider: Let’s say an NFC East team contending for a playoff spot is playing against a down-and-out AFC team playing for a draft pick. The next game the NFC East team has is a divisional game; unfortunately, during their current game, a player commits their third penalty that season and faces suspension for the far more important game. Two unsportsmanlike conduct penalties in a game resulting in disqualification is something pretty rare, but it does happen, and it changes the course of games. Now we can change future games? See what I’m getting at here? On paper it looks good, but how crummy would it be if a questionable defenseless-player flag came out just so the player gets suspended the following week (or two weeks later—point is, this puts too much power on the officiating crew). Keep in mind, the NFL is trying to instigate more replay on things like this, but there still isn’t a black-and-white review system of something that now has even further consequences than 15 yards. What about players that did commit the foul and it’s clearly on the tape, but they didn’t get flagged? Do they get a freebie when they should have been racking up strikes? To be fair, the odds of a player getting three of these distinct penalties in a single season are quite low—but that doesn’t mean it wouldn’t happen. How many times have the 49ers faced a running quarterback who slid all over the place collecting 15 yards? What is Dre Greenlaw to do now? If the NFL actually knew how to issue these calls in the first place, I wouldn’t be as skeptical. Thank goodness roughing the passer isn’t listed on here, because that would open up an entirely new can of worms. It still has the unfortunate result of singling out players and some unlucky breaks. Just by face value, it seems like something that wasn’t thought through very well. Don’t misunderstand: all of the hits listed need to get out of the game. The problem is that the people enforcing it have shown they can’t be trusted to call anything fair and right down the middle because of the speed of the said game they are watching. Giving them the ability to get future suspensions issued (or not) seems like a massive misfire. Before making a statement, maybe clarify exactly how this is enforced. Then again, maybe no one thought that far. This is PR. And we all know how much the NFL wants to look good while also being broken as a result.
author: Patrick Holloway

title: 3 position battles to watch in the 49ers preseason finale: The second safety spot remains up for grabs
summary: As the preseason winds down for the San Francisco 49ers, the roster decisions are starting to become clear for certain positions. Some positions aren’t as clear, as injuries might force the team’s hand. Obviously, nailing down the left guard spot is the biggest need, but what other position battles are in focus on Thursday night […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - JANUARY 17: Marques Sigle #36 of the San Francisco 49ers gets set during the second quarter of an NFL divisional playoff football game against the Seattle Seahawks at Lumen Field on January 17, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images As the preseason winds down for the San Francisco 49ers, the roster decisions are starting to become clear for certain positions. Some positions aren’t as clear, as injuries might force the team’s hand. Obviously, nailing down the left guard spot is the biggest need, but what other position battles are in focus on Thursday night against the Las Vegas Raiders? The second safety spot Malik Mustapha still hasn’t returned from injury. Marques Sigle should be the slam-dunk choice to start opposite Ji’Ayir Brown. Given Sigle’s preseason performance, that is anything but certain. The 49ers didn’t address the position in the draft, signaling confidence in what they had in-house, but a late offseason signing of veteran safety Ashtyn Davis likely meant the team wanted a veteran option after a look at the options during OTAs. Kyle Shanahan said there won’t be many starters, and while the focus is rightly on left guard, the second safety spot should be just as big of a concern without a clear-cut winner. Thursday night could go a long way to deciding who starts in Week 1. Cornerback Upton Stout is looking to return to practice next week, according to Shanahan. Deommodore Lenoir has been dealing with a shoulder injury, but will be fine for the Australia trip. Nobody seems to be discussing the spot opposite Lenoir, as Renardo Green is dealing with a hamstring injury. The logical choice would be veteran Jack Jones, who has impressed in the preseason, but what if upstart Ephesians Prysock has something to say about that on Thursday night? Darrell Luter, Jr always seems to find himself in the mix somehow, but the smart money should be on Jones to start if Green can’t. As we saw last week with Jacob Cowing, a big play can change everything, so it’s not set in stone. Linebacker One of the positions of concern this offseason was linebacker. However, the tide has shifted, and the 49ers now have a deep linebacker group with the emergence of Garrett Wallow, Jaden Dugger, and the potential of Nick Martin. I feel like a broken record, but injuries are running through the linebacker room, with Martin and Luke Gifford dealing with injuries. Deion Jones’ addition can be viewed as a camp body to get through the game, but a strong performance from the veteran could lead to a roster spot and a special teams contributor if Gifford’s injury lingers. The impact of the special teams ace shouldn’t be overlooked. Thursday night will be interesting for a few reasons.

title: Why the 49ers are taking a different approach than the Rams with their Week 1 travel
summary: The San Francisco 49ers and Los Angeles Rams have some unique circumstances for their Week 1 showdown in two weeks, as the two teams are traveling across the world to Australia. The game is set to be played on the morning of September 11th local time, with it being televised in the United States at […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - AUGUST 13: Head coach Kyle Shanahan of the San Francisco 49ers looks on from the sidelines against the Tennessee Titans during the second half at Levi's Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers and Los Angeles Rams have some unique circumstances for their Week 1 showdown in two weeks, as the two teams are traveling across the world to Australia. The game is set to be played on the morning of September 11th local time, with it being televised in the United States at 5:35 p.m. on September 10th. Despite the 17-hour time difference, Los Angeles plans to execute a similar plan to their London trip from a previous international game, where they arrived late and didn’t spend much time in the host country before the game, landing just the day before. The Rams proceeded to beat up on the Jacksonville Jaguars 35-7 in that London game, and flew back directly after. While head coach Sean McVay hasn’t confirmed any plans, he did mention earlier this offseason that the Rams will likely have a similar plan to that London game, minimizing their stay in Australia. The 49ers are doing a much different plan. They’re leaving to Australia a full week early to acclimate to the time change, with head coach Kyle Shanahan saying that was recommended by scientists. “I would love to just show up the day before and just play, but I’m not the best when it comes to the science and everything on that stuff,” Shanahan said this week. “So, you ask people who’ve done it a number of times, you ask people who study it, you take all their opinions in. “We’ve been strongly recommended to. When you’ve got a 19-hour flight and it’s a 16-hour-something difference, I forgot because I haven’t asked since we were making these decisions, but it’s a big adjustment on the body. So, the recommendation for everybody has been to tell us when to go, and it’s made a lot of sense. And I know how our players feel also. I was a little bit on the fence. Science wasn’t and what I was reported on and our players weren’t at all. So that helped me get off the fence.” San Francisco does have a lot on its plate ahead of the game with its number of injury decisions to go with the long plane ride. “I’m just hoping our team’s healthy enough and has the time to get there,” Shanahan continued. “Those are the challenges of it, just to get there to prepare for it. Guys still trying to recover to get there, the plane flight and things like that. But once you do get there and stuff, we’re going to have fun playing in another country and it’s going to be a cool atmosphere, things like that. That’ll all be good. But right now, I’m just thinking of the challenges of getting our team ready for those three and a half hours.” We’ll see if either travel strategy ends up having any residual effects, but the 49ers and Rams seem to be taking two vastly different approaches with the Australia travel. One has worked for one team before, while the other is brand new to the situation.
