title: Over or under? The teams we like to hit or miss on projected win totals
summary: Which NFL teams will exceed projections and which ones will fall short? Our analysts offer their best bets on teams' win totals.
full_text:
It seems simple enough. Take a team to go over or under a projected win total. Then injuries pop up, or perhaps an unknown star emerges, changing a team's trajectory.

 Seventeen NFL teams went over their totals last year, and 15 went under. The Arizona Cardinals ' number heading into last season was 8.5, and they finished with just three wins. The Kansas City Chiefs , who had been to three straight Super Bowls, were set at 11.5 and won six games. The Washington Commanders won five after entering with an over/under of 9.5 wins.

 

 Other teams hit the over with ease. The Jacksonville Jaguars had a total of 7.5 and went 13-4. And the Denver Broncos (9.5), New England Patriots (8.5) and Seattle Seahawks (8.5) all won 14 games.

 This season, nine teams projected for double-digit wins. The Los Angeles Rams and Baltimore Ravens are tied for the highest number at 11.5. The Miami Dolphins and Cardinals have the lowest at 3.5.

 Which teams will hit the over and which ones will fall short of win totals in 2026? We asked our analysts to break down the odds and offer their best bets.

 Note: Odds by DraftKings   and subject to change .

 
 Sign up for ESPN Fantasy Football . Play the No. 1 Fantasy game for free! 

 

   Cincinnati Bengals OVER 10.5 wins (+115) 

 Matt Bowen: I'm buying the Bengals -- and a healthy Joe Burrow -- with a revamped defensive front. Yes, Burrow's availability concerns have been an issue. But let's go back to the 2024 season, when Burrow played in all 17 games, throwing for 4,919 yards and 43 touchdowns, both of which were tops in the league. The league's best pocket thrower, Burrow has two premier targets in Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins , while Chase Brown is a productive starter in the backfield. Plus, with the trade for defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence II , who still has game-changing traits, and pass-rush help, Cincy is in a position (with the third-easiest schedule) to hit the over.

   Miami Dolphins UNDER 3.5 wins (+120) 
 

 Pamela Maldonado:  It's an extremely low bar, but Miami simply doesn't have the pieces to win games. This is a complete overhaul: new coaching staff, new quarterback, and Tua Tagovailoa , Tyreek Hill , Jaylen Waddle , Bradley Chubb and Minkah Fitzpatrick are all gone. QB Malik Willis gets his first real opportunity to start, but his supporting cast is dramatically different than the one he had in Green Bay. Miami is projected to have the league's worst receiving room, and first-round tackle Kadyn Proctor can't fix the offensive line by himself. De'Von Achane is the one proven difference-maker, but even his schedule against the run gets tougher. More concerning is a defense projected to be bottom of the league entering the season and playing the second-hardest schedule overall, including top-10 hardest slates for both passing and rushing offenses. Miami could be playing from behind a lot, which also puts Willis in exactly the type of game script he hasn't proved he can handle. The Dolphins might end up having the worst record in the NFL.

   New Orleans Saints OVER 7.5 wins (-120) 
 Eric Moody:  The Saints have a real shot at eight wins. New Orleans went 5-4 after Tyler Shough took over at quarterback last season, with the offense averaging 19.8 points and 235.2 passing yards per game over that stretch. Shough now gets another year with Kellen Moore and star wideout Chris Olave and has additions in first-round pick Jordyn Tyson and free agent Travis Etienne Jr . The schedule is favorable too, with one of the easiest slates in the league in a wide-open NFC South. The Saints' defense also came on late last season, allowing just 17.5 points per game from Week 10 on. Eight wins is well within reach.

   Tampa Bay Buccaneers OVER 8.5 wins (+115) 

 Liz Loza: After failing to win the division for the first time in four years, GM Jason Licht opted to overhaul much of Tampa Bay's operation. Zac Robinson, a former NFL quarterback who served as Baker Mayfield 's position coach in 2022, was brought in to implement a system that maximized the Bucs' offense under Liam Coen. Robinson's "true run-and-pass marriage," figures to elevate the running game and provide stability for Mayfield. This scheme is likely to be well supported by a top-three ranked offensive line, a deep backfield and an ascending group of young wide receivers. A shaky secondary and the retirement of LB Lavonte David are key gaps to fill, but the unit's infusion of pass-rushing talent should help balance the defense. Noting a favorable schedule (12th easiest), the Bucs should push toward 10 wins.

   Tennessee Titans UNDER 6.5 wins (-115) 
 Seth Walder:  I see multiple ways for this season to go wrong for Tennessee. The simplest path is that Cam Ward simply doesn't develop. If that's the case, then it doesn't matter how many pass catchers the team brings in -- the offense won't move. And while head coach Robert Saleh does lend confidence to the defense, I worry that the new cornerback tandem of Alontae Taylor and Cor'Dale Flott were overpays that won't be able to produce at their 2025 level at a notoriously volatile position. I'm open to lower bound alternate lines here, too (like under 4.5 wins at +320) for a big payout in the event that Ward really struggles.

title: How is NFL dealing with players heading back to college? 'Cluster of all clusters'
summary: NFL coaches, execs and agents tell ESPN they're sifting through questions and implications of a new reality, which seems to change by the hour.
full_text:
SEVEN DAYS IN  Cleveland epitomized the volatile landscape of eligibility in college sports -- and how the uncertainty is now seeping into the NFL.

 On Aug. 19, 33 athletes -- including then- Browns  and former  Ole Miss  tight end Dae'Quan Wright -- were granted a temporary restraining order by a Louisiana state court to return to college for one more season. The following day, Wright was one of more than a dozen former FBS players, including athletes who had signed contracts with NFL teams, who entered their names into the NCAA transfer portal.

 On Saturday, Wright donned a Browns uniform and warmed up with the team ahead of Cleveland's second preseason game. He didn't play in the game, and by Tuesday, Cleveland waived Wright with a noninjury settlement, and Wright reached an agreement to play for his former college coach, Lane Kiffin, who is now at LSU .

 "Man, isn't this s--- crazy? I don't even know what to say," Browns coach Todd Monken said after Saturday's preseason game.

 "I cannot believe this is being green-lit on any level," a scouting executive for an NFL club told ESPN on Sunday.

 

 That disbelief proved a good instinct. On Tuesday night, the SEC issued a ruling intended to bar Wright from returning to play college football, making all of this moot -- that is, until the next lawsuit is filed. And on Wednesday, the NFL sent a memo reminding clubs that a player who signed an NFL contract and then returned to college would not be allowed to sign with an NFL team again this season, referencing an eligibility rule in the player personnel handbook.

 The news of Wright's return to the NCAA, along with three other players who had been on NFL training camp rosters this summer -- former  New Orleans Saints  defensive lineman Zxavian Harris and former  Seattle Seahawks  running backs  TJ Harden and Anthony Hankerson -- has been the talk of the league over the past week. NFL coaches, executives and agents are sifting through questions and implications of the new reality, which seems to change by the hour.

 The NFLPA declined to comment to ESPN on Tuesday, and the NFL did not respond to a request for comment.

 Los Angeles Rams  coach Sean McVay perhaps summed it up best when asked about NFL players returning to college: "I feel like I took a freakin' gummy."

 

 IN RECENT WEEKS , there has been a litany of legal action -- in federal and state courts -- by outgoing seniors seeking a fifth year of eligibility and the right to return to play college football in 2026 after the NCAA in June passed new eligibility rules allowing athletes to play five seasons within a five-year window.

 A Colorado federal judge issued a late July preliminary injunction in a class action case brought by former Buffaloes basketball player Brock Wisne, opening the door for all athletes who started college in the fall of 2022 to return for a fifth season. However, last week the 10th Circuit Court of Appeals granted the NCAA a stay in an order reversing the lower court's decision.

 Since then, state lawsuits have sprouted across the country from athletes seeking to play a fifth collegiate season. The suit that Wright joined in a Louisiana court is one of the latest that will allow a group of outgoing seniors who were not considered exceptions for the NCAA's eligibility rule change to return to college. Athletes who have filed separate lawsuits in state court and have received restraining orders are not impacted by the Wisne decision.

 If this sounds confusing, it's because it is.

 A compliance director for a Power 4 college football program, who wasn't authorized by his school to speak on the record, told ESPN on Tuesday that his school has two players who started college in the fall of 2022 occupying roster spots and practicing with the team, even though they are currently not eligible to play.

 When the NCAA changed its eligibility rules, the compliance director said his school's coaching staff started reviewing its 2025 roster to determine which players might be interested in returning. When the two players returned to the team after going undrafted and unsigned in the NFL, they had what seemed, at the time, a clear path to eligibility under the Wisne decision. The players still needed to apply to the NCAA for reinstatement because they had professionalized themselves by signing with agents and being part of the 2026 draft class . But on Friday, the NCAA won a stay on the Wisne decision, meaning the two players needed to pursue independent litigation if they wanted to play this season.

 

 The compliance director said the communication they received from the NCAA states that the organization plans to continue fighting each eligibility case filed against it. 

 "We're two weeks out from the start of the season and a lot of this is not finalized, not resolved, and continuing to be fought," the director said Tuesday morning. "So yes, it could absolutely happen where someone is starting out the season playing and then that gets revoked in some way."

 Just a few hours after ESPN spoke to the compliance director, the Big Ten passed a rule barring any player who has declared for the NFL draft and has not withdrawn, appeared on an NFL roster, or signed a contract with a pro league from being on a member school's roster. The SEC later passed a similar rule prohibiting a player who signed a contract with an NFL team (or another professional football league) from appearing on a conference roster. And ESPN's Pete Thamel reported Wednesday that the Big 12 athletic directors agreed to ban professionals returning to their conference schools. There is also momentum in the ACC to join the Big Ten and SEC in banning players who have joined NFL rosters from returning to college rosters, per Thamel.

 In a span of five days, these two fifth-year college football players went from having a clear path to eligibility through NCAA reinstatement to needing to file their own lawsuit to get a restraining order to being banned from returning by their conference.

 "Even though these players are being given this relief at the state level and on this initial [Wisne] decision, the NCAA is still fighting this tooth and nail," the compliance director said. "It's very ticky-tacky because it comes down to the particular states and how they're reviewing things. So it's not one big thing to be decided. It's many, many fires that need to be put out for them."

 A veteran NFC scout said this is the most "bizarre" aspect of college football right now. "It feels like it only takes one judge to change a law."

 

 A Browns team source told ESPN that Wright, who originally signed with the Philadelphia Eagles as an undrafted free agent and joined Cleveland via waivers on Aug. 11, didn't factor into the team's long-term plans. However, this was an unprecedented situation, so the club consulted the NFL office for guidance on how they should roster-designate Wright.

 A source familiar with the league office's business said the NFL lawyers were looking into the consequences of the different designations to make sure they didn't put themselves at risk of a lawsuit, as the NCAA has.

 While the Browns and the league office examined the unfamiliar scenario last Wednesday, the day the plaintiffs in the Louisiana lawsuit received a restraining order, a rookie tight end had already arrived in town to replace Wright. He waited five days to sign.

 Though Wright was a long shot to make the Browns' 53-man roster , many around the league were curious about the domino effect of his departure and the precedent it could set.

 The conference bans have clouded the picture even further, and NFL sources have many unanswered questions, some of which may no longer even apply if the conference bans are successful. Does a college recruiting players on NFL rosters qualify as tampering? If undrafted players leave to go back to college, do clubs stop guaranteeing their salaries? Is there a future where players enter the…

title: Cowboys' leadership council is taking pressure off Prescott
summary: While Prescott is the de facto leader, players such as Quinnen Williams and Javonte Williams are stepping up.
full_text:
OXNARD, Calif. -- As the joint practice between the Dallas Cowboys and Los Angeles Rams came to an end on Aug. 11 in Woodland Hills, California, an interesting scene took place.

 With the Rams walking to their locker room after the two-hour practice, the Cowboys lined up on the goal line ready for some 20-yard sprints. More than one of the Rams shook their head or made some under-the-breath comments about it, almost glad they did not have to do something that is associated more with college or high school workouts.

 Linebacker  DeMarvion Overshown went up to quarterback  Dak Prescott after practice and asked if they were going to run their sprints.

 "I'm like, 'Yeah, if y'all want to run. ... I know we got it in us over here,'" Prescott said. "Yeah, just like a normal practice. Let's go get a run in, get better."

 

 So for an extra 10 minutes or so, all of the healthy players ran a series of sprints before taking off their pads and heading to the buses for the 45-minute bus ride back to Oxnard.

 It was actually the second straight practice the players asked to run the sprints. On Aug. 9, which was Family Day, coach Brian Schottenheimer had the players line up like normal and brought the group together, calling off the conditioning -- until the players requested to run the sprints like normal, even if it was Family Day at camp with wives, girlfriends, children, moms and dads in attendance.

 "We got the right guys," Schottenheimer said. "The leadership of this football team are some of our best players, and historically that means you're going to have a lot of success."

 

 August sprints may or may not impact September through January wins, although Schottenheimer told his players in the offseason that he wanted to have the best conditioned team in the league.

 But the fact that the players continued to do the sprints even when not required indicates a willingness of the group to work for the greater good.

 In his second year, Schottenheimer, with the recommendations of his coordinators, put together an 11-player leadership council. In his first season, Schottenheimer wanted a "one voice" approach -- his -- although he would often meet with players to get the pulse of what the locker room was feeling.

 The 11 players on the 2026 leadership council are Prescott, CeeDee Lamb , Tyler Smith , Tyler Booker , Jake Ferguson , Javonte Williams , Bryan Anger , Quinnen Williams , Kenny Clark , Rashan Gary , and Jalen Thompson .

 The council meets about every two weeks to discuss things that have happened and what might happen down the road. They each have a subset of players with whom they speak to get a feel for the locker room. From there, they give Schottenheimer ideas, feedback and suggestions.

 "At the end of the day, it's their council," Schottenheimer said. "It's not mine."

 Prescott was a given, of course. He has been this team's de facto leader almost since he arrived in 2016. But Clark carries a big voice on the council. Acquired a week before the season last year in the Micah Parsons  trade, the defensive tackle did not want to "step on anybody's toes" when he arrived. He led more by doing than talking.

 "Everybody's embracing everybody," Clark said. "I think it's just how you go about your business every day, how you lead the team, doing what you're doing."

 

 In recent years when leadership was talked about with the Cowboys, it was almost entirely about Prescott. His personality transcends the locker room, speaking with undrafted free agents as much as he speaks with stars like Lamb and George Pickens .

 While on the council, Prescott views himself as one of the 11.

 "That was purposeful. I couldn't be the, whatever you want to call it, the chief leader in there because I'm going to speak up. I'm going to talk," Prescott said. "I know what I know, and I'm not going to be hesitant to say it, but we need other guys to take that lead. And Kenny Clark, Rashan Gary and Tyler Smith have been those guys to step up and they're doing a hell of a job."

 Schottenheimer knows Prescott will always have a voice, but he is glad the responsibility is being shared.

 "I want those guys to speak up, and so it's really cool that those guys step up before Dak has to say things," Schottenheimer said.

 The burden of leadership has not worn down Prescott, but he is happy others are more involved.

 "When you've got guys like we do on that council, veteran guys, for me, it's good to have guys on different teams," Prescott said. "I know what I know. And sometimes it's a good thing, sometimes it's a bad thing. And so you've got other guys that can come in and say, 'This is a way that we've done it,' or 'I've had it like this in the past.' And not necessarily those are the right ways, but it gives you a different perspective, gives you a way to look at different solutions to get to things."

 Prescott's voice still carries a lot of weight. Clark, entering his 11th season, said he constantly learns from Prescott.

 "Dak's done so much for this organization, but just taking a little off of Dak, I mean, he's a total pro and does things the right way all the time," Clark said. "I think he's pretty happy he's got a bunch of guys behind him that's on the same type of time that he's on."

 Some of the other choices were of note. Of the four defensive players -- Quinnen Williams, Clark, Gary and Thompson -- none were with the team at this time a year ago.

 When the Cowboys signed Williams to a three-year contract extension worth $105.9 million on Aug. 10, one of the first things executive vice president Stephen Jones mentioned was his leadership.

 

 "We didn't have a lot of leadership on defense for the last couple of years," Jones said. "Now to have him and Kenny Clark and Rashan Gary, I think has really picked it up over there in terms of culture and the leadership."

 Booker is entering his second year and is only 22. He was a captain at Alabama. He was a captain at IMG Academy. During his rookie season, Schottenheimer encouraged Booker to speak up more.

 "That means a lot, first and foremost, to be seen as a leader by so many great men on this team and all my coaches," Booker said. "It really means a lot. It's truly a blessing, and that's something that I'm very proud of and I'm going to have to live up to the standard, too."

 There is a mix of personality among the group. Clark and Williams are more reserved. Ferguson is more outgoing. Smith learned from Zack Martin and Tyron Smith that when you speak is as important as how much you speak. Williams is more introverted.

 Schottenheimer admits he can run "hot and cold a lot" and wanted a group that would complement his style.

 "Kenny Clark, he is a man of few words, but I would follow that guy anywhere. I really would," Schottenheimer said. "And so Kenny's got to be himself. If you look at our leadership council, I would say that a lot of the guys on the council aren't jumping around going upbeat like I am. I mean, Quinnen's not that way. [Smith] isn't that way. But they're all what? They're all leading the way that they are. Jalen Thompson, Javonte Williams. I would follow Javonte Williams anywhere. Why? Because his heart's in the right spot. He loves football. He loves his teammates. He wants to win."

 Ultimately that's what matters most, but the council can help steer the direction when adversity hits in a way that coaches cannot.

 "There's a saying that the best team police themselves," Ferguson said. "It's one thing to have a coach or have somebody saying it, but when you got a guy who cares enough, a brother who cares enough to tell you and hold you accountable ... that's how you create that strong brotherhood. And that's all we're trying to do."

title: 2026 Green Bay Packers training camp: Latest intel, updates
summary: Catch up on our updates from Packers training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps are wrapping up around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. Packers reporter Rob Demovsky has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and, of course, the quarterbacks room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Packers camp. Will the revamped WR corps help QB Jordan Love and the offense take another step? Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Catch up on all the updates, including the Packers' top camp performer and biggest lingering question as preseason games begin.

 
 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest news out of Packers camp 
 
 Matt LaFleur, Mike LaFleur ready for Packers-Cardinals work 
 CB Keisean Nixon not guaranteed starting role with Packers 
 Aaron Rodgers wishes game at Lambeau, discusses retirement return 
 Packers QB Love expected to play in first preseason game 
 Micah Parsons: Playing vs. Cowboys in Week 6 'realistic' 
 Packers RT changes last name to Bako-Bewele to honor heritage 
 Packers star TE Tucker Kraft activated off PUP after ACL recovery 
 

 

 Wednesday, Aug. 26 

 For a team that spent a significant part of the offseason focusing on finishing better, Wednesday's joint practice with the Cardinals probably won't do much to convince anyone it has made progress in that area.

 
After a hot start by Jordan Love and the No. 1 offense, they fizzled out and were stopped by the Cardinals' No. 1 defense in a hotly contested two-minute period.

 
Love completed eight of his first 10 passes to start practice, including a spectacular 45-yard deep ball touchdown to Matthew Golden against double coverage from safety Budda Baker and cornerback Denzel Burke  as well as explosive gains on throws to Jayden Reed and Christian Watson .

 
However, Love was later intercepted twice and also was sacked on fourth down to lose the two-minute drive.

 
"We started off the day really hot and we were making a lot of plays," Love said. "And I think towards the end, we didn't finish as well. And I think that's obviously something we've harped on throughout the offseason, throughout training camp.

 "So, I think that was the kind of lowest point of the day was just [the] finish. And I think in training camp, the joint practices, I think it gets a little chippy, things happen, emotions start running a little higher. So, we got to find ways to be able to just dial back in, focus back in and be able to finish a practice."

 
In fact, the Packers lost all four two-minute situations. The Packers' No. 1 defense lost after Keisean Nixon was flagged for pass interference to set up Jacoby Brissett 's 1-yard touchdown toss to Marvin Harrison Jr.  over Brandon Cisse . The Packers' No. 2 offense lost when Tyrod Taylor was picked off, and the No. 2 defense gave up a touchdown, as well.

 
Green Bay coach Matt LaFleur put an emphasis on finishing better after they blew so many late-game leads last season and went from a 9-3-1 team to one that finished on a five-game losing streak, including the playoff collapse against the Bears.

 More observations: 

 
 Tight end Tucker Kraft took a couple of hard hits during the joint practice, including one that was flagged for a late hit. He didn't seem to mind or think it was dirty. "I needed some contact like that to wake up the nervous system and get ready for Week 1," said Kraft, who won't play in any preseason games but is expected to be full go for the opener. Kraft, who is coming off ACL surgery, practiced despite not having a contract extension done yet. "I would say we're on the same page that we'd like to get it done as soon as possible, prior to Week 1, for sure," Kraft said. 
 At least kicker Trey Smack is a gamer. The rookie has been perfect in three preseason games, including three 50-plus-yard field goals. He hasn't been as good in practice, and that continued Wednesday. He went 2-for-5 in practice with misses from 33 yards (wide left), 45 (wide right) and 58 (short) into the wind and makes from 38 and 53. 
 Starting nickelback  Javon Bullard (foot) practiced for the first time in more than two weeks but only during individual drills. Cornerback Benjamin St-Juste (hamstring) and edge Arron Mosby (illness) also returned. 
 General manager Brian Gutekunst held his final media session before roster cuts and said it's possible he might keep an extra running back on the initial 53-man roster in case Josh Jacobs gets suspended. Jacobs is still under investigation after being arrested in May on domestic violence allegations. "We'll deal with that if that transpires, but we could," Gutekunst said. "You're always usually going to keep three or four running backs, and I think we have enough to do that. But again, it comes down to choices and trying to figure that out. The one thing, particularly at that position, is elevating a guy from the practice squad. I don't want to say it's easy to do, but it's something we've done in the past and not something we'd shy away from." 
 The LaFleur family hung around the field for more than a half hour after practice catching up and taking pictures following the joint practice between Matt's Packers and Mike's Cardinals. 
 

 

 Monday, Aug. 24 

 Enter the names Matthew Golden and Barryn Sorrell into a search engine and you'll find a picture of them fishing together, a congratulatory social media post from Golden to Sorrell during the 2025 draft, a video on the Packers' website of the two of them engaged in a toy boxing match. 

 
The former teammates at the University of Texas even have lockers right next to each other at Lambeau Field.

 
None of that stopped them from getting into it during Monday's practice.

 
They started what was the closest thing to a training camp fight we've seen here this summer. Golden appeared to take exception to something Sorrell did at the end of a play, and tempers flared. Players came off the sideline and at least one player, linebacker Zaire Franklin , appeared to take a swing at someone.

 
"You know how it is when you've got a brother-type thing," Sorrell said, glancing at Golden's empty locker. "Me and Matt are always getting into it. It's just how our relationship is. Today it got out on the football a little bit and everybody thought we were like so serious. The whole time we were joking around a little bit. Like I said, it's football. It's how it gets. It's fun."

 
This on a day when Packers coach Matt LaFleur warned that there will be consequences if anyone fights during Wednesday's joint practice with the Cardinals.

 
Golden was not in the locker room after practice, but Sorrell said they made up quickly after a practice that was dominated by the defense.

 
"When [LaFleur] called us all up, we were dapping it up, we were joking about it and stuff and everything," Sorrell said. "It's just part of the game."

 More observations: 

 
 Running back Josh Jacobs took part in his first 11-on-11 work since his Aug. 6 groin injury. Jacobs had returned to practice last week on a limited basis but did not do any team periods until Monday. 
 Keisean Nixon , who appears to be in a fight for a starting cornerback job, made one of his biggest plays of camp with a leaping interception of  Jordan Love to score a win for the defense in the two-minute drill. Nixon and Brandon Cisse were the No. 1 cornerbacks Monday. Carrington Valentine and Domani Jackson worked with the second unit. Benjamin St-Juste (hamstring) did not practice. 
 Speaking of interceptions, Kitan Oladapo also went up in the air to pick off a Kyle McCord pass near the sideline. Oladapo and Kamal Hadden have been splitting time in the slot position that is normally manned by Javon Bullard (bruised foot). 
 The Packers got a scare when starting right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele was slow to get up after a play midway through…

title: How Chiefs offense is working to solve one of 2025's biggest issues
summary: Kansas City had one of the NFL's worst play-action passing attacks last season. Expect that to change in 2026.
full_text:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. -- Well before his usual offseason tradition of evaluating the Kansas City Chiefs ' offensive scheme, coach Andy Reid knew he had a major problem. Any time he turned on the film of last year's unit, one trend became worse and worse.

 "If you watch the level two defenders, the linebackers and or a safety coming up in the box, if we're selling a play-action and those guys are dropping [into coverage], they're not honoring the run game," Reid said last week. "There's something that they're seeing and not respecting."

 

 As last season progressed, one in which the Chiefs finished with a lackluster 6-11 record and missed the playoffs for the first time since 2014, opposing defenses never felt threatened by the appearance -- or the plausible possibility -- of quarterback Patrick Mahomes handing the ball to former running backs Isiah Pacheco and Kareem Hunt . The results led to the Chiefs having one of the NFL's worst passing attacks when utilizing play-action.

 Although the Chiefs used play-action on 178 snaps last season, the seventh most in the NFL, they produced just 977 passing yards from it, ranking 20th, according to ESPN Research. In fact, the Chiefs surrendered more sacks (nine) than they scored touchdowns (three).

 An example of a snap that illustrated the Chiefs' issue last season occurred early in the fourth quarter against the Houston Texans  in Week 14. With three tight ends on the field, Mahomes turned his back to the defense, executed a play-action fake with Hunt and then noticed that none of his three receiving options -- receiver Tyquan Thornton , tight end Travis Kelce and Hunt -- were open, leading him to throw the ball out of bounds.

 "Well, play-action has always been a big part of this offense," Reid said. "We look at the production of it. What are you getting out of it [on film]? You might as well just dropback and forget about the play-action."

 If the Chiefs are going to become a more potent offense this upcoming season, Reid and Mahomes have identified that the unit's play-action passing attack needs to have fangs that hurt opposing defenses.

 The Chiefs' biggest acquisition in free agency, running back Kenneth Walker III , is also part of the equation. As the reigning Super Bowl MVP, Walker has made it clear his running style preference is to work under center, which is expected to be a bigger part of the offense this season. The Chiefs know Walker presents a more dangerous threat that should force linebackers and safeties to move forward before Mahomes attempts a play-action pass.

 After all, Pacheco and Hunt combined for only one rushing attempt that gained more than 20 yards in 2025, which ranked last in the league. With the Seattle Seahawks last season, Walker was fourth in percentage of runs that gained 10 or more yards (minimum of 150 touches), according to NFL Next Gen Stats.

 

 "No. 9. That's all I can say," Mahomes said, referencing Walker's jersey number, when asked what intrigues him most about the offense. "That change and the ability to catch, run, pass protect, do everything. [He can] make a play out of nothing into a 20-yard gain. That's going to be the biggest impact, I think, we'll have -- just finding the ways to get him the ball."

 Last season, the Chiefs had Mahomes in the shotgun on 80.6% of their formations (excluding quarterback kneel-downs), which was the third most in the NFL, according to ESPN Research. Throughout training camp, though, Mahomes spent several reps under center. Those plays revealed Mahomes executing several different types of play-action passes -- true seven-step dropbacks, naked rollouts and even creative, nontraditional fakes that involved a receiver in motion.

 A sizable amount of those reps led to Mahomes throwing the ball more than 20 yards downfield. Those passes were most often caught by Kelce, Thornton and receiver Xavier Worthy . Mahomes attempted just seven passes last season in which his play-action pass traveled 20 or more yards downfield, according to ESPN Research. He completed just three of those passes.

 

 "We've got a lot of great players on this offense," Kelce said. "It's not just me. We've got some young guys that can play. [Worthy is] a man on a mission right now, and I love the way he's working and his attention to detail and how he's running his routes and just the aggression that he's running his routes in.

 "Pat has done an unbelievable job of not only getting himself ready, but working with these receivers and making sure that everybody's living up to that standard of how we're going to play this year."

 Even when in shotgun, Mahomes spent time in camp throwing intermediate passes in the middle of the field to work with his receivers on placing the ball behind linebackers who were retreating back into coverage. A receiver who caught many of those passes was Rashee Rice , who had eight such intermediate receptions between the numbers, according to ESPN Research.

 "Hopefully that works that way in the season," Reid said. "You want to put those level two defenders in a recovery mode. It creates seams and then you've got to be able to shoot the seams."

 One detail that Mahomes has worked to fix in camp is to show the ball longer to the defense -- and closer to Walker or the other running backs -- to better execute his fakes so that it mirrors closer to a true handoff. Too often last season, Mahomes showed the ball in front of Hunt or Pacheco and pulled it back quicker than he should have, which tipped opposing linebackers to the Chiefs' intentions of attempting a pass.

 "When you have a great run game, it opens up things down the field because it tends to have people play closer to the line of scrimmage," said offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy. "Kenneth has been very impressive. The thing that I love about him is his competitive spirit."

 

 One way Walker can help transform the offense is by becoming a true dual-threat player. Reid has been pleased with Walker's route-running ability, especially on plays when he is asked to run away from linebackers who are in man-to-man coverage.

 With Walker's receiving skills and ability to make defenders miss in the open field, Reid had the offense run one of his favorite passing concepts: the variety of plays where a play-action fake to the running back is executed before a short screen pass is thrown back to the same running back.

 "He looks like he's the full package," Reid said of Walker. "He works at it. That's the part I appreciate. He's always asking questions."

 Reid smiled last week when he made a joke in reference to the Chiefs' first offensive play of the preseason -- the lone snap against the Los Angeles Rams that included Walker.

 "We play-actioned on the first play," Reid said. "We ran a naked and everybody ran over there [toward Walker]. I go, 'OK, I like that.'"

title: 2026 Minnesota Vikings training camp: Latest intel, updates
summary: Catch up on our updates from Vikings training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. Vikings reporter Kevin Seifert has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and of course the quarterback room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Vikings camp. Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Catch up on all the updates, including the Vikings' top camp performer and biggest lingering question as preseason games begin.

 
 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest Vikings stories 

 
 What Kyler Murray as QB1 means for Vikings, J.J. McCarthy 
 Vikings, O'Neill reach $96M extension 
 Top Vikings storylines after minicamp, from QBs to new GM 
 Will Vikings start Caleb Banks, other rookies on defense? 
 Jefferson says decision on Vikings starting QB 'coach's call' 
 

 

 Wednesday, Aug. 26 

 The Vikings held quarterback J.J. McCarthy out of a full-pads practice Wednesday but are still hoping to start him in Friday night's preseason game at the Denver Broncos , coach Kevin O'Connell said.

 
McCarthy suffered a mild deltoid sprain in his ankle in Saturday's 13-3 loss to the Baltimore Ravens , O'Connell said. McCarthy was on the field Monday and Tuesday, which were light practices in shells, but O'Connell said he wanted to see if "we can put the ankle behind him a little bit" to help him prepare for Friday night and maximize his game reps in the preseason.

 "That's the goal," O'Connell said. "But also if we can't get him there, we can't get him there."

 O'Connell also did nothing to dissuade the notion that McCarthy remains in competition with Carson Wentz for the Vikings' No. 2 quarterback job. Wentz and No. 4 quarterback Max Brosmer are also scheduled to play Friday night.

 
"We want to make sure we give not only J.J. and Carson, but Max as well, with the good things that he's done, the ability to maximize what we can get out of these games and allow that competition," O'Connell said.

 More observations: 

 
  O'Connell said he spoke with veteran safety Harrison Smith as recently as this week. The Vikings are clearly leaving open the possibility that Smith could play in 2026 rather than retire. "I have had some conversations about where he's at, what he's thinking," O'Connell said, "and we'll keep you guys updated if there is an update on that." 
 O'Connell said that safety Theo Jackson (leg) and offensive lineman Caleb Tiernan (ankle) remain on track for a return to practice for the Vikings' Week 1 game against the Green Bay Packers 
 

 

 Thursday, Aug. 20 

 The Minnesota Vikings defense put on a dominant performance over two days of joint practices with the Baltimore Ravens .

 That has often been the case in recent years, when defensive coordinator Brian Flores' blitz schemes overwhelm offenses that are still learning their protection schemes. Linebacker Dallas Turner repeatedly broke into the backfield on pass rushers, and on the few occasions when the Ravens got the ball into the end zone, they celebrated wildly. Rookie receiver Ja'Kobi Lane spiked the ball with fury, for example, after catching a pass in the back of the end zone.

 The Vikings' offense, meanwhile, showed it is still catching up after spending the first two weeks of camp in a quarterback competition. Most notably, cornerbacks Marlon Humphrey and Nate Wiggins did strong work against Vikings receiver Justin Jefferson , who beat a double team for a touchdown Wednesday but had roughly a half dozen passes broken up as he tried to muscle for position.

 Jefferson said afterwards that the offense is making progress and acknowledged what quarterback Kyler Murray said this spring: Splitting reps was an added challenge.

 "Obviously [Murray] taking all of the 'ones' reps kind of allows us to get in the rhythm and get into the groove of things," Jefferson said. "And you don't really have to rely on having a catch on both footballs from two different people. So I mean, just like he said, he felt that the reps was a little short and he felt more comfortable having more reps.

 "So now he has it and the connection is definitely growing. Work needs to be done, but it comes with time and comes with just coming out here and just working together."

 
 Kicker Will Reichard converted four of six attempts during live kicking Thursday, with misses from 43 and 52 yards. The Vikings continued to split the holding duties between punters Johnny Hekker and Brett Thorson . 
 Safety Theo Jackson left practice with members of the Vikings medical staff after suffering what appeared to be a lower body injury. The team is relatively thin at safety and it has been notable that, even before Jackson departed, undrafted rookie Jacob Thomas was getting extensive first-team snaps. 
 Pro Football Hall of Fame receiver Randy Moss spent both days of joint practices with the Vikings, watching from the sidelines and sitting in on receiver meetings. "The information that he has is endless," Jefferson said. 
 

 

 Wednesday, Aug. 19 

 J.J. McCarthy took every second-team rep Wednesday in the Vikings' joint practice with the Baltimore Ravens , shortly after coach Kevin O'Connell reiterated with reporters that he considers McCarthy the No. 2 quarterback behind starter Kyler Murray .

 O'Connell, however, said he wants the quarterback position to remain competitive and did not rule out the possibility of  Carson Wentz  challenging McCarthy for the spot.

 
"We want Carson feeling like he can do the things consistently that he can do," O'Connell said, "and that we know exactly who and what he is. And we want J.J. feeling like, 'I'm one snap away, so I've got to prepare like I'm the starter anyway.' It's easy to say those things, but we wanted to have a room that forced it.

 "So we'll see how these next couple of weeks play out, and we're going to do what's best for our team, and proud of the way J.J.'s handled the last few days."

 McCarthy and Murray finished out the team portion of Wednesday's practices with big throws. Murray arced a pass roughly 40 yards into the corner of the end zone, allowing receiver Justin Jefferson to run past a double team and grab the ball for a touchdown. McCarthy then threw about a 30-yard pass over the middle to receiver Myles Price for a score.

 Other observations: 

 
 O'Connell acknowledged there have been some inconsistent snaps from center Blake Brandel to Murray during camp. He indicated it is largely an issue of Brandel anticipating where he is going to step first, triggering an inaccurate snap -- an unsurprising development for a player who hadn't played center before last season. "We have time," O'Connell said, "but not that much time, as I like to say." 
 Quarterback Max Brosmer (right wrist) did some light throwing Tuesday but did not participate in team drills. O'Connell said the Vikings are hoping Brosmer will be ready to play in Saturday's preseason game. 
 Rookie Caleb Tiernan , a third-round draft pick this spring who has been the second-team right tackle during training camp, is week-to-week because of an ankle injury, O'Connell said. 
 

 

 Who is the Vikings' top performer so far at camp? 

 Receiver Tai Felton has demonstrated remarkable improvement from his rookie year, when he struggled to catch the ball consistently in training camp and wound up with a near-exclusive special teams role during the season. He has made one-handed catches in the end zone, demonstrated soft hands at the end of deep routes and displayed his top-end speed while running quick hitters. Coach Kevin O'Connell said he has noted exceptional route running at times as well.

 Is Felton the Vikings' best player? Of course not. But no one has opened more eyes since camp began. He'll push veteran No. 3 receiver Jauan Jennings for playing time.

 What still needs to…

title: 2026 New York Giants training camp: Latest intel, updates
summary: Catch up on our updates from Giants training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. Giants reporter Jordan Raanan has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and, of course, the quarterbacks room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Giants camp. How will the Giants handle increased expectations and a new coach? Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Catch up on all the updates, including the Giants' top camp performer and biggest lingering question.

 
 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest news from Giants camp 
 
 New York Giants WR Calvin Austin carted off practice field 
 Players pulled from fight-filled Giants-Dolphins practice 
 Giants trade Daniel Faalele to Jaguars for 6th-round draft pick 
 Giants' Malik Nabers 'felt good' in 1st full-speed live drills 
 Giants QB Jaxson Dart 'puzzled' by latest concussion test request 
 A Harbaugh team meeting during training camp -- an inside look 
 

 
 Wednesday, Aug. 26 
 The Giants ran a generally light session in shorts and shoulder pads in their final practice of training camp. That didn't stop tempers from flaring a bit at the end.

 Running back Cam Skattebo caught a pass in a late-game drill and slid to the ground. Before they got to the next play, there was some pushing and shoving involving Skattebo and safety Jevon Holland and cornerback Greg Newsome II . It earned Skattebo a penalty flag from the officials.

 It left coach John Harbaugh not exactly thrilled.

 "Well, I mean, Skatt's great. He does bring a lot of energy. But he did get a 15-yard penalty at the end of practice. Did you notice that?" Harbaugh said. "That's not infectious. Well, it is infectious, actually. Infectious in a bad way, right? Like infectious disease type of thing (laughs). We don't want that. So, we want it to be directed in a positive way."

 Other observations: 

 
 Tight end Theo Johnson missed a second straight practice with a shoulder injury. Harbaugh said he should be fine. DT Shelby Harris worked on the side as the Giants continue to manage his workload. 
 WR Darnell Mooney saw an increased workload after the Giants lost Calvin Austin III for the season with a torn ACL. 
 The Giants concluded practice with a kicking competition. Both Dominic Zvada and Ben Sauls made field goals from 63 yards but missed from 69. Zvada again outkicked Sauls by hitting eight of his nine attempts. Saults hit 7 of 10. It would be surprising at this point if Zvada didn't win the job. 
 

 

 Tuesday, Aug. 25 

 The afternoon began for Odell Beckham Jr.  with one of his patented one-handed catches. It concluded with four receptions in live drills to complete one of his best practice performances of the summer.

 It comes at just the right time, with final cuts looming Sunday. Beckham has been presumed to be on the roster bubble after running mostly with the second team this summer. He also dropped a potential touchdown in Saturday's preseason game. But the injury to fellow wide receiver  Calvin Austin III could ultimately open the door for Beckham.

 "I know he's superfrustrated about that drop he had in the game the other day. We all know nine out of 10 times he's going to catch that," offensive coordinator Matt Nagy said of Beckham. "But I like where he's at."

 It wasn't just Beckham who had a strong practice Tuesday. Wideout  Darnell Mooney made a handful of big plays, including catching a deep touchdown from Jaxson Dart behind the defense.

 Other observations: 

 
 Coach John Harbaugh said over the weekend it's "an ongoing pecking order" at running back. The Giants listed Cam Skattebo as the starter on their weekly unofficial depth chart, with Tyrone Tracy Jr.  or Najee Harris or Devin Singletary next on an equal line. 
 TE Theo Johnson missed practice one day after colliding with outside linebacker Kayvon Thibodeaux . 
 G Francis Mauigoa (stinger) and RT Jermaine Eluemunor took part in individual drills after sitting out Monday. 
 

 

 Monday, Aug. 24 

 John Harbaugh huddled a group of veterans after practice. They went over schedules, practice details and other team-related items.

 This is how Harbaugh operates. He assembles a leadership group and consults with them on decisions.

 For the Giants, that consists of quarterback Jaxson Dart , left tackle Andrew Thomas , outside linebacker Brian Burns , middle linebacker Tremaine Edmunds , safety Jevon Holland , punter Jordan Stout , backup quarterback Jameis Winston and tight end Chris Manhertz . They were voted as leaders by their teammates.

 "We've been doing it for a long time. It's good," Harbaugh said of the leadership group. "I do kind of try to emphasize to the team that everybody's a leader and everybody has every opportunity to speak their mind. Talk to anybody.

 "But sometimes, it just kind of helps because guys don't always want to do that."

 They talk about everything. Harbaugh went on to say the Giants players asked Monday for a pool table in the locker room. He told them if they won enough games, they might even get a golf simulator.

 Other observations: 

 
 The Giants ran only a couple of periods of full-speed live drills. TE Isaiah Likely remains Dart's favorite target. The team keeps finding different ways to use WR Calvin Austin III ; the former Steelers wideout is going to have a significant role in this offense. 
 Tight end Theo Johnson left practice after a collision with Kayvon Thibodeaux . Harbaugh initially didn't think it was serious. 
 The Giants' offensive line was without RT Jermaine Eluemunor , G Francis Mauigoa (stinger) and G/OT Joshua Ezeudu (leg) at Monday's practice. All three should be back soon, possibly as early as Tuesday, when the Giants will be in full pads. 
 WR Jalin Hyatt (knee), TE Tanner Connor and DT Shelby Harris also didn't practice. 
 

 
 Thursday, Aug. 20 
 MIAMI GARDENS, Fla. -- This was the kind of practice you wanted to see from the Giants' offense -- and from quarterback Jaxson Dart .

 Dart had perhaps his best performances of the summer, going 17-of-23 passing in a joint practice against the Miami Dolphins that included several deep and intermediate gains. Six went to his favorite target, tight end Isaiah Likely .

 "I felt like I played clean," Dart said.

 This was an important day for Dart and the Giants' offense, which has been up and down most of the summer while learning a new system. They hadn't been able to hit many plays downfield.

 This was sort of a validation that this new offense can work.

 "We had a number of chunk gains off play-action, which was good to see," Giants coach John Harbaugh said. "It's one thing in theory, it's another thing in practice. You want to see it work. At the end of the day, did the play work? It could be a great play, but if it doesn't work, then there's a lot of things that go into making it work, including executing it well, then it's not a good play. I agree [it's validating]."

 

 More observations: 

 
 The Giants' offense probably wasn't even the team's best unit in the joint practice against the Dolphins. Outside linebacker Brian Burns said the defense was "dominant." When asked by a reporter if they had six sacks, Burns said no. In his estimation, they got to Dolphins quarterback Malik Willis even more than that. 
 How about this for a quick integration? Running back Najee Harris participated in live drills after just three days with the team. He even got a couple carries, including one on the goal line where he made an impressive cut and reached the end zone. Harris looked good for a player that supposedly wasn't going to be in football shape for a "couple weeks." 
 Another perfect practice for undrafted rookie kicker Dominic Zvada , who went 6-for-6, including one to end practice after the Giants drove the field on a…

title: Uar Bernard is the Eagles' newest quick study: 'Not of this world'
summary: There were so many hands in the defensive tackle's journey to make it possible for him to get drafted in April.
full_text:
MUSTAPHA MUSA SAID he didn't sleep for three days upon seeing the news that Uar Bernard was drafted in the seventh round by the Philadelphia Eagles , fearing he would wake up and realize it was all a dream.

 Sleep deprivation isn't new to Musa, an artist and designer by trade who also trains aspiring football players in Abuja, the capital of Nigeria, along with local gym coach Dike Christian.

 Abuja is some 5,000 miles away and five hours ahead of Pittsburgh where April's draft was held. It was around midnight Nigerian time when Bernard was selected by Philadelphia at No. 251 to play defensive tackle. Christian was following along closely but dozed off as the night wore on.

 "Musa called me and said, 'Dike, are you still sleeping? Our boy just got drafted!' I was like, 'Wait, are you serious? Are you serious?'" he said.

 "Then I saw Bernard called me ... He said, 'Coach. It has happened. God did it. Finally."

 It is hard to calculate the improbability of Bernard making it to the NFL. One in 17.5 million, maybe? That's the population of his home state of Kano. Bernard is the first NFL player from that area.

 Football wasn't even on his radar until 2022 when at age 17 he traveled six hours south from his home to Abuja for a basketball camp, which just so happened to be in the same facility as a flag football event put on by The Uprise Agency, led by former  New York Giants  defensive end Osi Umenyiora.

 

 Christian took one look at Bernard's "raw muscles" and "raw speed" and declared that the 6-foot-4 Bernard could excel as a football player if he dedicated himself. It didn't take much convincing: Bernard quickly fell for the sport and was all-in.

 Eventually the football world would see his unique gifts on display. He posted a 4.63-second 40-yard dash, a 10-foot, 10-inch broad jump and a 39-inch vertical jump at the International Player Pathway pro day -- all records for the event by a player over 300 pounds.

 "He looked like an action figure," said Jovan Gopie, who served as Bernard's defensive line coach as part of the IPP's predraft process. "Built by the gods, man."

 From initial discovery to the NFL, there were years of exhaustive work and rejection. He endured hunger. He wrestled with internal battles and nearly walked away from football altogether. But with support and sacrifice from his guardians, and led by the words of his late father, Bernard pulled off the near-impossible, emerging from the tunnel to the draft stage with a green-and-white Nigerian flag wrapped around his broad shoulders and gray suit.

 "I just see it as a miracle," Musa said.

 Many of those who had a hand in his journey pulled all-nighters and watched in elation as Bernard played his first official football snap in a preseason game against the Baltimore Ravens on Sept. 15, then again a week later as he recorded his first tackles versus the New England Patriots .

 "It was very much fun," Bernard told reporters following his first game. "People back home are proud of me, too, and I am proud of myself."

 

 

 THE LEGENDARY TREE  stands alone in a public park in Abuja.

 There is some grass and a sandpit and a hill nearby. With minimal resources to draw from, Musa and Christian needed to get creative to help turn the park into a training facility, which they named "The Trenches," for NFL hopefuls as part of their Pro Prospects Program.

 The athletes run the hill for conditioning, develop footwork in the sand and, without the benefit of tackling dummies, use the tree for everything from honing pass-rush moves to hand combat.

 "They've been hitting it so many times, you see the back of it peeling because a lot of them their hands got strong, to the extent that once they hit it, it peels off," Musa said.

 "I think the tree got them tougher because a lot of them would have been soft if they used the dummy. [Laughs.]"

 Musa dubbed it "The Legendary Tree" because a growing number of those who have struck it have risen to higher heights -- none higher than Bernard.

 He proved to be a quick study. Bernard asked a lot of questions and watched a lot of NFL film -- mostly of Aaron Donald, Christian said -- to refine his technique.  As gifted as he was, he lacked the necessary flexibility initially so Christian and Musa encouraged him to enroll in dance class.

 When he wasn't at the gym or in The Trenches, Bernard was at church. It was not uncommon for him to spend all night there keeping vigil and appear in front of his trainers early in the morning, red-eyed and looking to work. It was the same when he was running a fever. Sometimes they would have to decline his request, believing rest was more important in that moment.

 Musa linked Bernard being a "prayer warrior" to the death of his father when Bernard was 16 years old. Bernard described his dad as his "best friend" and said before he died, "He told me not to worry about anything. That if I put my trust in God, I will prevail through every situation. He was my inspiration ." 

 A big part of his motivation to make it to the NFL, Christian said, was linked to wanting to make life better for his mother and siblings, who lived in an area Christian described as "rough."

 "He told me that where he is from, the average annual income was $1,200 a year," Gopie said.

 The Pro Prospects Program is not paid for by the NFL;  it's actually self-funded by Musa and Christian, Musa said. Many of the athletes that come to them need housing and food and work. Musa and Christian use the money they get from being an artist and gym coach, respectively, to provide for the athletes. In doing so, they forego conveniences for themselves, like having a car.

 

 Bernard lived with Christian during his three years in Abuja and the trainers became like older brothers to him. When he was hungry or needed money, he would reluctantly go to them and they would offer what they had. It was not unusual for Bernard to have just one meal a day -- usually fufu, a doughy food made from the root plant cassava that can keep a person feeling sustained for long stretches.

 "He is the kind of person that even if he's hungry, he will never tell anybody apart from me or Dike. He will hold on to his hunger, and he will just manage himself," Musa said.

 "You know that this boy has the potential to be bigger but the nutrition he's getting is not as much as he should get. I'm sure you see the changes in his body now that he's actually under a team that is taking care of him. You can see he's getting bigger."

 Multiple attempts to make it into the IPP program failed, once because he was not old enough and once because it was deemed he did not have the necessary mobility. When he was denied entry into the camp in 2024, Bernard was "devastated," Musa said.

 "He was mentally down, broken, and he came to me. He was trying to go back to Kano. His mom is worried. She wants him to be around. She wants to see him because she feels like he's wasting time in Abuja chasing football," he said. "So he came to me. I was like, 'I'm not tired of training you, you understand. We are not tired of accommodating you. And we will push you till you get there.' I told him, 'Don't worry, just try it one more time,' and that was it."

 Bernard finally made it into the IPP program in 2025 despite another obstacle -- testing without shoes.

 According to Gopie, Nike sent a bunch of products to the NFL Academy in London for the athletes to test in. Problem was, there were no shoes to fit Bernard's Size 18 feet.

 "So this dude went and jumped a 39 vert without shoes the first time," Gopie said. "And that blew my mind."

 Once in, Bernard traveled to Florida for the IPP's 12-week predraft training -- an intense, 9-to-5, six-day-a-week program to prepare athletes for showcases and the combine.

 His numbers grew off the charts. He was hitting a 40-inch vertical and 40 reps of 225 pounds in the bench press. The goal was for him to become the first member of the "40-40" club at the…

full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. The  Seattle Seahawks ' camp is taking place in Renton, Washington, and Seahawks reporter Brady Henderson has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and, of course, the quarterbacks room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Seahawks camp. What is new with the defending Super Bowl champions? Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Catch up on all the updates, including the Packers' top camp performer and biggest lingering question as preseason games begin.

 
 Camp previews for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest news from Seahawks camp 
 
 CB Trevon Diggs signing 1-year deal with Seahawks 
 Sources: Seahawks still plan on signing Terrion Arnold 
 Cooper Kupp's latest route? Opening a new coffee shop 
 Seahawks, Witherspoon reach extension: 4 years, $132M, sources say 
 Seahawks' DeMarcus Lawrence confirms 2026 season his last 
 Facing charges, Terrion Arnold set to join Seahawks 
 WR Tory Horton healthy after cracking tibia last season 
 Seattle Pro Bowl DL Williams confirms deal talks 
 Seattle's Nick Emmanwori has ankle surgery, expected to play W1 
 Who are the Khoslas? Meet the family set to buy the Seahawks 
 
 

 Wednesday, Aug. 26 
 What has Jake Bobo meant to Seattle's wide receiver corps?

 The fourth episode of HBO's "Hard Knocks," which aired Tuesday, painted a colorful picture.

 In the opening scene, Seahawks receivers coach Frisman Jackson is giving Bobo a pep talk in the group's meeting room. He likens Bobo to a pitbull and tells him he's their version of Dennis Rodman, Udonis Haslem and Draymond Green -- NBA bad boys who were/are tasked with protecting the star players and doing things that don't show up in the stat sheet.

 "Your identity is that you're the goon, you're the enforcer," Jackson tells Bobo. "That dude is the f---er that we expect to see all the time: physical, a good in the run game, we throw you a ball, you make a play. That's it."

 The Seahawks will be without those attributes now that Bobo is out for the season because of a torn ACL he sustained last Friday in Seattle's joint practice against the  Tennessee Titans . The injury was a main storyline on "Hard Knocks," with one clip showing coach Mike Macdonald lamenting how his decision to sit a sore Cooper Kupp that day out of precaution meant that Bobo took more reps than usual.

 "That's an absolutely awful situation," Kupp said Wednesday, "and obviously everybody here feels for Jake."

 With Jaxon Smith-Njigba , Kupp and Rashid Shaheed , the Seahawks have as good a receiver trio as any in the NFL. The depth of that group was also supposed to be a strength, but Bobo is now out for the year and Tory Horton -- the projected No. 4 -- continues to deal with an undisclosed injury. It does not appear to be related to the leg fracture that cut Horton's rookie season short and required surgery, but it has been enough to sideline him for nearly two weeks, as Horton was again not on the practice field as warmups began Wednesday.

 Macdonald has not publicly disclosed what Horton is dealing with, only saying Friday that he's "still working through his stuff" and will be "out for a period of time."

 The Seahawks should be OK if Horton is sidelined into the regular season as long as their primary speed threat, Shaheed, remains healthy. But with Bobo not coming back, Seattle's receiver corps will miss its enforcer -- both on the field and off of it.

 "We're a group of men that come together every day to pursue a goal and have our own lives that all coalesce into this story that makes the season come alive," Kupp said. "Not having him be a part of that story moving forward for this year is tough. It's hard. I know he's going to get after things in terms of rehab and all that stuff, but not having Bobo the person around us is going to be tough."

 More observations: 

 
 Among those who were again not in uniform at the start of practice Wednesday were S Nick Emmanwori , TE AJ Barner , RB Emanuel Wilson , RG Anthony Bradford and OT Josh Jones (at this point of camp, reporters are only allowed to watch the warmup period of practice). 
 ESPN has obtained more details of CB Trevon Diggs ' one-year, $1.215 million contract with Seattle. According to a source, the deal has no guaranteed money, but it does include $2 million in incentives. Diggs would earn $500,000 for playing 42% of the defensive snaps, $750,000 for 50%, or $1 million for 60%. He'd earn $500,000 for three interceptions, $750,000 for five interceptions, or $1 million for seven interceptions. 
 

 

 Friday, Aug. 21 

 The Seahawks spent a second-round pick on safety Bud Clark after losing Coby Bryant in free agency, but don't pencil the rookie into the starting lineup just yet. Ty Okada doesn't look like he's giving up that job any time soon.

 "We love Ty," linebacker Ernest Jones IV said Friday after Okada provided a highlight of Seattle's joint practice against the Tennessee Titans . "I think where Ty has grown is that he's just more in command in his voice and speaking up when things aren't right. He's also just taken a next level to his game being ahead of plays and being that safety in the back that you depend on."

 Okada was dependable last season. The 2023 undrafted free agent gave Seattle starting-caliber play while Bryant and Julian Love missed a combined 11 games with injuries. But Friday's practice brought more evidence that Okada can also provide some playmaking when he jumped an over-the-middle throw from Cam Ward for a pick-six.

 "It was a really great call," Okada said. "I was coming down over the middle. I tried to get his eyes off of me and then on a crossing route, I was able to read it, play off of him, go out there and make a play. It felt good."

 Clark, the 64th overall pick, intercepted 15 passes over his final four seasons at TCU. But the ball production that was his calling card in college has yet to come alive with Seattle. It's among the reasons why Okada has taken almost all of the reps with the No. 1 defense, as all signs point to Seattle rolling with him opposite Love in their starting lineup.

 "He's got a ton of confidence," coach Mike Macdonald said. "He's taking on more of a leadership role, too, in terms of really holding our younger guys to a higher standard, which is great. We need that right now from those guys. From my stance, he's playing really good football."

 More observations:  

 
 RB George Holani got most of the reps with the No. 1 offense as top pick Jadarian Price (lower body soreness) continues to ramp back up after missing over a week of training camp. "It's not responsible to give him a thousand carries after being down for a minute, but I'm eager to watch the tape," Macdonald said. "I was looking forward to seeing him play today." 
 OLB Derick Hall is also working his way back from an undisclosed injury (Macdonald does not readily give injury information) that sidelined him for several days. Hall was in uniform Friday and went through early warmups before taking it easy for the remainder of practice. 
 

 

 Thursday, Aug. 20 
 What is Trevon Diggs ' mindset after joining the Seahawks?

 "I just want to come here, compete, earn my keep," the former Dallas Cowboys cornerback said Wednesday, "just do everything I can to earn a spot here and help this team win."

 Exactly what the Seahawks have in mind for Diggs will become more clear when the details of his one-year deal emerge. The fact that they were not initially reported seems telling in and of itself. So does the ending of Diggs' tenure in Dallas last season, as well as what he said after arriving at Seahawks headquarters about how he wants to "earn" a spot in Seattle.

 Nothing about the situation…

title: Four under-the-radar players, one position to watch for 49ers
summary: For the 49ers to return to the playoffs, it could depend on under-the-radar players like Demarcus Robinson and whoever starts at left guard.
full_text:
SANTA CLARA, Calif. -- Despite missing many of their stars for large chunks of last season, the San Francisco 49ers still won 12 regular-season games and advanced to the second round of the NFL playoffs.

 Much of the credit for that goes to the herculean effort of running back Christian McCaffrey , but the Niners wouldn't have gone as far as they did without some under-the-radar players. Most of those unsung heroes are back in San Francisco for the 2026 season , while the team also drafted some talented rookies who could make an early impact.

 Ahead of the 49ers' final preseason game against the Raiders on Thursday, here's a look at four players and one position that could help the 49ers make postseason noise again.

 

 Jump to: 
 Under-the-radar players 
 Position to watch 

 

 WR Demarcus Robinson 
 In a wide receivers room that has seen its fair share of upheaval from both offseason departures and training camp injuries, Robinson has been the constant, reliable option for quarterback Brock Purdy .

 Ricky Pearsall ( knee surgery ) is out for the season, and free agent signing Mike Evans has missed time with a quad issue. Deebo Samuel Sr . is back and rookie De'Zhaun Stribling has impressed , but Robinson has been the one lining up at every spot and producing in practice.

 "I think he's just one of the best receivers that I've played with in terms of the one-on-one matchup and his feel for the game," Purdy said. "I learned a lot about him last year, but this offseason, watching film on him, it's like, all right, we can give this guy more [opportunities] and have him be a huge part of our offense."

 Out of the players on this list, Robinson had the best postseason performance with six catches, 111 yards and a touchdown in their wild-card win over the Eagles. His exact role remains to be seen and might depend on Evans' health, but it's a safe bet that the team will give Robinson plenty of snaps as it sorts through injuries and youthful growing pains.

 

 
 DT C.J. West 
 In 2025, West gave the Niners something they otherwise lacked in the middle of the defensive line: A powerful run stuffer. When West was on the field, opponents averaged 3.3 yards per attempt on 120 attempts. When he was on the sideline, opponents averaged 4.7 yards per rush on 304 attempts.

 The 49ers' run defense remains a question and having West take another step forward in 2026 would go a long way in providing an answer.

 "He's been a big-time run stopper and a guy that can really hold up, particularly towards the end of the season to do some things in that nose tackle position," defensive coordinator Raheem Morris said. "I'm really fired up to see where he goes from here and what he's able to do and how he can contribute to that line."

 The team has played it safe with West this preseason (he sat out of the first exhibition game), but he suffered a concussion in a practice last week before returning Sunday. The injury opened the door for an undrafted rookie such as  James Thompson Jr . or  Bryson Eason to make the roster. Now that West is back in the mix, don't be surprised if he has a big role in this defense, particularly on early downs.

 
 S Ji'Ayir Brown 
 After starting 13 games last season, Brown is entering the fourth and final year of his rookie contract. The first three seasons have been full of fits and starts, as Brown has struggled to find the consistency to earn a second deal.

 Through it all, Brown has remained confident, noting repeatedly that he sees himself as the top safety in the league. To that end, Brown has pointed to Morris taking over as defensive coordinator as a reason this could be his best season yet.

 During camp, Brown said Morris has allowed the safeties to play more freely and trust their instincts to make plays. For now, that is Brown's focus, not his pending free agency.

 "When I get out on that field, I don't think about none of that," Brown said. "This game is so detailed that your mind just has to be on the day, the moment, the now. So that stuff, I don't even worry about that. I'm here to play football."

 With Marques Sigle and Malik Mustapha as the options for the other safety spot, the 49ers need Brown to provide stability at a position that desperately needs it.

 
 LB Jaden Dugger 
 Dugger is one of at least five rookies who could play an important role right away, but he might have the most difficult job. Throughout the preseason, the Niners have worked Dugger at multiple linebacker spots and he has even worked in with the edge rushers during individual drills.

 

 While Dre Greenlaw (weak side) and Fred Warner (middle) have the primary linebacker jobs nailed down, Dugger looks like he's the favorite to fill the "fever 'backer" hybrid position and serve as the backup to Greenlaw.

 "For a rookie to be asked to do a lot of different things, play a lot of different positions, whether it's off the ball, whether it's on the ball, whether it's on the edge, where he's being asked to do a lot of things and the fact that it's not too much for him, that's how you know that he's got a good feel of the game and being able to retain a lot of information," Warner said.

 The 49ers will be in nickel defense plenty, but Dugger's combination of length (6-foot-5 with a 7-foot wingspan) and speed (4.6-second 40-yard dash) should get him on the field early and often. How he develops will go a long way in determining whether San Francisco's young defense takes a step forward in 2026.

 

 

 Position to watch: Left guard 
 After losing incumbents Ben Bartch and Spencer Burford  to the Lions and Raiders, respectively, in free agency, the Niners didn't spend big bucks for a replacement.

 Instead, San Francisco cobbled together a competition featuring low-cost free agent Robert Jones , second-year Connor Colby and a fourth-round rookie converting from tackle in Carver Willis . No one has separated himself from the group during training camp.

 "It's still a competition," coach Kyle Shanahan said. "No one has really completely made it easy on us yet. I still think we've got a lot more time to go, not a ton, but enough for guys to step up and do it."

 As the only incumbent, Colby had an early lead but was unable to nail down the job. Jones got the next turn but has battled a calf injury. Willis is the latest player to get a shot and though he has flashed promise, his lack of experience inside could make it hard to start immediately.

 Swing tackle Austen Pleasants even worked at left guard recently before a knee injury in the preseason game against the Chargers. That this battle has grown rather than narrowed suggests that their best option is possibly not even on the roster yet.
